articles.titulo: Deficiency of peripheral serotonin caused by Tph1 abrogation attenuates cerebral malaria severity.
articles.autores: Turco A, Rossini G, Vaccaro L, Vascelli G, Mandarano M, Floridi C, Sidoni A, Renga G, Miglio A, Antognoni MT, Barbetta A, Colliva C, Giacchè N, Gargaro M, Sulla A, Iacomelli G, Lombardi M, Bicchieraro G, Wong AYW, Fallarino F, Oikonomou V, Zelante T, Spaccapelo R
articles.resumo_original: In cerebral malaria (CM), the most severe neurological complication caused by Plasmodium falciparum infection, accumulating evidence suggests that tryptophan metabolism mediates disease severity by modulating inflammation and, consequently, blood-brain barrier disruption. Here, we have established an experimental CM mouse model to dissect the differential role of the host tryptophan-serotonin metabolic axis in regulating disease pathogenesis. Peripheral serotonin-deficient mice (Tph1 -/- ) displayed reduced mortality and blood-brain barrier permeability defects. In addition, we found that in the absence of serotonin synthesis via the enzyme Tph1, mice develop inflammation characterized by a mixed type 1 and type 2 cytokine signature. Pharmacological depletion of peripheral serotonin through injection of the Tph1 inhibitor telotristat in wild-type mice significantly improved resistance against CM. Thus, we propose that targeting serotonin synthesis through Tph1 antagonism could have a therapeutic role in P. falciparum infection and may act as a potential treatment strategy for CM.

articles.titulo: CD8+ T cells induce RIPK1-regulated brain endothelial cell death in cerebral malaria.
articles.autores: Hadjilaou A, Christodoulou P, Brandi J, Engler JB, Matcharashvili A, Goncharov T, Johnson C, Vladimirov N, Schubert C, Mohanty S, Sahu PK, Drewicke L, Binder S, Kretz O, Krasemann S, Bal LC, Woo MS, Konrath S, McGuinness D, Vieira V, Richardt U, Steeg C, Bauer S, Taylor T, Nyirenda J, Renné T, Seydel KB, Hoffmann A, Kuhle J, Huang Z, Vandenabeele P, Woehler A, Moxon CA, Schwaninger M, Wassmer SC, Puelles VG, Vucic D, Jacobs T, Friese MA
articles.resumo_original: Cerebral malaria (CM) is a potentially lethal complication of Plasmodium falciparum infection characterized by blood-brain barrier disruption and brain hemorrhage. Although immune-mediated endothelial damage is central to CM pathology, the mechanisms linking cytotoxic immune responses to endothelial injury remain unclear. Here, we show that CD8+ T cells induce receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1)-regulated cell death of brain endothelial cells in mouse CM, while RIPK1 phosphorylation is increased in brain endothelial cells in human CM. Using magnetic resonance imaging, three-dimensional tissue-cleared brain imaging, cross-species pathology, endothelial translatomics, immunocerebrovascular interactomics, and genetic association testing, we identify a CD8+ T cell-dependent, RIPK1-centered mouse endothelial cell death program. Combined RIPK1 and caspase inhibition protected cross-presenting endothelial cells from CD8+ T cell-mediated death in vitro. In vivo, brain endothelial-specific genetic inactivation or systemic pharmacological inhibition of RIPK1 kinase activity prolonged survival in mouse CM without altering parasitemia. These findings support RIPK1 inhibition as a promising therapeutic strategy to counter CD8+ T cell-induced endothelial death in CM.

articles.titulo: Identification of Plasmodium sporozoites using angle-resolved scattered light pulse shapes.
articles.autores: Devaraj V, Kahler S, Kage D, Levashina EA, Kaiser T
articles.resumo_original: Flow cytometry is widely used to identify and sort rare cells, but conventional approaches rely on fluorescent labels. Label-free discrimination of rare targets in complex, heterogeneous samples remains challenging. Here, we introduce a label-free strategy that combines multi-angle pulse shape flow cytometry (MAPS-FC), which exploits the full temporal structure of the signal pulses during cell or particles transit through the laser spot, with a deep learning-based analysis. As a biologically relevant test case, we focus on Plasmodium falciparum sporozoites, the infectious stage of the malaria parasite, which need to be isolated from mosquito salivary glands and are embedded in a heterogeneous mosquito-derived background. Using a GFP-expressing reporter line for validation, we trained a long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network to classify sporozoites solely from their scattering pulse shapes captured through MAPS-FC. Using training data from multiple days and setting a threshold on the classification confidence, the network can distinguish sporozoites from mosquito debris without fluorescent labels. This work establishes MAPS-FC with deep learning as a platform for label-free identification of rare parasites in complex biological samples.

articles.titulo: Navigating Malaria in a Border Zone: A Qualitative Study of Behavioural Determinants, Structural Barriers and Elimination Challenges in Tak Province, Thailand.
articles.revista: Tropical medicine & international health : TM & IH
articles.autores: Chiraphatthakun P, Kanthawee P, Inchon P, Thu AM, Rahayu SR, Azam M
articles.resumo_original:
Malaria elimination in the Greater Mekong Subregion (GMS) is still struggling with barriers in border regions, where population mobility, occupational exposure, and health system fragility continue to drive ongoing malaria transmission. Tak Province is a typical example of such challenges along the Thailand-Myanmar border. Qualitative evidence of the lived experience of frontline health actors is crucial for the design of contextually placed elimination strategies.
This qualitative descriptive study was conducted in Khane Chue Subdistrict, Mae Ramat District, Tak Province, a malaria-endemic area bordering Myanmar. A total of 17 informants participated: 13 village health volunteers, two health workers and two non-governmental organization staffs. Semi-structured instruments were developed to suit each group of participants and used to guide the in-depth interviews. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to analyse data, applying both deductive and inductive coding.
Five factors related to malaria prevention behaviours were identified: cross-border mobility and migration; occupational exposure of agricultural and forest workers; a knowledge-behaviour gap related to malaria risk normalization and availability of free treatment; lifestyle routines that coincide with peak vector biting hours; socioeconomic and environmental vulnerability. Five programmatic bottlenecks were also prominent: funding cuts after USAID's exit, human resource shortages and low rates of compensation for community health workers (CHWs), fear-based avoidance of health care services by undocumented migrants, poor uptake of long-lasting insecticidal nets and compounding external shocks such as Myanmar's political instability and COVID-19 pandemic.
Malaria control in this border area is influenced by the interaction of many behavioural, environmental, and health system determinants on multiple levels. To achieve elimination will need migrant-inclusive health policies, occupation-specific vector control, active surveillance for a prolonged period, cross-border programmatic coordination and stable financing. Findings provide specific recommendations for health planners in similar border contexts in Southeast Asia.

articles.titulo: The Immunity Paradox of Bed Nets: Why Reducing Exposure Can Still Strengthen Malaria Control.
articles.autores: Ouemba Tassé AJ, Ghakanyuy BM, Taboe HB, Ngwa GA, Ngonghala CN
articles.resumo_original: Insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs) are central to malaria control. They serve as physical barriers and chemical agents that deter and kill mosquitoes, thereby reducing transmission; however, this form of protection reshapes the immunology of malaria by reducing exposure to Plasmodium parasites and weakening the development of naturally acquired immunity. Against this background, the present study develops a modeling framework to investigate how this tension between protection and immunity alters malaria dynamics once vaccination is introduced as a complementary control strategy and the optimum combination of ITN and vaccine coverage required for malaria control. Unlike standard models that use a fixed proportional reduction in transmission, this study models ITN coverage and efficacy as coupled, time-dependent processes and immunity driven by exposure to infection and vaccination. Rigorous analysis of the model identifies existence conditions for equilibria and shows that malaria can be contained through the synergistic interaction of vaccination, vector control, and immunity-mediated host dynamics. Parameter values of the model are estimated by fitting the model to confirmed malaria case data and the estimated baseline reproduction number using these parameter values is 1.41 (95% confidence interval: 1.34-1.48), confirming sustained transmission. Simulations of the model show that, although ITNs reduce immunity acquisition, their net effect is to reduce infections and improve recovery and survival. Hence, population-level benefits of ITNs outweigh their immunity-reducing effects (particularly when combined with vaccination), leading to a reduced malaria burden. Comprehensive sensitivity analysis indicates that malaria burden is driven mostly by mosquito biting intensity, population capacity, and transmission probabilities; while mosquito mortality, effective treatment, ITN performance, and vaccine efficacy cause the most significant reductions. Additionally, malaria is uncontrollable with universal ITN use and vaccination at baseline efficacy. While individual interventions can achieve control under low transmission, neither 100% ITN coverage nor 100% vaccine coverage can achieve control under moderate-to-high transmission. However, a strong synergy between ITNs and vaccination allows combinations of high efficacy to achieve containment at realistic coverage levels, suggesting that integrated malaria control involving effective vector control, vaccination, and prompt treatment is needed.

articles.titulo: Oblique Back-Illumination Microscopy Enables Phase-Gradient Optical Sensing of Malaria-Induced Intracellular Heterogeneity.
articles.autores: Lee MKH, Guan Y, Huang C, Guha A, Barman I
articles.resumo_original: Malaria remains a major global health burden, with diagnosis often relying on ex vivo analysis of infected red blood cells (RBCs), which incompletely samples key stages of parasite development. In particular, early ring-stage parasites exhibit subtle structural perturbations, while a significant fraction of parasite burdenincluding immature gametocytesis sequestered within the microvasculature and is not readily captured in peripheral blood smears. Here, we present a label-free imaging and analysis framework that integrates oblique back-illumination microscopy (OBM) with data-driven classification to detect malaria infection by sensing parasite-induced intracellular heterogeneity. Unlike stained brightfield microscopy and quantitative phase imaging (QPI) methods that depend on interferometric acquisition and phase reconstruction, OBM directly converts intracellular refractive-index gradients into measurable intensity variations through noninterferometric phase-gradient contrast. By exploiting multiply scattered illumination and asymmetric detection, OBM enhances sensitivity to parasite-induced refractive-index gradients associated with Plasmodium falciparum development, capturing morphological complexity across the intraerythrocytic lifecycle. This enables the discrimination of uninfected cells, early ring-stage infections, and mature gametocytes. Fourier-domain analysis further reveals infection-stage-dependent redistribution of spatial-frequency content, providing a physically interpretable description of progressive intracellular remodeling during parasite development. Using synchronized in vitro cultures with brightfield validation, we demonstrate automated classification of infected RBCs with accuracies of 95% for binary classification and 82% for multiclass classification, with consistent precision, recall, and F1-scores across repeated randomized data splits. Together, these results establish OBM as a scalable, label-free sensing strategy that leverages intracellular heterogeneity as a diagnostic signal while providing access to stage-resolved optical phenotypes that remain difficult to interrogate with existing approaches. By building on prior studies of in vivo phase-gradient imaging, this framework provides a pathway toward integrating OBM with real-time analysis for noninvasive and field-deployable malaria diagnostics, particularly where conventional ex vivo measurements are limited by parasite sequestration.

articles.titulo: The CCCH-type zinc-finger PfMD3 promotes translation for malaria parasite transmission.
articles.autores: van Biljon R, Bhatnagar S, Kumar R, Gliozzi ML, Xu G, Tripathi AK, Ashrafi A, Swearingen KE, Sinnis P, Llinás M, Painter HJ
articles.resumo_original: Sexual maturation and fertility of the malaria-causing parasite, Plasmodium spp., are critical to transmission between hosts. This developmental process involves an intricate gene expression regulatory network that drives gametocyte commitment, development, and the production of male and female gametes. Here, we characterize the role of the CCCH-type zinc-finger protein Plasmodium falciparum Male Development 3 (PfMD3) in the formation of gametes. Genetic disruption of PfMD3 reveals a male fertility defect that decreases infectivity to mosquitoes. Molecular characterization of PfMD3 reveals its binding to mRNA transcripts is associated with male gamete development through a specific RNA sequence. Gametocyte proteins encoded by these PfMD3-bound transcripts decrease significantly in PfMD3 knockout parasites, suggesting that PfMD3 impacts translation. In addition to RNA-binding, PfMD3 also interacts with proteins involved in mRNA processing and nuclear export that influence translational regulation. This study establishes PfMD3 as an RNA-binding protein that impacts lineage-specific translation and male gamete fertility.

articles.titulo: MIF deficiency exacerbates Plasmodium berghei ANKA induced cerebral malaria, associated with enhanced intracerebral T lymphocyte infiltration.
articles.autores: Xu D, Guan W, Guo H, Zhao Y, Lian Y, Yang S, Xie Y
articles.resumo_original: Cerebral malaria (CM) is the most severe and life-threatening neurological complication of Plasmodium falciparum infection, responsible for substantial mortality and long-term neurological sequelae in patients from endemic settings. Macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF), a pleiotropic immunomodulatory molecule, regulates lymphocyte responses in diverse infectious and inflammatory diseases. However, whether and how endogenous MIF modulates the progression of CM remains unclear. In this study, Plasmodium berghei ANKA (PbA) infected red blood cells were intraperitoneally inoculated into wild-type (WT+PbA) and MIF-knockout (KO+PbA) C57BL/6 mice to establish the experimental cerebral malaria (ECM) model. The roles of MIF in regulating ECM pathological progression were observed. To preliminarily explore the underlying mechanisms, splenic lymphocytes were detected by flow cytometry, intracerebral lymphocyte infiltration was evaluated via immunohistochemistry, and semi-quantitative brain injury scores were analyzed based on hematoxylin-eosin staining. The results showed that KO+PbA mice exhibited a significantly reduced proportion of splenic CD8⁺ T cells compared with the WT+PbA mice. And PbA infection also significantly reduced splenic CD8⁺ T-cell numbers in MIF KO mice but not in WT mice. Meanwhile, a trend toward enhanced cerebral infiltration of CD3⁺ T cells (used as a surrogate marker for infiltrating CD8⁺ T lymphocytes), more severe cerebral microvascular injury and increased haemorrhages were observed in KO+PbA mice, which finally showed a trend toward exacerbated ECM symptoms and significantly shortened survival time. The observation here, together with previous data on markedly aggravated blood-brain barrier breakdown observed in PbA-infected MIF-knockout mice from our previous study, suggest that MIF deficiency exacerbates ECM-associated cerebral injury and accelerates mortality, potentially associated with the enhanced intracerebral T cell infiltration, and even possibly a redistribution of CD8⁺ T cells between the spleen and the brain. These findings suggest a potential role for host MIF in ECM and provide a basis for future studies aimed at clarifying its precise function in cerebral malaria.

articles.titulo: Political Continuity and Malaria Dynamics in the Brazilian Amazon, 2004-2024.
articles.autores: Corder RM, Paula GA, Castro MC, Ferreira MU
articles.resumo_original: Malaria control in Brazil was historically implemented through a centralized vertical program, but decentralization in the early 2000s gradually transferred responsibility to state and municipal governments. In decentralized health systems, political turnover may disrupt institutional continuity and affect the sustainability of control activities. To assess whether municipal administrative continuity is associated with malaria incidence, we linked municipality-level electoral data from the 2008-2020 election cycles with national malaria surveillance records from 2004-2024 for municipalities in the Brazilian Amazon. The primary outcome was malaria incidence during the four-year mayoral term following each election. We estimated multivariable negative binomial regression models, adjusted for pre-election malaria trends and baseline transmission intensity, and found that municipalities experiencing new political leadership had significantly higher cumulative malaria incidence over the subsequent term compared with municipalities with administrative continuity (incidence rate ratio [IRR] = 1.204; 95% CI: 1.078-1.343; P = 0.001), corresponding to a 20.4% increase. These findings suggest that administrative continuity at the municipal level is associated with lower malaria incidence in Brazil, where malaria control is decentralized. Political turnover may disrupt institutional capacity and weaken the implementation of control activities. Strengthening mechanisms that preserve technical expertise, programmatic continuity, and institutional memory across political cycles may enhance the resilience of malaria control programs.

articles.titulo: Spatial patterns of mosquito communities and monkey malaria vectors in a tropical riverine forest in Sabah, Malaysian Borneo.
articles.autores: Matsuda I, Manin BO, Yahiro T, Lambut P, Tangah J, Huffman MA, Bernard H, Kumar VS, Chua TH
articles.resumo_original:
Understanding how vector ecology intersects with host behaviour is essential for predicting zoonotic malaria risk in tropical ecosystems. In Malaysian Borneo, zoonotic transmission of monkey malaria parasites such as Plasmodium knowlesi is shaped by interactions among mosquito vectors, non-human primate reservoir hosts, and human activities across heterogeneous landscapes. However, fine-scale spatial structuring of mosquito communities within tropical riverine forests remains poorly characterized.
We conducted a two-year mosquito survey (November 2016-October 2018) in a lowland riverine forest along the Menanggul River, Sabah, Malaysian Borneo. Mosquitoes were sampled on 44 nights using CO2-baited light traps repeatedly deployed across horizontal (0 m, 250 m, and 500 m from the river) and vertical (ground and canopy) gradients, yielding 244 trap collections. A total of 9,928 mosquitoes were collected, dominated by Culex spp. (91.4%), whereas Anopheles spp. were rare (153 individuals; 1.5%). Female Anopheles mosquitoes (n = 57) were more frequently detected near the river and tended to occur more often in ground traps. Zero-inflated negative binomial generalized linear mixed models based on the female mosquito dataset revealed significant effects of river distance and trap height on mosquito abundance, while short-term microclimatic variation showed little explanatory power. The Anopheles assemblage was dominated by Anopheles balabacensis, a recognized vector of monkey malaria parasites in Sabah. Molecular screening detected monkey Plasmodium DNA in two An. balabacensis individuals, including P. knowlesi, together with other monkey Plasmodium species.
Our findings suggest that river-edge habitats may function as localized contact hotspots where mosquito vectors, non-human primate reservoir hosts, and human activities repeatedly overlap in space and time, potentially facilitating zoonotic malaria transmission even when vector densities are low. These results support the growing view that zoonotic malaria risk in tropical landscapes is shaped less by overall vector abundance than by fine-scale ecological overlap among vectors, wildlife, and humans.

articles.titulo: Effects of Biosynthesized Silver Nanoparticles on Feeding Behavior, Selected Insecticide Resistance-Associated Gene Expression, and Permethrin Susceptibility in Anopheles gambiae: A Laboratory Study.
articles.revista: Vector borne and zoonotic diseases (Larchmont, N.Y.)
articles.autores: Abbasi E
articles.resumo_original:
Insecticide resistance in Anopheles gambiae threatens malaria control. This study evaluated biosynthesized silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) derived from the endophytic fungus Aspergillus niger for their effects on mosquito feeding behavior, resistance-associated gene expression, and permethrin susceptibility.
AgNPs were biosynthesized using cell-free extracellular metabolites of an A. niger isolate and characterized by ultraviolet-visible spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), dynamic light scattering, zeta-potential analysis, and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy. The nanoparticles were predominantly spherical, with mean TEM and hydrodynamic diameters of 25.6 ± 4.2 and 28.3 ± 5.1 nm, respectively, a polydispersity index of 0.21, and a zeta potential of -32.4 ± 2.8 mV. Adult A. gambiae were exposed to 0.1, 0.5, and 1.0 mg/L AgNPs.
AgNP exposure significantly and concentration-dependently delayed host-seeking, reduced feeding success and blood-meal volume, and decreased responsiveness to a standardized human-odor stimulus (p < 0.001). Expression of the resistance-associated genes Cyp6m2, Cyp6p3, and Ace1 decreased by up to 71%, 66%, and 59%, respectively (p < 0.001). Permethrin-induced mortality increased from 45.8 ± 5.1% in controls to 89.3 ± 4.2% at the highest AgNP concentration, indicating enhanced permethrin-associated mortality but not restoration of full susceptibility.
Biosynthesized AgNPs altered behavioral and selected molecular endpoints and enhanced permethrin-associated mortality in resistant A. gambiae under controlled laboratory conditions. These findings provide laboratory-scale evidence supporting further investigation of fungal-derived AgNPs as potential adjuncts to vector control. However, operational effectiveness, environmental persistence, nontarget effects, ecological safety, and effects on malaria transmission were not evaluated and require validation in mechanistic, semifield, ecological, and field studies.

articles.titulo: The mosquito-stage transcriptome of the neglected malaria parasite Plasmodium malariae reveals species-specific gene expression signatures and functional adaptations.
articles.autores: Ruiz JL, Díaz-Terenti B, Lefèvre T, Yerbanga SR, Otto TD, Gómez-Díaz E
articles.resumo_original:
To survive and multiply in different host niches, malaria parasites require sets of proteins that are expressed during the life cycle in a timely manner. Plasmodium malariae is a human malaria parasite that is present in most malaria-endemic regions. This species remains enigmatic due to the inability to maintain it in long-term culture, the low parasitemia observed in human infections, and its frequent co-infection with other malaria species.
We investigate the transcriptome of P. malariae during transmission in the vector by analyzing RNA-seq data from midgut and salivary gland parasite stages obtained in two experimental mosquito infections with field P. malariae isolates. Our analysis identified 3,699 expressed genes, of which 263 are developmentally regulated and 309 are P. malariae-specific, including genes with unknown functions and without orthologs in other Plasmodium spp. We detected unique expression patterns of the ApiAP2 family of transcription factors, many of which appear to function as master regulators during sporogony. Several members of multigene families, such as pir, phist, and fam-l, were found to be expressed, and new families potentially showing transcriptional heterogeneity were described.
Our findings indicate that the P. malariae transcriptome is largely conserved; however, a distinct set of expressed genes lacking detectable orthologs may contribute to differences in transmission and virulence. Given the scarcity of genomic and transcriptomic data for this pathogen and considering the global distribution of P. malariae and its potential role in sustaining malaria transmission, this study has direct implications for malaria control and elimination efforts.

articles.titulo: Comparing watershed-based spatial units and administrative boundaries for malaria prediction in the Peruvian Amazon.
articles.autores: Barja A, Ascencio EJ, Fernandez-Camacho B, Revilla LC, Qquellon J, Carrasco-Escobar G
articles.resumo_original: Malaria continues to pose a major public health threat in the Peruvian Amazon, where climate variability influences transmission patterns. This study assessed whether watershed-based spatial units (hydrobasins) outperform traditional administrative boundaries in predicting P. vivax and P. falciparum cases in Loreto, Peru. A retrospective ecological analysis was conducted using village-level geocoded malaria case data from 2009 to 2018, aggregated at the district level and three hydrobasin levels (levels 6, 7, and ANA). Environmental and meteorological variables were derived from satellite data and incorporated into Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial regression and machine learning models (Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and XGBoost). Model performance was evaluated using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) and Akaike Information Criteria (AIC). Among 297,324 malaria cases analyzed (79.48% P. vivax, 20.52% P. falciparum), hydrobasin level 7 consistently showed superior predictive accuracy. For P. falciparum, hydrobasin level 7 consistently produced the lowest prediction errors across modelling approaches. Among machine learning models, XGBoost achieved an RMSE of 15.79 (95% CI: 10.42-21.03), whereas the corresponding ZINB-PCA model achieved an RMSE of 39.19 (95% CI: 17.09-62.24). District- and ANA-based ZINB-PCA models yielded RMSE values of 50.89 (95% CI: 23.65-77.87) and 59.22 (95% CI: 33.26-82.21), respectively. For P. vivax, XGBoost achieved an RMSE of 38.44 (95% CI: 26.90-49.19), whereas the corresponding ZINB-PCA model achieved an RMSE of 63.87 (95% CI: 46.38-80.95). District-, hydrobasin level 6-, and ANA-based ZINB-PCA models produced RMSE values of 102.81 (95% CI: 73.15-131.77), 175.87 (95% CI: 116.08-232.61), and 263.78 (95% CI: 144.98-389.87), respectively. These findings suggest that the choice of spatial unit affects predictive accuracy, with hydrobasin level 7 producing the lowest prediction errors; the associations captured by the models are predictive and are not interpreted as causal effects. Integrating hydrologically defined boundaries into surveillance systems may enhance malaria control strategies in environmentally complex regions.

articles.titulo: Peer-country support for HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria programmes, Benin, Burkina Faso, Niger and Togo.
articles.revista: Bulletin of the World Health Organization
articles.autores: Manzengo C, Baissa M, Moyenga L, Kaaga YL, Saizonou R, Baza D, Ba NS, Diasso-Tingueri R, Aboubakar F, Koudema WL, Bachabi M, Affolabi D, Dandonougbo C, Kompaore SC, Soma DN, Combary A, Yahaya A, Ganda OR, Soumana A, Dagnra AC, Gbadamassi AG, Atekpe A, Manzengo B, Guire I, Moussa OS
articles.resumo_original:
In the World Health Organization's Regional Office for Africa, the previous inter-country technical support arrangements could not fully meet the growing and diverse needs of the 47 Member States.
The Regional Office therefore introduced multicountry assignment teams in 2022 to provide timelier, country-centred and integrated technical assistance. The multicountry assignment team for Benin, Burkina Faso, Niger and Togo organized comparative data analysis, thematic webinars, quarterly data reviews, peer-country visits and a best-practices workshop to strengthen the programme performance in human immunodeficiency virus, tuberculosis, malaria and hepatitis.
The four West African countries together have about 75 million people and have different programme performance levels. The countries also face different security constraints and service-delivery challenges. These factors create a strong rationale for structured peer learning and adaptation of proven practices.
The initiative strengthened routine data use for decision-making, promoted peer support between countries and facilities, and contributed to practical service-delivery adaptations, including improved implementation of hepatitis B prevention of mother-to-child transmission after peer learning from Burkina Faso.
Structured peer-country support can accelerate programme improvement when it is anchored in routine data, focused on practical bottlenecks and translated into simplified, decentralized and task-shared service-delivery models.

articles.titulo: Blood donation candidates who are deferred in the State of Roraima, Brazilian Amazon: reasons for unsuitability and seroprevalence of transfusion-transmitted pathogens.
articles.autores: Roque DR, Granja F, Carvalho-Costa FA
articles.resumo_original:
Blood donation candidates who are deferred are not targeted by any health policy.
To describe sociodemographic characteristics of unsuitable blood donation candidates, the causes of unsuitability and compare the prevalence rates of transfusion-transmitted infections in deferred and eligible blood donors.
A cross-sectional survey was conducted to obtain sociodemographic data and blood samples; 8,159 blood donation candidates were screened (21.1% rejected, 78.9% approved). A sample of 212 deferred candidates was established.
Most rejected candidates were female, young adults, with high school or university education, self-declared white, born in the North region and single. Main reasons for unsuitability were low haemoglobin concentration, potential exposure to malaria and risky sexual behaviour. The comparison of seropositivity rates in deferred and eligible blood donation candidates generated the following prevalence ratios (PR) and respective 95% confidence intervals (CI): human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), PR = 6.75 (1.46 - 31.05), p = 0.046; syphilis, PR = 1.47 (0.46 - 4.64), p = 0.463; anti-HBc, PR = 2.84 (1.24 - 6.50); p = 0.023; anti-HCV, PR = 4.67 (1.06 - 20.58), p = 0,080; Chagas disease, PR = 60.75 (5.53 - 667.43), p = 0.003.
Treating anaemia in women and controlling malaria in Roraima will reduce the pool of rejected blood donation candidates in the State.

articles.titulo: AP2-L-Dependent Processes Promote PVM Maintenance and Plasmodium Liver-stage Development.
articles.revista: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
articles.autores: Kidane DT, Thaniana A, Mosaddeque F, Louvat C, Subudhi A, Pain A, Bhanot P
articles.resumo_original:
Successful malaria infection requires transformation of Plasmodium sporozoites into replicative exo-erythrocytic forms (EEFs) within hepatocytes, a process requiring a functional parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM) and interactions with host cellular pathways. ApiAP2 transcription factors regulate developmental progression throughout the Plasmodium life cycle. AP2-L consists of an extended amino terminal region and two AP2 domains and is highly expressed in asexual stage trophozoites, sporozoites and early EEFs, but its role in these stages is poorly understood. We characterized the functional consequences of deleting the entire P. berghei ap2-l coding sequence on the erythrocytic cycle in vivo , sporozoite gene expression, liver-stage development, and hepatocyte-parasite interactions. AP2L-KO parasites maintained erythrocytic replication, but sporozoite inoculation failed to establish blood-stage infection in mice. AP2-L loss decreased transcripts encoding proteins involved in sporozoite gliding motility, host-cell entry, and rhoptry secretion. Motif discovery upstream of a subset of these genes suggests possible direct targets of AP2-L. Infected HepG2 cells showed reduced EEF numbers and sizes, impaired parasite DNA replication, and abnormal parasite positioning relative to the host nucleus. PVMs of AP2L-KO parasites exhibited aberrant localization of proteins, absence of tubular vacuolar network extensions, and sensitivity to detergent. These abnormalities were accompanied by increased accumulation of the host's autophagy-associated protein around parasites, suggesting efficient host-mediated elimination. Additionally, AP2L-KO parasites displayed reduced association with the host microtubule-organizing center, Golgi compartments, and COPB2-positive vesicular structures, suggesting an impairment in uptake of nutrients. Together, these findings demonstrate that AP2-L directs both vacuolar biogenesis and host cytoskeletal/vesicular capture in liver-stage parasites.
Before causing symptomatic malaria, Plasmodium parasites multiply silently inside liver cells within a specialized protective structure called the parasitophorous vacuole. Understanding how the parasite builds and defends this essential niche is critical for developing strategies to prevent malaria. In this study, we demonstrate that the parasite transcription factor AP2-L controls a gene expression program vital for liver-stage survival. By analyzing parasites with a complete gene deletion, we show that AP2-L, directly or indirectly, activates genes required for vacuole membrane formation and maintenance. Without AP2-L, parasites form compromised vacuoles, fail to evade host cell autophagic clearance, and cannot capture host cell organelles needed for growth, completely halting infection. These findings establish AP2-L as a key regulator connecting nuclear gene expression to vacuole integrity and host cell manipulation, processes that are fundamental to intracellular pathogen survival.

articles.titulo: Maternal Vaginal Pathogenic Bacterial Colonization and Early-Onset Neonatal Sepsis in Mwanza City, Tanzania: A Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.revista: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
articles.autores: Matovelo D, Sabuni PA, Kajungu GW, James M, Kidenya B, Magoma M, Downs JA, Seni J
articles.resumo_original:
Early-onset neonatal sepsis (EONS) remains a major cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality in low- and middle-income countries. Maternal vaginal pathogenic bacterial colonization and HIV infection may increase the risk of EONS through vertical transmission and immune dysregulation, but prospective evidence from sub-Saharan Africa is limited. This study assessed the association between maternal HIV status, vaginal pathogenic bacterial colonization, and EONS among women delivering at five selected health facilities in Mwanza City, Tanzania.
A prospective comparative cohort study was conducted between August 2023 and February 2025 among 580 pregnant women delivering at five selected health facilities in Mwanza City. A maternal lower vaginal swab was collected before delivery for bacterial culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Neonates were followed for seven days after birth to identify EONS using standardized clinical and laboratory criteria, with culture confirmation where applicable. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression were used to estimate incidence rates and identify independent predictors of neonatal sepsis.
Overall, 89 neonates developed EONS, yielding a cumulative incidence of 15.3% and an incidence rate of 2.42 per 100 person-days (95% CI: 1.97-2.98). Twenty-four (27.0%) cases were culture-confirmed, while 65 (73.0%) were clinically diagnosed. Neonates born to colonized mothers had substantially higher sepsis incidence than those born to non-colonized mothers (3.41 vs. 0.34 per 100 person-days). After adjustment, maternal vaginal bacterial colonization was the strongest predictor of neonatal sepsis (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 9.52, 95% CI: 3.47-26.09; p<0.001). Maternal HIV infection independently increased the hazard of neonatal sepsis by 76% (aHR 1.76, 95% CI: 1.14-2.73; p=0.011), while maternal malaria doubled the risk (aHR 2.74, 95% CI: 1.43-5.22; p=0.002). Escherichia coli ( E. coli ) accounted for 58.3% of culture-confirmed neonatal infections, followed by both Klebsiella pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus (20.8% each).
Maternal vaginal pathogenic bacterial colonization was strongly associated with early-onset neonatal sepsis. Maternal HIV infection and malaria were also independently associated with increased sepsis. The findings support strengthening maternal infection prevention, neonatal surveillance, and microbiological diagnostic capacity, while prospective intervention studies are needed to determine whether targeted screening and prevention of maternal bacterial colonization can reduce neonatal sepsis.

articles.titulo: An integrated approach to prioritizing areas for imported malaria re-establishment prevention in Chongqing, China.
articles.revista: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
articles.autores: Jiang D, Tan Y, Yang M, Chen S, Guan H, Yang S, Bai H, Luo F, Chen JH, Zhou S
articles.resumo_original:
This study integrated spatiotemporal analysis of imported malaria cases, ecological niche modeling of Anopheles sinensis, and field-measured vector density to prioritize county-level areas for imported malaria re‑establishment prevention in Chongqing, China. The findings facilitate a stratified and targeted response strategy, thereby providing evidence-based guidance for mitigating the risk of re-establishment arising from imported cases.
Data on imported malaria cases in Chongqing (2014-2024) and vector surveillance records were compiled for this study. The vector data comprised two components: occurrence records (2011-2025) for ecological niche modeling and quantitative density measurements (2011-2024) for priority mapping, with density expressed as captures per trap-night during the peak mosquito activity season (June-October). Spatiotemporal pattern analysis was performed using R 4.5.2. Based on the vector data, ecological niche modeling was implemented via biomod2 (v.3.5.1), whereas all spatial operations-including map overlays and priority zoning-were conducted in ArcGIS 10.8.
Of the 301 imported malaria cases documented in Chongqing during 2014-2024, 75.08% were attributed to P. falciparum and 12.29% to P. vivax. The affected population was predominantly male (94.35%), aged 21-50 years (84.71%), and predominantly composed of outbound migrant workers (60.80%). Cases originated from 32 African countries (90.37%), with the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Nigeria accounting for the highest proportions. Spatially, cases were mainly clustered in the metropolitan area and western districts. Among the 39 P. vivax cases (including mixed infections), relative concentrations were observed in Yubei, Hechuan, and Pengshui, and 20 (51.28%) were reported during the peak mosquito activity season (June-October). The ensemble niche model for An. sinensis identified bio5, NDVI and bio11 as the leading environmental determinants, with predicted suitable habitats largely concentrated in the metropolitan and western areas. Field surveillance revealed substantial spatial heterogeneity in vector density, with the highest densities recorded in Wanzhou, followed by Yunyang, Fengjie, and Fengdu, whereas densities in the metropolitan districts were uniformly low except in Jiulongpo.
Suitable habitats for An. sinensis were predicted across most of Chongqing, yet imported cases were primarily concentrated in the metropolitan area and western Chongqing. After further overlaying imported P. vivax cases and empirical vector density data. Wanzhou, Yubei, Hechuan, Tongnan, Pengshui, and Jiulongpo were identified as top-priority districts, whereas Tongliang, Shapingba, Jiangjin, Yongchuan, Dazu, Rongchang, Fuling, Wulong, Xiushan, Zhongxian, and Wushan were classified as moderate-priority districts. Enhanced surveillance should be prioritized to ensure timely detection and standardized clinical management of imported cases, coupled with vector suppression during the peak mosquito activity season-so as to eliminate opportunity for re-establishment.

articles.titulo: Malaria in an informal settlement of a socioeconomically disadvantaged population in Rajasthan, a non-endemic state of India, 2024: an epidemiological investigation.
articles.autores: Taylor PK, Choudhary R, Vedachalam SK, Choudhary S, Chauhan A, Sharma S, Aswal P, Bahl A
articles.resumo_original:
In 2024, there were an estimated 3900 malaria deaths in the World Health Organization's South-East Asia Region (WHO-SEAR), of whom India accounted for 89%. In November, 2024, three suspected malaria deaths were reported from an informal settlement near Village A, Sirohi district, Rajasthan, a malaria non-endemic Indian state with malaria cases < 1 per 1000 population. We investigated to confirm the cause of these deaths, search for additional cases, describe the epidemiology, and identify contributing factors.
We conducted verbal autopsies for the three deceased children. A suspected case was defined as fever between October 11th-December 10th, 2024, in the settlement resident; a malaria case was a suspected case that tested positive for Plasmodium falciparum (Pf) or P. vivax (Pv) via rapid antigen test or blood smear microscopy. The settlement was surveyed house-to-house, to identify suspected cases. Identified suspected cases were interviewed to collect demographic and clinical data, assess exposures; and tested to confirm malaria. We identified larval breeding sites, and captured larvae and adult mosquitos. Blood smear preparation by field workers was observed and microscope quality was assessed.
All three deceased children (aged two, five, and 11 years) were siblings with fever lasting 6-10 days. Two died at home untreated; one was hospitalized and confirmed as Pf, and died in hospital. The settlement had 752 residents in 137 households. Among 752 residents, 41 suspected cases were identified, among whom 21 were confirmed (18 Pf, 3 Pv) (attack rate: 2.8%); six needed hospitalization (all Pf). There were three deaths, with case fatality rate 14.3 (3/21)%. Larval breeding was found in six of 160 water bodies. Of 278 adult Anopheles mosquitoes collected, Anopheles subpictus (29.3%), An. stephensi (20%), An. fluviatilis (19%), and An. culicifacies (12.5%) were predominant. Most (95%) cases slept outdoors without mosquito nets. Microscopy facilities were nonfunctional, and incorrect slide-preparation practices were observed in the nearest health facility. The settlement was unmapped and excluded from routine surveillance and control activities.
A laboratory-confirmed seasonal increase in malaria incidence, leading to three deaths, occurred in an informal settlement near Village A, probably due to outdoor sleeping habits of cases, in proximity to mosquito breeding sites, absence of surveillance and control activities, and limited diagnostic capacity of the health facility, delaying diagnosis. We trained the field staff in slide preparation, conducted source-reduction and community-awareness activities, and recommended strengthening laboratory diagnostics.

articles.titulo: Anopheline diversity, ace-1 resistance and climate-driven habitat projections for Anopheles peditaeniatus in Lao PDR border regions.
articles.autores: Zhang J, Zhao X, Yan Z, Yang R, Wu L, Luo C, Zhang C, Zhang Y
articles.resumo_original:
Over the past two decades, the Lao People's Democratic Republic (Lao PDR), one of the Greater Mekong Subregion (GMS) countries, has made remarkable progress in malaria control, but heterogeneous transmission, insecticide resistance, cross-border parasite importation and climate-driven vector habitat shifts still hinder malaria elimination. Systematic studies on species composition, insecticide resistance and habitat suitability of Anopheles mosquitoes are essential for targeted interventions.
Mosquitoes were overnight collected using battery-operated CDC light traps at four transboundary sites across Laos, Cambodia and Thailand from 2017 to 2019. Species identification was conducted by combining cytochrome c oxidase subunit 2 (COII) and internal transcribed spacer 2 (ITS2) sequencing. Insecticide resistance profiles were evaluated via targeted sequencing of the knockdown resistance (kdr, L1014F) and acetylcholinesterase-1 (ace-1, G119S) loci. Maximum Entropy Model (MaxEnt) ecological niche modeling was employed to predict habitat suitability for Anopheles peditaeniatus using 108 occurrence points and 19 bioclimatic variables from WorldClim version 2.1 at a spatial resolution of 2.5 arc minutes (baseline climate: 1970-2000; future projections: 2021-2040 under various Shared Socio-economic Pathway (SSP) scenarios, derived from the Beijing Climate Center Climate System Model version 2-Medium Resolution (BCC-CSM2-MR) global climate model.
Fifteen Anopheles species were identified, with An. kochi (38.46%) and An. sinensis (21.69%) being the dominant species. Among the 18 collected An. peditaeniatus individuals, ace-1 genotyping revealed that 5 were homozygous susceptible (GG) (27.8%), 12 were heterozygous carriers (GS) (66.7%), and 1 was homozygous resistant (SS) (5.6%), while no kdr L1014F mutations were detected in any of the tested species. MaxEnt models showed good performance, with BIO6 (Min Temperature of Coldest Month), BIO18 (Precipitation of Warmest Quarter), and BIO4 (Temperature Seasonality) acting as the key climatic drivers. Under the SSP245, SSP370 and SSP585 scenarios, highly suitable habitats for An. peditaeniatus expanded markedly in the tri-border region; SSP126, by contrast, induced habitat fragmentation, with core suitable areas confined to major wetlands.
Molecular and morphological identification of 650 Anopheles specimens identified 15 species whose assemblages displayed marked spatial heterogeneity across the four sampling sites; the overall mosquito community was predominated by An. kochi (38.5%) and An. sinensis (21.7%). The high frequency of the ace-1 G119S mutation in An. peditaeniatus (one of the Anopheles hyrcanus group) highlights the necessity of tailored insecticide rotation strategies to mitigate resistance development. MaxEnt modeling projections pinpoint future hotspots of vector activity for this species. Incorporating these insights into cross-border surveillance systems and targeted intervention measures will enhance malaria elimination efforts amid climatic changes and persistent insecticide resistance threats in the GMS.

articles.titulo: Spatial and temporal dynamics of insecticide resistance in the Anopheles gambiae complex, with a focus on Anopheles coluzzii, in Burkina Faso.
articles.autores: Ki HD, Bayili K, Badiel A, Sow BBD, Bayili B, Diabri B, Kientega M, Traoré N, Bazongo T, Yaméogo KB, Maiga H, Namountougou M, Diabaté A
articles.resumo_original:
Insecticide resistance is widespread among malaria vectors in Burkina Faso. Although resistance in Anopheles coluzzii has been extensively documented, studies integrating spatial variation and long-term temporal trends in both field and laboratory populations remain limited in Burkina Faso. Understanding these dynamics is essential for evidence-based vector control strategies.
Spatial variation in insecticide resistance was assessed using WHO susceptibility bioassays on Anopheles gambiae s.l. collected from four localities, combined with molecular species identification and genotyping of the kdr-L995F mutation in An. coluzzii. Temporal dynamics were investigated over five consecutive years in a sentinel site (Vallée du Kou) and over 2 years in a laboratory colony using the same methods.
A total of 6,700 mosquitoes were tested in susceptibility bioassays and 1,264 An. coluzzii specimens were genotyped. Populations of An. gambiae s.l. and An. coluzzii were fully susceptible to pirimiphos-methyl (100% mortality), while responses to bendiocarb varied across localities (94.9-100%), years (96.1-100%), and laboratory generations (86.3-100%). In contrast, high levels of resistance were observed to pyrethroids and DDT, with mortality ranging from 0 to 18.4% for deltamethrin, 1-5.9% for permethrin, and 1-41.6% for DDT. Pre-exposure to PBO partially restored susceptibility to deltamethrin, increasing mortality by 27.5-68 percentage points across all datasets. Significant spatial and temporal variations in kdr-L995F frequency were detected in both field and laboratory populations of An. coluzzii. Allele frequencies ranged from 0.27 in Ziniaré to 0.50 in Banfora. In Vallée du Kou, the frequency declined from 0.51 in 2021 to 0.31 in 2025, while in the laboratory colony it decreased from 0.74 (generation F5) to 0.21 (generation F27).
Despite persistent pyrethroid resistance, the marked decline in kdr-L995F frequency in both field and laboratory populations of An. coluzzii suggests the involvement of additional resistance mechanisms. These findings underscore the need for integrated phenotypic and molecular surveillance to support insecticide resistance management.

articles.titulo: Strengthening insecticide resistance management in malaria vectors control in Côte d'Ivoire: from evidence to action.
articles.autores: Gbalegba CGN, Fodjo BK, Wolie RZ, N'Guessan R, Clarke SE, Lines J, Abeku TA
articles.resumo_original:
Malaria remains a major public health challenge in Côte d'Ivoire, particularly among young children and pregnant women. Insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) have significantly reduced transmission, but their effectiveness is increasingly threatened by widespread insecticide resistance in malaria vectors. In response, Côte d'Ivoire developed a national insecticide resistance management (IRM) plan (2017-2020) to preserve the effectiveness of vector control interventions. This review examined coherence between planning and practice, the responsiveness of strategies to emerging resistance trends, and the integration of resistance management into broader malaria control efforts.
To characterize the interventions implemented under the IRM plan and their impact on the targeted outcomes a mixed-methods approach was used. This included document reviews, analyses of epidemiological and entomological data, and interviews with key stakeholders and subject matter experts.
Key achievements included the stratified deployment of insecticide-treated nets (ITNs), limited implementation of indoor residual spraying (IRS), and pilot larval source management (LSM). Resistance to pyrethroids, carbamates, organochlorines and organophosphates was found to be widespread across the country. Indeed, nine studies conducted across 54 localities in Côte d'Ivoire reported mortality rates below 80% to these insecticides. Furthermore, resistance to newer insecticide classes such as neonicotinoids and pyrroles was also detected in certain localities. Funding constraints emerged as a major barrier, resulting in gaps in implementation and delayed activities.
This case study shows that although progress has been achieved in term of vector control strategies, and strengthened entomological surveillance, current interventions remain insufficient to keep pace with the spread of resistance. Some limitations can be highlighted after IRM implementation. The study relied on secondary data sources, national reports, and stakeholder interviews, with no direct entomological field assessments or efficacy trials, and was further constrained by the absence of a comprehensive national entomological database, which may have introduced reporting bias and limited the depth of resistance trend analysis. Côte d'Ivoire's experience provides lessons for other malaria-endemic countries facing similar insecticide resistance challenges.

articles.titulo: Detection of Plasmodium falciparum-infected Anopheles sergentii with reduced insecticide net susceptibility in a dryland ecosystem of the Kenyan Rift Valley: implications for malaria surveillance and vector control.
articles.autores: Tchouassi DP, Rotich G, Mustapha AM, Otieno FG, Kamau L, Oruni A, Torto B, Wondji CS
articles.resumo_original:
In Kenya, parts of the dryland ecosystems have disproportionately witnessed a surge in malaria burden amidst poor understanding of the entomologic risk factors. This study investigated whether this trend is linked to shifts in the vector landscape, including the cryptic role of potential new vectors.
Adult female anopheline mosquitoes were collected in a village in semi-arid to arid Marigat subcounty, Baringo County of the Kenyan Rift Valley. This was achieved using paired CDC light traps placed indoors and outdoors in randomly selected households during sampling periods, in August 2023, August 2024, and July 2025. A subset of the mosquitoes morphologically identified as Anopheles funestus (s.l.) were analysed by PCR and sequencing for species identification, malaria parasite infection and host meal sources. In addition, using cone bioassays, the efficacy of single and dual-ingredient insecticide-treated nets was evaluated on the mosquito population.
Analysis of the mosquitoes revealed presence of established Anopheles sergentii populations infected with Plasmodium falciparum (overall infection rate 8.9%, 27/302) in 2023, 2024, and 2025. An. sergentii exhibited low anthropophagy (~ 8%) but high plant-feeding rates (~ 85%). Despite its predominant outdoor activity evidenced from high representation among infected mosquitoes outdoors (25/290) than indoors (0/12), mortality remained low (8-53%) after exposure to piperonyl butoxide- and pyriproxyfen-treated bed nets. Five An. longipalpis C specimens were also found infected with P. falciparum (1.7%; 5/302).
We provide evidence of An. sergentii, beyond its historical record in Kenya, as a potential malaria vector, underscoring the need to mainstream molecular analysis into routine malaria surveillance activities. The reduced efficacy of dual-ingredient nets against An. sergentii could present a serious challenge to their future deployment in the region, including outdoor control tools with similar active ingredients. This mosquito, and cryptic malaria vectors, such as An. longipalpis C could pose additional threat to malaria control efforts in Kenya.

articles.titulo: Association between entomological indices and malaria test positivity rates in Western Kenya: implications for surveillance.
articles.autores: Omala B, Mburu D, Ombok M, Moshi V, Gimnig J, Achee NL, Grieco JP, Abong'o B, Ochomo E
articles.resumo_original: The relationship between malaria entomological indices and epidemiological outcomes remains poorly understood at local scales in western Kenya, limiting evidence-based surveillance strategies. This study evaluated associations between malaria test positivity rates and vector densities, human biting rates, and entomological inoculation rates (EIR) in a high-transmission setting. The study was conducted in five villages within Teso South sub-County, Busia County, Kenya, from March to June 2021. Village-level entomological indices including vector densities, human biting rates (HBR), and entomological inoculation rates (EIR) were calculated for Anopheles funestus and An. gambiae s.l. Concurrent malaria test positivity rates were obtained from outpatient department registers in the health facilities serving the five villages (n = 2377 cases). The relationship between entomological indices and malaria test positivity was analyzed using multilevel logistic regression models, accounting for individual- and village-level factors. During this period 1950 female anopheline mosquitoes, predominantly An. gambiae s.l (89.0%) and An. funestus (11.0%) were collected. Malaria test positivity rates varied significantly across villages (range: 23.6%-68.7%). Multilevel analysis revealed significant associations between malaria test positivity and both anopheline mean density (OR 1.11, 95% CI 1.08-1.15, p < 0.0001) and HBR (OR 1.35, 95% CI 1.17-1.57, p < 0.0001). However, an association between EIR and malaria test positivity was not observed (OR 1.04, 95% CI 0.96-1.13, p = 0.316). These findings suggest that one solution to address foci with higher malaria cases is to target transmission through vector control based on health facility surveillance. This information could be valuable for national malaria control programs in optimizing surveillance strategies and evaluating intervention effectiveness.

articles.titulo: Decline to near-zero malaria hospitalisation over 35 years on the Kenyan Coast.
articles.autores: Kamau A, Musau MM, Mturi N, Mohammed S, Mwambingu G, Walumbe D, Nyaguara A, Williams TN, Bejon P, Snow RW
articles.resumo_original:
Few longitudinal studies have examined the long-term health impact of changing malaria prevention and treatment strategies in Africa. This study analyses 35 years of clinical surveillance among paediatric malaria admissions in Kilifi, Kenya.
Children aged 1 month to 14 years who were residents of rural Kilifi Health and Demographic Surveillance System and admitted to Kilifi County Hospital between January 1990 and December 2024 were included. Community malaria exposure was estimated using infection prevalence among children admitted for trauma, elective surgery, bites and neoplasms. Malaria admissions were defined as hospitalisations with a positive blood slide and a primary or co-morbid malaria diagnosis. Severe malaria phenotypes including severe anaemia, cerebral malaria, hyper-parasitaemia and in-hospital mortality were also examined. Binomial and Poisson regression models assessed temporal differences, using 1990-1996 as the reference period.
Community malaria prevalence declined from 35% (95% CI 31, 39) in the 1990s to 2% (95% CI 1, 4; p < 0.001) in 2020-2024. Malaria hospitalisations declined from a peak of 25.5 per 1,000 children per annum (p.a.) (95% CI 24.4-26.6) in 1999 to 0.65 (95% CI 0.59-0.72; p < 0.001) between 2020-2024. The median age of malaria increased from 19 months (IQR: 12, 39) between 1990-1996 to a peak of 48 months (IQR: 28, 78) between 2012-2019. Cerebral malaria became proportionally more common than severe anaemia over time. Malaria-specific hospitalised mortality rates declined from 0.43 per 1,000 children p.a. (95% CI 0.38-0.49) in the 1990s to 0.03 (95% CI 0.02-0.05; p < 0.001) during the period 2020-2024.
Hospital admission with malaria among children in Kilifi is now uncommon. Sustained reductions in parasite exposure have altered the clinical profile of disease presentation, including both phenotype and age distribution, without resulting in a cumulative increase in disease burden. Expanded and sustained coverage of effective long-lasting insecticidal nets, together with improved access to effective treatment, have likely contributed to this epidemiological transition.

articles.titulo: Submicroscopic malaria parasite carriage and hemoglobin levels among outpatients attending the laboratories of the Korle Bu Teaching Hospital.
articles.autores: Mensah BT, Otu H, Armah DNO, Abuanor CT, Amenga-Etego L, Antwi-Baffour S
articles.resumo_original:
Malaria remains a major public health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa, where asymptomatic infections continue to hinder elimination efforts. Although the effects of microscopic infections are well documented, the health implications of submicroscopic Plasmodium falciparum infections remain poorly understood, particularly in Ghana. Beyond serving as reservoirs for sustained transmission, emerging evidence suggests these infections may contribute to adverse health outcomes. This study assessed the burden of submicroscopic P. falciparum infections and their association with anemia among outpatients attending Korle Bu Teaching Hospital.
A cross-sectional study involving 345 participants was conducted. Malaria infection was assessed using mRDT, blood smear microscopy, and LAMP-PCR for parasite detection and species identification. Hemoglobin levels and red blood cell indices (MCV, RDW, RBC count, MCHC, and HCT) were measured using a hematology analyzer. Statistical analysis was performed using STATA version 14, applying Pearson's chi-square test and logistic regression.
The overall prevalence of asymptomatic P. falciparum infection was 35.0% (117/334), with 18.9% microscopic and 16.1% submicroscopic infections. Both infection types were significantly associated with lower hemoglobin levels after adjusting for age and anemia severity (p = 0.024). Low MCHC emerged as the strongest predictor of submicroscopic infection (p = 0.04).
Asymptomatic P. falciparum infections are common in this population, with a substantial proportion occurring at submicroscopic levels. Their association with reduced hemoglobin suggests a potential contribution to anemia despite the absence of symptoms. The findings underscore the need for sensitive diagnostics and targeted interventions to support malaria elimination efforts in Ghana.

articles.titulo: Inpatient mortality and predictors among adults hospitalized with severe malaria: a prospective cohort study in Southwest Ethiopia.
articles.autores: Tesfaye K, Lamessa A, Kitessa M, Gudeta B, Yilma D
articles.resumo_original:
Severe malaria remains a major public health challenge in tropical and subtropical regions, frequently resulting in multi-organ dysfunction and high mortality. Despite intensified control strategies and widespread use of antimalarial therapy, mortality rates remain unacceptably high. Moreover, data regarding inpatient mortality and its predictors at Jimma Medical Center (JMC) in Southwest Ethiopia remains limited.
This study aimed to determine the inpatient mortality and predictors among adults hospitalized with severe malaria at JMC from March 1, 2024, to February 28, 2025.
A prospective cohort study design was conducted among 250 adult patients hospitalized with severe malaria, using a consecutive sampling technique. Data were collected using Kobo Toolbox and analyzed with IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, version 27.0. Categorical variables were summarized using frequencies, percentages, and graphs, while continuous variables were summarized using means or medians with standard deviations. Logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with inpatient mortality among patients with known final outcomes (n = 225). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Crude and adjusted odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals were used to assess the strength of associations.
Of the 250 adult patients hospitalized with severe malaria, 37 died during hospitalization, yielding a crude inpatient mortality rate of 14.8% (95% CI: 10.0-19.0%). In the multivariable logistic regression analysis, presence of comorbidity (AOR = 21.6, 95% CI: 4.646-50.799, P < 0.001), cerebral malaria (AOR = 12.4, 95% CI: 3.069-30.814, P < 0.001), acute kidney injury (AOR = 9.8, 95% CI: 2.828-23.867, P < 0.001), illness duration > 5 days (AOR = 6.1, 95% CI: 1.644-22.489, P = 0.007), and leukocytosis (AOR = 3.9, 95% CI: 1.135-13.866, P = 0.031) were independently associated with increased odds of inpatient mortality. Conversely, female sex (AOR = 0.20, 95% CI: 0.047-0.621; P = 0.007) and formal education (AOR = 0.20, 95% CI: 0.059-0.685; P = 0.010) were independently associated with an 80% lower odds of inpatient mortality.
The inpatient mortality rate among adults hospitalized with severe malaria was relatively high. Presence of comorbidity, cerebral malaria, delayed presentation beyond 5 days, acute kidney injury, and leukocytosis were independently associated with increased odds of inpatient mortality. In contrast, female sex and formal education were associated with lower odds of inpatient mortality. These findings underscore the need for timely case detection, improved access to healthcare, and early clinical intervention to reduce mortality from severe malaria.
Not applicable.

articles.titulo: Ownership, coverage, and determinants of utilization of long-lasting insecticidal nets in a high malaria transmission setting in Uganda: a cross-sectional study.
articles.autores: Owori B, Mugerwa J, Nduhukyire L, Muyunga A, Naturinda K, Akol G, Ngolobe B, Nalule NR, Babirye JP, Tukwasiibwe D, Fred B, Kintu IS, Tumwine G
articles.resumo_original:
Malaria remains highly endemic in many parts of Uganda despite repeated rounds of universal coverage campaigns distributing free Long-Lasting Insecticidal Nets (LLINs) to strengthen control efforts. While household-level LLIN ownership has reached near-universal levels nationally, utilization is still low. This study assessed ownership, coverage, and determinants of utilization of LLINs in a high malaria transmission setting in Eastern Uganda.
A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 441 households selected from four sub-counties with the highest malaria burden in Bugiri District. Structured questionnaires adapted from the Roll Back Malaria Monitoring and Evaluation Reference Group indicators were administered to collect data on LLIN ownership, coverage, and use. Modified Poisson regression analysis was performed to determine factors associated with LLIN use among household heads. Prevalence ratios (PR) were reported with their 95% confidence intervals, with significance set at p < 0.05.
LLIN ownership was nearly universal, with 95.7% (95% CI 93.3-97.2) of households reporting at least one LLIN. However, only 47.6% (95% CI 42.9-52.3) had adequate coverage (≥ 1 net per two persons). Overall, 72.9% (95% CI 70.9-74.9) of the study population reported sleeping under a LLIN the previous night and 93.4% (95% CI 91.5-94.9) of existing nets were utilized. In multivariable analysis, rural residence (aPR = 1.14, 95% CI 1.05-1.24, p = 0.002), and adequate household LLIN coverage (aPR = 1.09, 95% CI 1.01-1.19, p = 0.037) were significantly associated with LLIN use. Net material was also significantly associated with use, with polyester (aPR = 1.21, 95% CI 1.09-1.33) and polyethylene nets (aPR = 1.16, 95% CI 1.04-1.30, p = 0.008) being more likely to be used than LLINs made of both types of materials.
While LLIN ownership remains high, gaps in household coverage continue to undermine universal protection. Consistent use is more likely where households have adequate LLINs and when the material aligns with user preferences. Ensuring that every household receives an adequate number of LLINs, while also accounting for the practical factors that shape their use, remains central to the success of Uganda's malaria control strategy.

articles.titulo: Co-administration of traditional remedies and orthodox antimalarials in southwestern Nigeria: prevalence, demographic correlates, and implications for treatment policy.
articles.autores: Odediji SA, Busari LO, Olawuyi AO, Amoo KO, Amoo-Adeboye BO, Yusuff YO, Odediji M, Surakat OA, Adeleke MA
articles.resumo_original:
The efficacy of first-line artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) in Nigeria is threatened by non-adherence to clinical guidelines. This includes the widespread use of traditional and herbal medicines (THMs) and discontinued monotherapies. This study aimed to quantify the prevalence of these practices, identify the populations most at-risk, and elucidate the treatment pathways involved to inform targeted public health interventions.
A community-based cross-sectional survey was administered to 1500 adults in Osun State, Nigeria, using multi-stage sampling. Data on socio-demographics, treatment-seeking behaviour, and antimalarial/THM use were collected. Logistic regression analyses identified factors independently associated with THM use and high-risk practices.
40.7% of respondents reported using THMs for malaria. Their use was independently associated with age ≥ 30 years (aOR: 3.21, 95% CI 2.45-4.21), female gender (aOR: 1.68, 95% CI 1.30-2.17), education at secondary level or below (aOR: 7.45, 95% CI 5.89-9.42), and rural residence (aOR: 13.10, 95% CI 10.15-16.91). THM users were significantly more likely to initiate treatment through informal sources (54.9 vs. 3.4%, p < 0.001) and to report using chloroquine (57.4%) and injectable artemisinin monotherapies. Overall awareness of drug resistance (34.2%) and ACT completion importance (25.3%) was low. Critically, all antimalarial therapy must be preceded by parasitological confirmation, as treating undifferentiated febrile illnesses in high-transmission settings can exert sub-therapeutic selective pressure on concurrent asymptomatic parasitemia.
The co-administration of THMs and non-recommended antimalarials is common and follows distinct demographic and behavioural patterns. These practices, facilitated by informal treatment channels and low therapeutic literacy, represent a clear deviation from national policy and threaten ACT effectiveness. The findings provide an evidence base for the Nigerian Malaria Elimination Programme to design community-specific interventions, including vendor regulation and education campaigns targeting high-risk groups.

articles.titulo: Global characterization of diversity and selective pressures in five Plasmodium falciparum loci identified by whole-genome sieve analysis as putative antigens.
articles.autores: Scalsky RJ, Dwivedi A, Guo B, Lyke K, Silva JC
articles.resumo_original:
Previously conducted, whole-genome sieve analyses (SAWG) using whole genome sequencing data from Plasmodium falciparum isolates collected in two placebo-controlled vaccine trials identified twelve single-copy loci as putative protective antigens. Here, five of those loci were investigated to characterize their diversity and mode of evolution.
The five selected loci were PF3D7_0711200, PF3D7_0808100, PF3D7_1324300, PF3D7_1335900 and PF3D7_1361800. Each locus was reference-based reconstructed in 2053 clinical isolates sampled from 24 geographic locations throughout Africa, Asia, and Oceania, using publicly available data from MalariaGEN Pf7. Nucleotide diversity (π) was estimated for each location, partitioned by synonymous (πS) and nonsynonymous (πN) sites, and examined on a sliding window. Encoded protein variants were used to determine protein heterozygosity and to infer networks on which to visualize the geographic distribution of common variants. Tajima's D and McDonald and Kreitman (MK) tests were conducted to identify putative signals of positive selection.
Higher malaria transmission was associated with increased π. PF3D7_1335900 (Pftrap) was the most diverse locus by several fold, indicative of a markedly different mode of evolution. A πN/πS >  > 1 in Pftrap revealed strong positive selection. Heterogenous π across the length of all loci, with peaks in diversity common to all continental regions, indicated common selective pressures. Protein variant networks showed geographic structure in all three chromosome 13 loci, suggestive of recent region-specific polymorphisms originating independently in each region. Protein networks and haplotype diversity results showed extensive global diversity of variants and that the Pf3D7 protein variant is rare or altogether absent in most geographic regions. This may result in vaccine evasion when vaccine efficacy is allele-specific and only the Pf3D7 allele is used in vaccine formulations.
Our results show that all three loci in chromosome 13 have negligible synonymous diversity, possibly due to recent selective sweep(s) or chromosome region-specific phenomena, but that positive (diversifying) selection acting on Pftrap is sufficiently strong to have enabled new nonsynonymous polymorphisms to rise to detectable frequencies, consistent with a mode of evolution characteristic of antigens. These results suggest that despite their speculative role in naturally acquired malaria immunity, pre-erythrocytic antigens can be subjected to selective pressure imposed by the vertebrate immune system.

articles.titulo: Genome-wide SNP analysis identifies population structure and genetic differentiation in Anopheles stephensi.
articles.autores: Sumitha MK, Kalimuthu M, Kumar A, Rahi M, Gupta B
articles.resumo_original: Anopheles stephensi, a major urban malaria vector in South Asia and the Arabian Peninsula, has recently spread to several African countries, raising significant public health concerns. Understanding its genetic structure is important for tracing invasion pathways; however, population genetic studies have been limited by sparse genome-wide datasets particularly from India, its native range. Here, we sequenced five An. stephensi samples from southern India and integrated them with 33 publicly available genomic datasets from India and Ethiopia to enable a comparison across native and invasive populations. Genome-wide analysis across 38 samples, revealed higher genetic diversity and evidence of broad-scale population differentiation among Indian and Ethiopian samples. Genetic differentiation between regions was moderate (FST = 0.14). A total of 813 SNPs were fixed (FST = 1) between populations, with 586 fixed in Ethiopian samples and 227 in Indian samples. Several fixed SNPs were concentrated in genes involved in sensory perception, ion transport, development, and transcriptional regulation, highlighting candidate genomic regions associated with population-specific differentiation that warrant further investigation. Overall, the results provide evidence of genetic differentiation between native and invasive populations and highlight genomic regions that may contribute to population-specific divergence in An. stephensi.

articles.titulo: Genomic analysis reveals selection pressure and the emergence of molecular insecticide resistance in the malaria vector, Anopheles gambiae, from Western Ethiopia.
articles.autores: Gemechu F, Bennett KL, Dugassa S, Hernandez-Koutoucheva A, Eukubay A, Miles A, Abera D, Clarkson CS, Golassa L
articles.resumo_original:
Insecticide resistance poses a significant challenge to malaria control, driven by diverse molecular mechanisms, whose distribution remains poorly characterized in Ethiopia. This study presents the first results using whole-genome sequence data of Anopheles gambiae from Ethiopia, confirming its presence in the western region of the country and expanding its known geographical distribution.
Analysis of single-nucleotide polymorphisms and copy number variants focussed on key target-site insecticide resistance genes, including the voltage-gated sodium channel (Vgsc), acetylcholinesterase-1 (Ace-1), the gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-gated chloride channel (Rdl) gene, as well as metabolic resistance loci such as cytochrome P450s (Cyp6m2, Cyp6aa/p, Cyp9k1) and carboxylesterases (Coeae2f, Coeae2-7g).
Genomic analysis revealed high frequencies of Vgsc-L995F (kdr-west) mutations, alongside amplifications at Cyp6aa/p, Cyp9k1, and Gste2. Notably, frequencies of Vgsc and Gste2 variants exhibited differences on a local scale, while Vgsc and Cyp9k1 variant frequencies also fluctuated seasonally. Findings highlight the need for site-specific monitoring on a fine temporal scale. Furthermore, genome-wide selection scans using phased haplotypes identified emerging signals of selection at loci with a potential link to insecticide resistance, including a signal spanning 2L:33,767,545-34,391,778, which expands the catalogue of candidate loci for functional validation.
Together, the presence of high frequencies of known insecticide resistance markers suggests that An. gambiae populations may be largely refractory to pyrethroids and moderately resistant to organophosphate (OPs) insecticides in western Ethiopia. Findings necessitate a better understanding of the An. gambiae geographical distribution in Ethiopia, accompanied by resistance-informed malaria control interventions targeting the vector.

articles.titulo: First report of co-occurrence of Anopheles gambiae and An. arabiensis (Diptera: Culicidae): comparative blood meal sources and infection rates in Ethiopia.
articles.autores: Yewhalaw D, Tsegaye A, Assefa G, Ayala A, Endale M, Zeleke K, Keya M, Alemayehu B, Degefa T, Alemayehu E, Abiy E, Worku A, Yohannes G, Olana D, Balkew M
articles.resumo_original:
Entomological surveillance is critical for understanding the species composition, behavior, and transmission roles of malaria vectors to guide evidence-based control strategies. This study aimed to determine the species composition, blood meal sources, and infection rates of the Anopheles gambiae complex in three regions of Ethiopia.
Surveillance was conducted from July to November 2024 in six sites across three regions (Southwest, Gambella, and Oromia) of Ethiopia. Mosquitoes were collected using human landing catches, CDC light traps, and Prokopack aspirators. Specimens were identified morphologically, followed by species-specific PCR. Blood meal sources and Plasmodium infection rates were determined using PCR and Circumsporozoite Enzyme-linked Immunosorbent Assay (CSP-ELISA), respectively.
Of 284 morphologically identified An. gambiae s.l., PCR identified 39.8% as An. gambiae, 26.7% as An. arabiensis, and 6% as An. amharicus (27.8% non-amplified). Anopheles gambiae was present in all sites, with the highest prevalence in Godere (96.2%) and South Bench (60%). In contrast, An. arabiensis predominated in Seka Chekorsa (67.9%). Blood meal analysis results showed that the human blood index (HBI), bovine blood index (BBI) and goat blood index (GBI) for An. gambiae was 41.8%, 18.2% and 14.5% respectively while HBI, OBI and GBI for An. arabiesnsis was 0%, 28% and 71.4%, respectively. An. gambiae infection rates for Plasmodium falciparum and P. vivax were 2.8% and 0.9%, respectively and no Plasmodium infection was detected for An. arabiensis.
This study provides the first report of An. gambiae in three regions of Ethiopia and its co-occurrence with the major malaria vector, An. arabiensis was also documented for the first time in Ethiopia. The high HBI and infection rates suggest that An. gambiae could contribute to local malaria transmission in Ethiopia. Hence, the national control/elimination program should prioritize indoor residual spraying (IRS) and insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) to target this indoor-resting species (An. gambiae) in these areas.

articles.titulo: Malaria and Chikungunya outbreak in Marsabit County, Kenya, May 2023: a descriptive study.
articles.autores: Kanyina E, Okunga E, Langat D
articles.resumo_original:
Acute febrile illnesses are common causes of seeking health care in Sub-Sahara Africa especially among the under-five years. Understanding their causative pathogen is critical for optimal patient management. We characterized a febrile illness outbreak in Marsabit County to determine the magnitude of an outbreak, describe the epidemiology and clinical characteristics of the outbreak and conduct Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE).
