A retrospective review of laboratory registers and patients' clinical notes was done at Kargi Health Centre, Korr Health Centre and Laisamis Sub-county Hospital. A case of febrile illness was any person living in or has travelled to Laisamis Sub-county presenting with fever ≥ 380 C or headache at the health facility or in the community from 1st May to 24th May 2023. Cases of febrile illness were interviewed using a structured questionnaire to collect clinical and epidemiologic information. Approximately 4-5 ml of blood was collected from cases of febrile illness for laboratory differential diagnosis. Risk Communication and Community Engagement activities were conducted included interpersonal communication, focused manyatta group discussions and sensitization of community health promoters.
A total of 184 febrile cases were line listed. Eighteen cases of Chikungunya and 12 cases of malaria were confirmed from the 72-blood specimen analysed during the investigation period. Of the 12 samples that tested positives for malaria, 11 were P. falciparum and one P. vivax. Of the 72 blood specimen analysed, three had dual infection. One mortality was reported, involving a case co-infected with Malaria P. falciparum and Chikungunya. Thirteen Manyattas were visited where interpersonal communication was conducted as well as focused group discussion among manyatta residents and manyatta leaders. Two hundred Community Health Volunteers were sensitized on mosquito-borne diseases prevention and control in Laisamis Town. There was low knowledge on causes of febrile illness especially malaria.
The outbreak was driven by two infections; Chikungunya virus infection and Malaria infection. Sustained surveillance, vector control programs and awareness promotion are needed for early detection and control of possible mosquito-borne outbreaks.

articles.titulo: Clinical presentation of severe malaria in children who received the RTS,S/AS01E malaria vaccine, seasonal malaria chemoprevention or the combination of both interventions in Burkina Faso and Mali.
articles.autores: Issiaka D, Zongo I, Sidibe Y, Compaoré YD, Yerbanga RS, Kaya M, Zoungrana C, Zerbo RO, Dicko OM, Kone Y, Tapily A, Traore S, Sanogo K, Diarra M, Barry A, Mahamar A, Haro A, Thera I, Ali MS, Snell P, Grant J, Kuepfer I, Lee CK, Ockenhouse CF, Ofori-Anyinam O, Milligan P, Sagara I, Tinto H, Ouedraogo JB, Chandramohan D, Greenwood B, Dicko A
articles.resumo_original:
Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria is a leading cause of death in sub-Saharan Africa, with most deaths occurring in children younger than five years of age. The RTS,S/AS01E (RTS,S) malaria vaccine delivered seasonally with Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention (SMC) led to a two-third reduction in severe malaria and malaria deaths compared with either intervention given alone. The aim of this study was to assess and compare the clinical phenotype distribution among severe malaria admissions by intervention groups and country.
We conducted a secondary ad-hoc analysis of hospital admissions in children aged 5 to 17 months of age when enrolled in the RTS,S + SMC trial in April 2017 in Houndé, Burkina Faso, and Bougouni, Mali, and who were followed until they reached five years of age.
Among the 5,920 children enrolled in Burkina Faso and Mali, 337 serious adverse events were reported during the trial with 222 (65.9%) in Burkina Faso and 115 (34.1%) in Mali, and 48.1% (162/337) due to severe malaria. The mean age of children with severe malaria was 2.9 years; 79.0% (128/162) of the cases occurred in children aged 3 years or less and 21.0% (34/162) in those aged 4 to 5 years. The most common presentation was severe anemia reported in 50% (81/162) of children, followed by repeated convulsions 25.3%, (41/162), prostration 11.1%, (18/162), hyperparasitaemia 8.0%, (13/162) and cerebral malaria 6.2%, (10/162). The proportion of children with the severe malaria anemia phenotype was higher among severe malaria cases in the SMC alone arm 62.1%, (36/58) compared to those in the SMC + RTS,S arm 37.1%, (13/35), p = 0.048. There was no significant difference in the proportion of other clinical presentations between the study arms. Most severe malaria cases, 85.8% (139/162) occurred during the transmission season (July to December).
Severe anemia was the most common presentation of severe malaria in study children and its proportion among severe malaria cases was highest in the SMC alone arm. Children aged 3 years or less were the most affected and almost all the severe malaria cases occurred between July and December. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04319380.

articles.titulo: Microbiota modulation impacts life history traits and mating success in male Aedes aegypti mosquitoes.
articles.autores: El-Dougdoug NK, Magistrado D, Perry KI, Short SM
articles.resumo_original:
Aedes aegypti mosquitoes transmit multiple arboviruses, but population suppression through the mass release of sterile or incompatible male mosquitoes can effectively reduce populations. These methods depend on the reliable mass-rearing of healthy, robust males that can successfully mate with wild females. The microbiota is a critical component of the larval diet, and its modulation can dramatically influence life history traits relevant to mass-rearing and male quality. Here, we used axenic (microbe-free), monoxenic (inoculated with Escherichia coli), and "laboratory community" mosquitoes (inoculated with an undefined microbiota derived from laboratory mosquitoes) to show that longevity was significantly enhanced in axenic and monoxenic males compared to laboratory community males. Moreover, monoxenic males more efficiently obtained mates in non-competitive mating scenarios compared to laboratory community males. However, microbiota treatment had no effect on mating success when males from different treatments competed for a mate. Our findings suggest that the microbiota is a key determinant of male mosquito life history, with direct implications for optimizing production of males for control programs.
The microbes found in association with mosquitoes are crucial to mosquito development and have the capacity to influence multiple life history traits. In the current study, we comprehensively and functionally evaluate the role of the microbiota in mating success and other life history traits of male mosquitoes. Males are crucial to disease transmission, via their role in mating, and via their use in mosquito population control. By focusing on males, the understudied sex in mosquito research, we provide novel and foundational insight into how microbial communities influence male life history traits and mating success. Moreover, our findings establish a critical framework for understanding how the microbiota may affect male quality, production efficiency, and performance in vector control programs that involve mass production of adult male mosquitoes.

articles.titulo: Protection Induced by a Novel Circumsporozoite Protein Malaria Vaccine is Associated with the Quality of Antibody Responses.
articles.autores: Robben PM, Hutter JN, Zhu L, Galli H, Koren MA, Moon JE, Brown DR, Robinson TM, Duncan EH, Belmonte AD, Sedegah M, Lakhal-Naouar I, Peel S, Bolton JS, Wijayalath W, Soisson L, Rao M, Matyas GR, Angov E, Bergmann-Leitner ES, Regules JA, Dutta S
articles.resumo_original:
Malaria remains an intractable global health problem. We report results of a single-center, open-label Phase 1 trial of a nearly full-length soluble recombinant Plasmodium falciparum CSP (FMP013) formulated in the Army Liposome Formulation containing QS21 (ALFQ).
Healthy malaria-naïve adults (n=29) were enrolled into three groups. Standard (STD) group volunteers received FMP013/AFLQ (20 µg/0.5 mL) on a 0-1-2-month schedule (n=10). Delayed group (DEL) received the same dose on a 0-1-6-month schedule (n=10). Delayed Fractional Dose (DFD) volunteers (n=9), vaccinated at 0-1-6-months, received a fractional third dose (4 µg/0.1 mL). Immunized and unvaccinated control participants underwent P. falciparum-infected mosquito bite challenge three weeks after the third immunization and safety, tolerability, efficacy, and immunogenicity were analyzed.
All regimens were well tolerated. 5 of 9 DEL (vaccine efficacy [VE], 55.6%, 95% confidence interval [CI], 21.2-86.3%; P< 0.001), 1 of 7 DFD (VE 14.3%, CI 0.0-57.9%), and 1 of 9 STD (VE 11.1%, CI 0.0-48.3%) subjects had sterile protection. Delayed blood-stage infection was observed in 3 DEL, 2 DFD and 1 STD subjects. The FMP013/ALFQ vaccine elicited C-terminal biased responses and protection in the DEL regimen was associated with higher C-terminal avidity, and junction, minor repeat epitope-specific responses.
A soluble protein CSP vaccine, akin to particle vaccines, can elicit a protective response when delivered using a potent adjuvant and an extended vaccination schedule. These data encourage further evaluation of FMP013/ALFQ efficacy and durability in the field.

articles.titulo: Development of an infection via sugar meal (IVSM) technique to infect mosquitoes (Diptera: Culicidae) with arthropod-borne viruses.
articles.autores: Drahun I, Williams AJM, Barelli LR, Krokovsky L, Hunter FF
articles.resumo_original: The global expansion of mosquito vectors is increasing human exposure to arboviruses, highlighting the need for rapid and practical approaches to assess vector competence. Standard artificial laboratory infection methods rely on infectious blood meals or intrathoracic inoculation, both of which can be resource-intensive and limit the capacity to conduct timely experiments, particularly in high-containment facilities. We developed an infection via sugar meal (IVSM) technique to determine whether mosquitoes can acquire and transmit arboviruses by ingesting virus-spiked sucrose. Using IVSM, we tested the vector competence of Aedes albopictus and Culex quinquefasciatus for West Nile virus (WNV), Mayaro virus (MAYV), and Zika virus (ZIKV) following 1-hour or 24-hour exposures. Viral RNA copy numbers were quantified in the body, legs/wings, and saliva at 7 and 10 days post-infection. Both species supported WNV infection and dissemination, with the virus detected in saliva. Aedes albopictus exhibited high MAYV infection and dissemination rates, whereas Cx. quinquefasciatus was largely refractory. ZIKV infection and dissemination were limited in both species and did not progress to saliva. High feeding success, low vector mortality, and reproducible outcomes across trials demonstrate that IVSM is an accessible and practical alternative to blood-based infection models and provides a framework for investigating vector competence under conditions that utilize natural feeding behavior.

articles.titulo: Climate-driven morphological change in mosquito vectors: implications for vector competence, distribution and disease transmission-a systematic review.
articles.autores: Ekeleme UG, Dozie UW, Omire JC, Nnadozie EC, Chinemerem OM, Iwuala CC, Chikaodi NO, Okereke CCA, Chukwuocha UM
articles.resumo_original:
Climate change is altering the thermal environments experienced by mosquito vectors during development, with consequences for adult morphology and potentially for vector competence and pathogen transmission dynamics.
This systematic review synthesizes evidence on climate-associated morphological change in mosquito vectors, focusing on body size and wing morphology, and examines how these changes may relate to vectorial capacity, geographic distribution, and disease transmission.
This systematic review follows the PRISMA 2020 reporting framework and uses the Population, Exposure, Comparator, Outcome (PECO) structure. Searches were conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE (n = 31), Elsevier Embase (n = 28), Clarivate Web of Science Core Collection (n = 22), and CAB Direct/CAB Abstracts (n = 14), yielding 95 records. After removal of 34 duplicates, 61 unique records underwent title/abstract screening, 37 underwent full-text assessment, and 24 sources were retained for synthesis.
Twelve primary empirical studies and twelve contextual or methodological sources were included. Across the primary evidence base, warmer developmental conditions generally reduced adult body or wing size, although responses varied by species, population and nutritional environment. The transmission implications were parameter-specific: smaller mosquitoes may exhibit compensatory increases in feeding frequency, whereas larger mosquitoes may show greater competence per infectious bite in some experimental systems. Temperature also affected adult survival and extrinsic incubation in non-linear ways, so no uniform directional effect on transmission could be inferred.
Climate-associated thermal change can alter mosquito morphology through biologically plausible plastic and potentially heritable mechanisms. However, the net effect on pathogen transmission remains contingent on the joint effects of biting frequency, vector competence, survival, development, extrinsic incubation, and local ecological conditions. Wing geometric morphometrics may provide a useful supplementary surveillance measure where validated locally.
https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261483189, CRD420261483189.

articles.titulo: First evidence of plasmodium falciparum-plasmodium ovale co-infection with delayed clinical presentation in an Ivorian patient: observations and diagnostic challenges.
articles.autores: Akhoundi M, Guedri G, Brun S, Marteau A
articles.resumo_original:
Malaria remains highly endemic in Côte d'Ivoire, where repeated exposure to infective mosquito bites increases the risk of both mono- and mixed-species Plasmodium infections. While Plasmodium falciparum predominates and accounts for most acute clinical cases, co-infections with non-falciparum species are under-recognized due to diagnostic limitations and complex interspecies interactions.
Unlike previous reports of concomitant mixed infections, we report the first case of P. falciparum and P. ovale infection in a 69-year-old Ivorian patient residing in France, who experienced latent recurrent malaria episodes following travel to the Man District in the western part of the country. Initial episodes were attributed to P. falciparum, whereas a subsequent episode, occurring in the absence of any re-exposure, was diagnosed as P. ovale infection. This report highlights the critical role of a putative co-infection and species-specific incubation strategies in malaria pathophysiology. The temporal dissociation between P. falciparum and P. ovale detection strongly suggests an initial co-infection, with P. ovale likely remaining subclinical due to low parasitemia (0.02%) and plausible interspecies competition. Unlike P. falciparum, P. ovale is capable of forming dormant hepatic stages (hypnozoites), leading to delayed clinical recurrence 4 months after the primary infection. The late clinical presentation observed in this patient, without recent travel and new exposure, supports the hypothesis of hypnozoite reactivation rather than reinfection.
This report underscores the importance of considering mixed-species malaria infections and variable incubation periods in diagnostic and clinical management. It also highlights the importance of sensitive molecular diagnostic tools and appropriate radical treatment strategies targeting both blood-stage parasites and dormant hepatic forms.

articles.titulo: Evaluation of the immunogenic properties of a chimeric protein against West Nile virus: in-silico analysis and assessment in mouse.
articles.autores: Arezoumandi M, Baghini SS, Rad N, Taghipour E, Pouriayevali MH, Frootan F, Motallebi M, Salmanian AH
articles.resumo_original:
West Nile virus (WNV) is a mosquito-borne flavivirus that represents a significant public health concern, and the development of effective vaccine candidates remains a priority. This study aimed to design a chimeric multi-epitope protein against WNV using immunoinformatics approaches and evaluate its immunogenicity in mice.
Selected regions of the WNV envelope (E) and non-structural 1 (NS1) proteins were analyzed to identify B- and T-cell epitopes using immunoinformatics tools. The selected epitopes were incorporated into a chimeric construct fused with cholera toxin B subunit, and its antigenicity, allergenicity, structural properties, and TLR3 interaction were evaluated in silico. The optimized construct was expressed in Escherichia coli, purified by Ni-NTA affinity chromatography, and confirmed by SDS-PAGE and western blotting. BALB/c mice were immunized with the recombinant protein plus adjuvant, and immune responses were assessed using ELISA, cytokine assays, and flow cytometry.
Immunized mice developed high IgG antibody titers and showed detectable IFN-γ and IL-5 production, suggesting induction of Th1-associated responses with limited Th2-related cytokine production. The chimeric protein also stimulated CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell responses, indicating activation of both humoral and cellular immunity.
The designed chimeric protein showed immunogenic potential and induced humoral and cellular immune responses in mice, supporting further evaluation as a candidate for WNV vaccine development.

articles.titulo: Persistent neutralizing antibodies against chikungunya virus eight years after infection.
articles.autores: Zhu XL, Wang MF, Kong M, Ma YM, Wang XJ, Wan S, Cao GP, Chen RR, Cheng YM, Li LL, Xi J, Yang LP, Zhan BD, Ma MJ
articles.resumo_original: Chikungunya fever, caused by the mosquito-borne chikungunya virus (CHIKV), poses a significant global health burden, with an estimated 16.9 million infections annually. Although CHIKV infection induces neutralizing antibody responses, data on their long-term persistence remain limited. In July 2017, an imported outbreak caused by the CHIKV East/Central/South African genotype occurred in Zhejiang Province, China. To assess the longevity of neutralizing antibodies, we conducted a cross-sectional follow-up study in August 2025, approximately eight years after infection. Two laboratory-confirmed patients from the outbreak were enrolled, and serum samples were collected. Serum neutralizing antibodies were measured using both pseudovirus and authentic CHIKV neutralization assays. Remarkably robust and sustained responses were observed in both patients. The pseudovirus neutralization titers were 225,677 and 134,460, respectively, and authentic virus neutralization titers were 9,133 and 4,951, respectively-which substantially exceeded the established protective threshold of 150. As no subsequent CHIKV outbreaks were documented in this non-endemic region, these high neutralizing antibody titers indicate that durable immunity may be derived from a single infection rather than repeated boosting. These findings suggest that natural CHIKV infection can elicit neutralizing antibodies that persist at high levels for at least eight years, providing evidence to inform the development of vaccines and vaccination strategies.

articles.titulo: Investigation of Aedes koreicus vector competence for dengue virus in Italy.
articles.autores: Montarsi F, Dal Molin E, Di Luca M, Fortuna C, Toniolo F, Sgubin S, Garziera T, Gradoni F, Pacenti M, Barzon L, Gobbo F
articles.resumo_original:
The increasing incidence of dengue in Europe, combined with the spread of invasive mosquito species, raises concerns about the emergence of new vectors. Aedes koreicus, an invasive mosquito rapidly expanding in several European countries, has shown competence for some arboviruses, but its role in dengue virus transmission remains unknown. This study aimed to assess, for the first time, the vector competence of an Italian population of Ae. koreicus for dengue virus serotype 1 (DENV-1).
Laboratory-reared Ae. koreicus females originating from northeastern Italy were orally infected with DENV-1 via an artificial blood meal. Mosquitoes were maintained at 26 ± 1 °C and analysed at 7, 14, 21 and 28 days post-infection (dpi). Infection, dissemination and transmission were evaluated by RT-qPCR and droplet digital PCR, while the presence of infectious virus in saliva was confirmed by virus isolation in Vero E6 cells.
Aedes koreicus was susceptible to DENV-1 infection, with infection rates ranging from 30 to 60% across time points. Viral dissemination to legs and wings was detected from 14 dpi onwards, reaching 100% at 21 and 28 dpi. DENV-1 RNA was detected in saliva at 28 days post-infection (dpi), indicating a relatively long extrinsic incubation period. Overall transmission rate and efficiency were 33.3% and 20%, respectively, at later time points. Infectious virus was successfully isolated from saliva samples confirming transmission capability.
Aedes koreicus was shown to be susceptible to DENV-1 infection and capable of transmitting the virus, although with low efficiency and a long extrinsic incubation period. Despite these limitations, its increasing abundance, longevity and capacity to feed on humans suggest that it may act as a potential dengue vector under favourable conditions. These findings highlight the need to include Ae. koreicus in entomological surveillance and risk assessments for dengue transmission in Europe.

articles.titulo: Association between the december 2020 mass long-lasting insecticidal net distribution campaign and reported malaria incidence in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo: an interrupted time-series analysis of routine surveillance data.
articles.autores: Mbuku N, Mandja BA, Muntenge G, Nsabatien V, Lukanu P, Wanet S, Mpongo T, Matela B, Zanga J, Gonzalez JP, Luhata C, Matulonga B, Mvuama N
articles.resumo_original:
Long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) remain a cornerstone of malaria vector control in sub-Saharan Africa. Although mass LLIN distribution campaigns substantially increase household ownership and access, their population-level effect on malaria incidence may vary over time. We assessed the association between the December 2020 mass LLIN distribution campaign and malaria incidence in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), from 2018 to 2023.
We conducted an ecological interrupted time-series (ITS) study using monthly routine malaria surveillance data from Kinshasa between January 2018 and December 2023. Negative binomial regression models were fitted with population included as a logarithmic offset. The primary segmented ITS model included three explicit ITS terms: calendar time, a binary intervention indicator, and post-intervention time. Seasonality was controlled for using a binary seasonal indicator and Fourier harmonic terms. Sensitivity analyses were conducted using January 2021 and February as alternative intervention start dates and by applying heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC/Newey-West) standard errors. Residual temporal autocorrelation was assessed using autocorrelation function (ACF) and partial autocorrelation function (PACF) plots and formal Ljung-Box tests.
In a simple pre/post model, the post-distribution period was associated with higher malaria incidence than the pre-distribution period (incidence rate ratio [IRR] = 1.23, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.07-1.41; p = 0.003). After adjustment for harmonic seasonal terms, this association remained significant (IRR = 1.16, 95% CI: 1.03-1.32; p = 0.013). In the primary segmented ITS model, the post-intervention period was associated with a higher incidence level (IRR = 1.18, 95% CI: 1.07-1.31; p = 0.001), while post-intervention time was associated with a modest but significant monthly increase in incidence (IRR = 1.01, 95% CI: 1.01-1.02; p < 0.001). Sensitivity analyses using January 2021 and February 2021 as alternative intervention dates, as well as HAC/Newey-West standard errors, yielded highly consistent findings. Significant residual autocorrelation remained present across model specifications.
This ecological ITS analysis did not demonstrate a sustained decline in reported malaria incidence following the December 2020 LLIN distribution campaign in Kinshasa. Findings were robust across alternative intervention dates and autocorrelation-consistent sensitivity analyses but should be interpreted cautiously because of residual autocorrelation, potential reporting changes, the absence of a control group, and the ecological nature of the study.

articles.titulo: Hypoxia in lymphoma: Mechanistic remodeling of the tumor microenvironment, disease progression and therapeutic resistance (Review).
articles.autores: Zhu Y, Zhang C, Zhang M, Hong Q, Han Y, Tang X, Chen N
articles.resumo_original: Hypoxia is increasingly recognized as a determinant of tumor behavior across multiple malignancies; yet, its role in lymphoma remains incompletely defined and is frequently generalized across biologically distinct disease entities. In lymphoma, hypoxia is not merely a consequence of rapid tumor expansion and abnormal vascularization, but an active driver of tumor microenvironment remodeling, metabolic adaptation, immune escape, angiogenesis and therapeutic resistance. Emerging evidence suggests that hypoxia‑inducible signaling, lactate accumulation, adenosine metabolism, macrophage polarization and altered mitochondrial fitness collectively shape lymphoma progression and treatment response. However, the strength of evidence varies markedly by lymphoma subtype and a notable proportion of mechanistic assumptions is still derived from solid tumors or non‑lymphoma systems. The present review provides a structured summary of current knowledge regarding hypoxia in lymphoma, with emphasis on microenvironmental regulation, disease progression and resistance to chemotherapy, radiotherapy, antibody‑based therapy and cellular immunotherapy. Particular attention is given to the distinction between direct lymphoma‑derived evidence and indirect extrapolation. The present review also highlights major unresolved questions, including subtype‑specific heterogeneity, differences between acute and chronic hypoxia, and the need for clinically actionable biomarkers and combination strategies. A more rigorous understanding of hypoxia in lymphoma may improve biological stratification and identify context‑specific therapeutic vulnerabilities.

articles.titulo: Lactylation in the regulation of macrophage polarization: Mechanisms pathophysiological significance (Review).
articles.autores: Wang XY, Liao DX, Yang L, Xie Q, Huang QQ, Wen Y
articles.resumo_original: Macrophage polarization is regulated by metabolic reprogramming epigenetic modifications. The discovery of histone lysine lactylation has revealed that lactate is not merely a glycolytic end product but also an important metabolic signal linking cellular metabolic status to gene expression programs. Lactylation modulates both histones (such as H3K18la) non‑histone proteins (such as nuclear factor‑κB p65 hypoxia‑inducible factor‑1α), thereby influencing macrophage polarization through transcriptional regulation signal transduction. Its functions are highly context‑dependent. In the tumor microenvironment, it predominantly promotes M2‑type immunosuppression; in certain neuroinflammatory conditions, it may be associated with M1‑like phenotypes; in metabolic diseases, it may exacerbate pro‑inflammatory damage. This modification involves extensive crosstalk with acetylation, methylation, other epigenetic modifications, constituting a complex regulatory network. However, current research faces critical bottlenecks: The intracellular source metabolic flux of lactyl‑CoA remain unclear; the substrate specificity physiological relevance of candidate writers, such as E1A‑binding protein p300 CREB‑binding protein, erasers, such as sirtuin 2, remain controversial; a bona fide reader domain that specifically recognizes lactylated lysine has not been identified; in vivo causal evidence remains limited. Future efforts should integrate multiomics technologies, genetic manipulation tools, precision delivery systems to decipher the spatiotemporal regulatory networks of lactylation, thereby facilitating the identification of new therapeutic targets strategies for inflammatory, neoplastic, metabolic diseases.

articles.titulo: Metabolic reprogramming of myeloid‑derived suppressor cells in colorectal cancer: Mechanistic insights and immunometabolic targeted rehabilitation (Review).
articles.autores: Zhu LX, Jiang GJ, Gao FH, Du YQ
articles.resumo_original: Metabolic reprogramming of myeloid‑derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) plays a role in immunotherapy resistance in colorectal cancer (CRC). This metabolic reprogramming appears to be coordinated by oncogenic mutations (such as adenomatous polyposis coli, KRAS and TP53) through a proposed self‑reinforcing 'mutation‑metabolism‑suppression' axis. In the present review, four core metabolic pillars sustaining MDSC pathogenicity and the epimetabolic regulation that durably locks them into a suppressive state were examined. Furthermore, two emerging dimensions were highlighted: The spatial metabolic antagonism through which MDSCs may construct a metabolically hostile zone to limit the functional activity of tertiary lymphoid structures, and the remote manipulation of MDSC function by gut and intratumoral microbiota‑derived metabolites. To transcend the limitations of non‑specific myeloid depletion, immunometabolic rehabilitation is proposed as a potentially transformative framework targeting intrinsic metabolic vulnerabilities to functionally reprogram MDSCs from an immunosuppressive to a homeostatic or immunostimulatory phenotype. By integrating emerging spatial omics for precise target validation, artificial intelligence‑guided rational drug design and microbiome modulation, this paradigm provides a strategic roadmap for next‑generation precision immunotherapy, aiming to achieve durable responses across both microsatellite stable and microsatellite instability‑high CRC.

articles.titulo: Functional involvement of AMPK in Lumpy skin disease virus replication and associated cellular stress responses.
articles.autores: Zhong L, Li C, Ren J, Tang F, Dai J, Xue F
articles.resumo_original: Lumpy skin disease virus (LSDV) infection induces extensive cellular stress responses and metabolic reprogramming in host cells. However, the regulatory mechanisms linking these changes to viral replication remain unclear. In this study, MAC-T cells were used as an in vitro infection model to investigate LSDV-induced cellular stress responses and their impact on viral replication. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that LSDV infection activated pathways associated with energy stress, oxidative stress, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, suggesting disruption of cellular energy homeostasis and redox balance. Transmission electron microscopy further demonstrated mitochondrial structural damage in infected cells. Subsequent analyses showed that the ATP/AMP ratio and lactate metabolism decreased during infection, accompanied by elevated mitochondrial calcium levels and excessive reactive oxygen species accumulation. Mechanistically, LSDV infection activated the PERK-eIF2α-ATF4-CHOP and IRE1α-JNK-BECN1 pathways, indicating induction of ER stress-related signaling. Given the role of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) as a central metabolic stress sensor, we further examined its function during LSDV infection. LSDV infection enhanced AMPK activation, as evidenced by increased phosphorylation of Thr172. Inhibition of energy stress, oxidative stress, or ER stress reduced AMPK phosphorylation to varying degrees, suggesting that multiple stress responses collectively contribute to AMPK activation. Furthermore, AMPK inhibition impaired LSDV replication, while downstream analysis revealed that AMPK activation promotes autophagosome formation. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that LSDV-induced cellular stress responses activate AMPK signaling to facilitate viral replication, providing new insights into host metabolic regulation and identifying AMPK as a potential antiviral target.

articles.titulo: Fatty acid‑binding proteins at the inflammation‑cancer interface: Isoform‑specific metabolic‑immune mechanisms and therapeutic implications (Review).
articles.autores: Hah YS, Ju YT, Lee SJ, Hwang J, Kwag SJ
articles.resumo_original: Fatty acid‑binding proteins (FABPs) comprise ten mammalian isoforms (FABP1‑FABP9 and FABP12), each a small intracellular lipid chaperone traditionally viewed as a mediator of fatty acid uptake, trafficking and metabolic partitioning. Evidence from metabolic disease, immunology and oncology indicates that selected FABP isoforms also regulate inflammatory signaling, immune‑cell metabolism and tumor‑stromal crosstalk. Prior reviews have mainly emphasized single isoforms of FABPs or single disease categories. The present narrative review organized FABP biology as a context‑specific evidence map across the inflammation‑cancer interface, in which each principal claim is reported together with the experimental system, with the outcome and limits of extrapolation described. The main mechanistic focus was FABP4, FABP5 and FABP7. The structural determinants of isoform specificity, ligand routing to nuclear receptors and the non‑classical secretion of FABP4 as a circulating adipokine were summarized. The evidence supports a model in which FABPs may contribute to, rather than fully explain, the progression from metabolic stress to chronic low‑grade inflammation, premalignant remodeling and the establishment of the tumor microenvironment. In the present model, FABP4 links adipocytes, macrophages, endothelial cells and tumor cells through fatty acid shuttling and inflammasome/cytokine signaling; FABP5 connects retinoic acid and peroxisome proliferator‑activated receptor β/δ signaling with tumor‑cell growth and T helper/regulatory T‑cell balance; and FABP7 regulates neural‑lineage tumor plasticity through ligand‑dependent retinoid X receptor α signaling. In addition, translational evidence was stratified into clinically observed biomarkers, preclinical therapeutic targets and conceptual future technologies. Particular attention was paid to biomarker confounding by obesity, diabetes, age and sex, and to the therapeutic paradox in which FABP5 inhibition may suppress T helper 17 cell‑driven inflammation while enhancing regulatory T‑cell‑mediated immunosuppression in cancer. This synthesis provides a restrained conceptual framework for stage‑, isoform‑ and cell‑type‑specific FABP research.

articles.titulo: Long non-coding RNA prompts immune-related adverse events risk and immunotherapy response in pan-cancer.
articles.autores: Dong L, Zhang L, Song L, Qu C, Wang X, Xiao S, Tian M, Wang P, Zhi H, Zhao Y, Ning S, Gao Y
articles.resumo_original: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) improve cancer outcomes but can cause immune-related adverse events (irAEs) that compromise treatment. Using FAERS real-world data, we developed a two-layer network algorithm to identify irAE-associated lncRNAs (irAEsLncs) across 18 cancer types. The irAEsLnc network showed organ-specific patterns and cancer-specific irAE susceptibility, while irAEsLncs were associated with immune infiltration, inflammatory responses, immune activation, and checkpoint molecules. Single-cell analysis of ICI-induced colitis linked irAEsLncs to inflammatory macrophage and T cell states and metabolic reprogramming. irAEsLnc-derived signatures independently predicted prognosis and responses to targeted therapy and immunotherapy, with ALAL-1/CD80/MEF2C predicting ICI efficacy in lung adenocarcinoma. Knockdown of ALAL-1 and SEC61G-DT suppressed tumor cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and macrophage-mediated inflammation. These findings connect irAE-associated lncRNAs with toxicity and antitumor immunity and support their potential as biomarkers for treatment stratification.

articles.titulo: Succinate promotes multiple myeloma cell proliferation through TCA cycle oxidation.
articles.autores: Gudgeon N, Fulton-Ward T, Stavrou V, Haslam A, McIlroy G, Giles H, Pratt G, Dimeloe S
articles.resumo_original: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell malignancy that develops within the bone marrow. The bone marrow metabolome is altered in myeloma, with implications for malignant cell growth. Here, the impact of elevated bone marrow levels of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle metabolite, succinate, was interrogated. Succinate was found to promote proliferation of several myeloma cell lines. This was linked to its uptake and oxidation in the TCA cycle, as indicated by increased ATP-coupled mitochondrial respiration and incorporation of succinate-derived carbons into downstream TCA cycle intermediates, which also occurs in primary myeloma cells. Succinate-driven proliferation was dependent upon mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and abrogated by ATP synthase inhibition. Furthermore, interrogation of large-scale transcriptomic data identified that elevated expression of a mitochondrial succinate transporter associates with accelerated disease progression in myeloma, indicating this mechanism may promote plasma cell growth in vivo and highlighting a target for therapeutic intervention.

articles.titulo: Metabolic and biochemical predictors of glycemic response after bariatric surgery: a scoping review.
articles.autores: Netto MPS, Duval-Araujo I, Tinoco A
articles.resumo_original:
Bariatric and metabolic surgery is one of the most effective treatments for severe obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), promoting metabolic changes beyond weight loss. However, the biochemical determinants of postoperative glycemic response remain incompletely understood.
A scoping review was conducted following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus were searched for studies published between 2016 and 2025 evaluating metabolic and biochemical variables associated with glycemic outcomes after bariatric surgery.
Twenty-two studies were included, comprising eight randomized controlled trials and fourteen cohort studies. Bariatric surgery was consistently associated with reductions in HbA1c and significant rates of T2DM remission. Improvements in insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), beta-cell function, and incretin response-particularly GLP-1-were associated with better outcomes. Reductions in inflammatory markers, including IL-6, IFN-γ, and TNF-α, were also reported.
Glycemic improvement after bariatric surgery is associated with complex metabolic interactions involving insulin sensitivity, incretin modulation, and inflammatory changes. These findings support the role of bariatric and metabolic surgery as a metabolic and immunometabolic intervention, although the descriptive design of a scoping review precludes causal inference.

articles.titulo: Effects of intradermal lymphocyte therapy in patients with recurrent pregnancy loss: secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial investigating purinergic signaling, inflammation, and cellular energy status.
articles.autores: Yildirim O, Gundogdu H, Abbas-Kabiri D, Naseri A, Baharaghdam S, Chakari-Khiavi F, Aghapour A, Miahipour A, Hakimi P, Pourlak T, Roshangar L, Yousefi M
articles.resumo_original:
Recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL), a multifactorial and complex reproductive disorder, is diagnosed when there are two or more documented back-to-back failed pregnancies. Intradermal lymphocyte therapy (ILT) emerged as a promising intervention, aiming to modulate the intricate immunological milieu implicated in RPL. This study was designed to assess the effects of ILT on pregnancy and live birth rate and also provide insight into potential immunometabolic mechanisms underlying the clinical efficacy of lymphocyte therapy in RPL.
The study included 100 patients with RPL, who received ILT (treated group, n = 50) or routine treatment (untreated group, n = 50), as well as 30 healthy women with a history of successful pregnancy as a control group. Low-dose ILT (Three injections of 20 × 10^6 PBMCs) was administered according to a standardized protocol, and flow cytometric analysis of CD39 and CD73 expression, ELISA measurement for serum levels of TNF-α, TGF-β, IL-1, and IL-10, as well as intracellular ATP and AMP using commercially available enzymatic colorimetric assay kits, were conducted.
Pregnancy and live birth rate were significantly higher in the treated group compared with the untreated group (p < 0.001). In patients with successful pregnancy, across all measured cytokines (TNF-α, TGF-β, IL-1, and IL-10), as well as ATP/AMP ratio and CD39⁺CD73⁺ cell frequency, treated patients exhibited significant pre- to post-treatment changes, whereas routine treatment patients showed no statistically meaningful differences. After treatment, between-group differences were statistically significant across all measured outcomes, although the level of statistical significance varied across outcomes.
Low-dose ILT may be associated with improved successful pregnancy and live birth rates in RPL patients. These clinical outcomes coincided with changes in purinergic signaling, inflammatory cytokines, and cellular energy status; however, formal mediation cannot be inferred from the present analysis.

articles.titulo: Immunometabolic crosstalk in intervertebral disc degeneration: a narrative review of neutrophil extracellular traps, macrophage polarization, and metabolic reprogramming.
articles.autores: Li F, Peng Y, Wu H, Song C, Fu Z, Liu Z
articles.resumo_original: Intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) is a major pathological contributor to chronic low-back pain. Long viewed merely as a mechanical "wear-and-tear" condition, IVDD is now thought to be substantially driven by reciprocal immunometabolic interactions between infiltrating immune cells and disc-resident nucleus pulposus (NP) cells. This narrative review synthesizes and critically appraises available evidence for three core pathological components: neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation and its pro-inflammatory consequences, dysregulated macrophage plasticity within the degenerative microenvironment, and metabolic crisis triggered by mitochondrial impairment and maladaptive glycolytic reprogramming. We integrate these elements into a unified conceptual model of bidirectional immunometabolic crosstalk operating within the unique hypoxic, avascular, low-glucose intervertebral-disc niche. Importantly, many mechanistic links within this network remain hypothetical and are partly extrapolated from non-disc inflammatory models; we explicitly distinguish experimentally-supported observations from unvalidated causal hypotheses and summarize key unresolved mechanistic questions. We further outline molecular mediators mediating immune-metabolic communication and highlight stage-dependent therapeutic opportunities together with major translational bottlenecks. Finally, emerging intervention strategies targeting this immunometabolic network-including PAD4-directed NET inhibition, macrophage phenotype reprogramming, and restoration of mitochondrial and metabolic homeostasis - are discussed to inform future mechanism-oriented therapeutic research for IVDD.

articles.titulo: Metabolomic Changes in Biofilm of Pseudomonas aeruginosa Under Early-Stage Tobramycin Treatment Identified by 2D NMR-Based COLMARq.
articles.autores: Choo M, Li DW, Lee K, Sindeldecker D, Bruschweiler-Li L, Brüschweiler R
articles.resumo_original: Biofilms are estimated to account for a large proportion of persistent microbial infections and are associated with substantial mortality in hospitals. Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilms exhibit higher resistance to antibiotics compared to their planktonic growth form, making them difficult to eradicate and contributing to the mounting global challenge posed by infectious diseases. To gain deeper insights into the metabolic response of biofilms to antibiotic pressure, we conducted a quantitative, untargeted metabolomics analysis using heteronuclear 2D NMR spectroscopy. Biofilms were grown in the presence of sub-inhibitory concentrations of tobramycin, and metabolic alterations were identified and quantified using the COLMARq analysis platform. Our analysis revealed significant metabolic shifts even at low doses of tobramycin with key metabolites such as UDP-glucose increasing and putrescine decreasing. Pathway enrichment analysis highlighted alterations in amino acid biosynthesis, energy metabolism, and stress response pathways. Notably, the accumulation of glutathione disulfide indicates enhanced oxidative stress, while the depletion of β-alanine, succinate, and GABA suggested metabolic shifts linked to biofilm adaptation. These findings provide new insights into the metabolic reprogramming of biofilms under antibiotic treatment and offer perspectives into biofilm behavior in the case of Pseudomonas aeruginosa when exposed to antibiotics from an early stage of infection.

articles.titulo: Engineered synbiotic microspheres enable system-level reprogramming of the gut-immune-vascular axis in chronic inflammatory vascular disease.
articles.autores: Shen L, Zhai M, Yang Z, Yu J, Pang Z, Fang Z, Ding X, Xu J, Hu Y, Fang S, Shu G, Yang Y, Lv L, Zhang S, Xu J, Wu J, Chen W, Lu C, Chen M, Ji J
articles.resumo_original: Chronic inflammatory vascular diseases are increasingly recognized as systemic disorders sustained by maladaptive cross-organ immunometabolic coupling, yet current therapeutic strategies remain largely lesion-centered and fail to address upstream drivers of disease persistence. Here, we identify the gut-immune-vascular axis as a system-level pathogenic unit that integrates gut microbial dysbiosis, intestinal barrier dysfunction, metabolic imbalance, and vascular immune activation into a self-reinforcing pathological circuit. Through integrated clinical profiling and cross-species validation, we demonstrate that disruption of this axis is characterized by coordinated probiotic depletion, expansion of proinflammatory taxa, translocation of microbial endotoxins, accumulation of microbiota-derived metabolites, and macrophage polarization toward a proinflammatory phenotype along the gut-vascular continuum. To therapeutically target this axis, we engineer enzyme-responsive synbiotic microspheres that codeliver probiotics, a microbial metabolic pathway inhibitor, and a prebiotic within a protective polymeric matrix, enabling site-specific intestinal activation and coordinated microbiota-metabolic modulation. This engineered system restores intestinal barrier integrity, reprograms microbial ecology and metabolite output, suppresses immunometabolic dysfunction, and robustly attenuates pathological vascular remodeling across cellular, murine, and large-animal models, with in-stent restenosis serving as a representative disease context. Collectively, this work establishes axis-oriented immunometabolic reprogramming as a generalizable therapeutic paradigm and highlights engineered synbiotic platforms as scalable tools for system-level intervention in chronic inflammatory diseases.

articles.titulo: Metabolic Landscape and Immune Microenvironment in Ovarian Cancer: Mechanisms of Remodelling and Therapeutic Opportunities.
articles.autores: Zhao Y, Wang Y, Huang L, Tian T
articles.resumo_original: Ovarian Cancer (OC) is the most lethal gynaecological malignancy worldwide, with a 5-year survival rate of less than 50%. Most patients still face tumour recurrence and drug resistance, which is mainly attributed to its highly complex tumour immune microenvironment (TIME) and metabolic heterogeneity, where metabolic remodelling severely suppresses immune cell function. OC cells exhibit distinctive metabolic reprogramming during tumour development and progression. In addition, various cells such as tumour-associated macrophages and neutrophils collectively construct an immunosuppressive network through their respective metabolic pathways. In the hypoxic peritoneal niche, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α directly drives the expression of galectin-1 and intersects with the IDO1-kynurenine-AhR axis, jointly reinforcing regulatory T-cell expansion and T-cell exhaustion. Targeting metabolic reprogramming to reshape the TIME has become a research hotspot, and emerging strategies including the delivery of metabolic inhibitors via nanoplatforms have shown synergistic antitumour potential. This article elaborates the mechanisms of metabolic reprogramming between OC cells and various cell types within the TIME, focusing on breaking immune tolerance by correcting metabolic disorders, so as to provide theoretical support for novel therapeutic regimens for OC based on immunometabolic regulation.

articles.titulo: Hypoxia Orchestrates the Natural History of Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Opportunities.
articles.autores: Luque MVS, Moreno ASA, Angarita-Planchez ME, Múnera-Rodríguez AM, López-Enríquez S, Casado-Jurado D, de Miguel M, Palomares F
articles.resumo_original: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) arises from a dynamic interplay between epithelial dysfunction, immune activation, microbial dysbiosis and tissue remodelling. Although hypoxia was initially regarded as a consequence of intestinal inflammation, it is now recognized as an active regulator of epithelial, immune and stromal responses that coordinate disease progression. Here, we propose that hypoxia acts as a biological organizer linking oxygen sensing to the transition from intestinal homeostasis to chronic inflammation and structural tissue damage. We use this term in a mechanistic rather than a hierarchical sense: oxygen availability is a shared upstream constraint on epithelial, immune, microbial and stromal programmes, not a single initiating event. This review integrates evidence connecting oxygen sensing with epithelial barrier integrity, immunometabolism, microbial ecology and stromal remodelling, with emphasis on advances in single-cell transcriptomics, spatial biology and microbiome research. Physiological low-oxygen gradients support epithelial metabolism, barrier integrity and immune tolerance, whereas persistent inflammatory hypoxia drives oxidative stress, metabolic reprogramming and maladaptive epithelial-immune-microbial interactions. Hypoxia also contributes to spatially distinct epithelial, immune and stromal niches that may sustain chronic inflammation and fibrotic progression. Microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids and succinate, together with iron metabolism and ferroptosis, further link oxygen sensing to tissue injury, adaptation and repair. These findings position hypoxia-responsive signalling as a pharmacologically actionable network rather than a downstream consequence of inflammation. Targeting selected components may promote mucosal healing and limit structural disease progression, although successful translation will require cell- and isoform-selective modulation, adequate tissue exposure and careful assessment of long-term safety.

articles.titulo: Proteomic and functional analyses identify an ISG15-TLR3-NF-κB signaling axis associated with the antibacterial response to Streptococcus agalactiae infection in Nile tilapia.
articles.autores: Li LY, Zhang JH, Bai Y, Pan JM, Sun LB, Xia JH
articles.resumo_original: Streptococcus agalactiae (GBS) is the leading cause of streptococcosis in Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus). Interferon-stimulated gene 15 (ISG15) is widely recognized as an antiviral effector, but its role and molecular targets in bacterial infections are still unknown. Here, we employed 4D-DIA proteomics to profile spleen and head kidney responses in GIFT tilapia 24 h post-GBS infection, identifying 8280 and 8491 proteins, among which 383 and 461 were differentially expressed (DEPs), respectively. These DEPs revealed tissue-specific immune programs: inflammatory and coagulation pathways in the spleen versus energy metabolic reprogramming in the head kidney. Parallel reaction monitoring (PRM) validated 28 DEPs and pinpointed ISG15 as a pivotal regulator. GST pull-down coupled with mass spectrometry identified 927 ISG15-interacting proteins. Co-immunoprecipitation and dual-luciferase assays confirmed that ISG15 associates with TLR3 via its two ubiquitin-like domains, which bind to the LRR and TIR domains of TLR3, recruiting TRIF and MyD88 to dose-dependently activate NF-κB and induce seven pro-inflammatory cytokines plus IL-10. This study identifies an ISG15-TLR3-NF-κB signaling axis associated with the antibacterial response in teleosts, based on cell-based and in vitro evidence, adding a mechanism fundamentally distinct from mammalian TLR2/8/4 pathways. These findings expand ISG15 function beyond antiviral immunity. As the interaction was characterized in vitro and in overexpression systems, whether the contact is direct or mediated by bridging proteins, whether endogenous complexes form during infection, and whether the axis enhances bacterial clearance or survival in vivo remain to be established.

articles.titulo: A multi-omics study with in vitro and in vivo interventions targeting the leptin-mediated Hypoxia-Inducible Factor-1 Alpha metabolic-inflammatory axis in gastroesophageal reflux disease.
articles.revista: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Molecular basis of disease
articles.autores: Wang Z, Zhang Q, Wufuer A, Li Z, Hong T
articles.resumo_original: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is characterized by persistent inflammation of the esophageal mucosa, and acid-suppressive therapy may not fully reverse an established inflammatory microenvironment. We integrated two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR), multi-omics profiling, and in vivo and in vitro experiments to examine a leptin-HIF-1α metabolic-inflammatory axis. MR using the European-ancestry, adiposity-adjusted leptin phenotype linked to GCST90007310 identified a modest, hypothesis-generating association with GERD risk rather than definitive causal proof. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses implicated HIF-1α-related glycolysis and inflammatory pathways in diseased esophageal tissue. In epithelial and animal models, leptin-associated HIF-1α activation was accompanied by increased glycolytic activity, lactate and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, inflammatory signaling, and loss of barrier proteins. LEPR expression and receptor-dependent signaling, HIF-1α turnover, PX-478 target engagement, systemic AAV9-CMV-Hif1a distribution, and single-agent controls were examined to define the experimental boundaries. The single-agent analyses showed direct drug effects, particularly for 2-DG, and PX-478 also affected HIF-2α under hypoxia; therefore, the pharmacological data are interpreted as pathway-intervention evidence rather than proof of isoform-specific or toxicity-free rescue. These findings support a mechanistic framework linking leptin-associated signaling, HIF-related metabolic reprogramming, inflammation, and epithelial barrier injury in GERD, while the directionality and translational relevance require further validation.

articles.titulo: PD-1 deficiency impairs Treg differentiation in Trichinella-infected mice via inhibition of fatty acid oxidation.
articles.autores: Zhang Y, Hao Y, Wu C, Li C, Huang J, Zhu X, Cheng Y
articles.resumo_original: Helminth infections establish long-term host persistence by inducing regulatory immune responses that limit pathology while promoting parasite survival. Programmed death 1 (PD-1), an inhibitory receptor expressed on activated T cells, plays an essential role in maintaining immune homeostasis during chronic infections. Regulatory T cells (Tregs) expand during helminth infection and are critical for controlling excessive inflammation; however, the metabolic mechanisms linking PD-1 signaling to Treg differentiation during helminth infection remain poorly defined. Here, we investigated the role of PD-1 in regulating Treg differentiation during Trichinella spiralis infection, focusing on metabolic reprogramming in CD4⁺ T cells. Using a murine infection model, we compared wild-type and PD-1-deficient (PD-1⁻/⁻) mice and evaluated Treg differentiation in vivo and in a bone marrow-derived dendritic cell (BMDC)-CD4⁺ T-cell co-culture system stimulated with muscle larval excretory-secretory products (MES). PD-1 deficiency significantly reduced splenic FoxP3⁺ Treg frequencies following infection and impaired MES-induced Treg differentiation and Treg-associated cytokine production in vitro. Metabolic profiling revealed that CD4⁺ T cells from infected PD-1⁻/⁻ mice exhibited markedly reduced fatty acid oxidation (FAO), accompanied by decreased expression of Carnitine Palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A), a key rate-limiting enzyme in FAO. PD-1 deficiency was associated with enhanced PI3K-Akt-mTOR signaling and suppressed AMPK activation. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of PI3K partially restored FAO activity and rescued Treg differentiation in PD-1⁻/⁻ CD4⁺ T cells. These findings suggest that PD-1 supports Treg development during T. spiralis infection, at least in part, through a CPT1A-associated FAO pathway, highlighting a PD-1-associated metabolic pathway that may contribute to helminth-induced immune regulation.

articles.titulo: Astrocytic endoplasmic reticulum stress as an amplifier of neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's disease: a narrative review.
articles.autores: da Silva Lima B, Dos Santos YTP, Farias GC, de Lima Souza EFR, de Lima PDL, Quaresma JAS, da Costa Vasconcelos PF, de Sousa JR
articles.resumo_original: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is increasingly recognized as a multicellular neuroimmune disorder in which proteostatic failure, metabolic dysfunction, and sustained glial activation interact to accelerate synaptic loss. This narrative review examines endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress in astrocytes as a mechanistic link among the unfolded protein response (UPR), neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neurodegeneration. The three canonical UPR branches, mediated by protein kinase R-like ER kinase (PERK), inositol-requiring enzyme 1 (IRE1), and activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6), initially reduce protein-folding burden and reinforce ER quality control. When stress persists and adaptive capacity becomes insufficient, sustained PERK and IRE1 signaling may favor apoptosis, inflammatory transcriptional programs, cytokine production, calcium dyshomeostasis, and oxidative injury, whereas ATF6 remains predominantly associated with proteostatic reinforcement in a context-dependent manner. In astrocytes, persistent UPR activation may impair neuronal metabolic support, synaptogenic signaling, and astrocytic contributions to neurovascular homeostasis while promoting complement component 3 (C3) expression and bidirectional inflammatory crosstalk with microglia. ER-mitochondria contact sites further integrate calcium transfer, reactive oxygen species generation, bioenergetic failure, and intrinsic apoptotic signaling. Experimental evidence therefore supports a self-reinforcing neuroglial circuit in which astrocytic ER stress is proposed to function as an amplifier rather than merely a consequence of AD pathology. Therapeutic strategies targeting UPR signaling, chemical chaperones, extracellular vesicles, gene modulation, and cell-selective delivery systems remain under investigation, and their translation will require temporally controlled, cell-type-specific, and safety-conscious modulation of stress responses.

articles.titulo: Tissue-resident memory T cells: central regulators of chronicity and relapse in autoimmune diseases-from mechanistic insights to precision interventions.
articles.autores: Wang G, Yin S, Hou X
articles.resumo_original: Tissue-resident memory T cells (TRM), a subset of memory T cells that persist long-term within peripheral tissues without recirculating, play a dual role in adaptive immunity. They serve as the frontline defense against pathogen reinfection, yet accumulating evidence implicates TRM cells as pivotal effectors driving chronicity, tissue-specific damage, and clinical relapse in various autoimmune diseases. This review systematically examines the central role of TRM cells in autoimmunity by dissecting the molecular mechanisms underlying their development, maintenance, and activation. We highlight how specific cytokine networks, alongside metabolic programs and sustain their pathogenic potential. Emphasis is placed on the heterogeneous functions of TRM cells in diseases such as psoriasis/psoriatic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and primary Sjögren's syndrome. Furthermore, we analyze the dysregulation of tissue immune checkpoints through interactions between TRM and regulatory T cells (Treg), which disrupt immune homeostasis. Finally, we critically evaluate current therapeutic strategies targeting TRM cells and propose future precision intervention approaches leveraging immune metabolic reprogramming, nanotechnology, and artificial intelligence to improve disease management and prevent relapse.

articles.titulo: From cave adaptation to ageing resilience: the Mexican cavefish Astyanax mexicanus.
articles.autores: Lagunas-Rangel FA
articles.resumo_original: The Mexican cavefish, Astyanax mexicanus, is a powerful evolutionary model for investigating how adaptation to extreme environments reshapes vertebrate physiology. Multiple cave populations have independently evolved under subterranean conditions, acquiring traits including insulin resistance, persistent hyperglycaemia, increased adiposity, altered sleep patterns, hypoxia tolerance and extensive metabolic reprogramming. Despite these differences, cavefish exhibit lifespans comparable to those of surface fish, while selected traits, including fertility and locomotor performance, appear to be better preserved with age. These observations challenge the assumption that persistent metabolic dysfunction necessarily entails accelerated functional decline and raise the possibility that cavefish have evolved mechanisms of ageing resilience. This narrative review examines evidence linking cave adaptation to biological processes relevant to ageing, focusing on nutrient sensing, lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, redox homeostasis and immune regulation. Rather than eliminating metabolic stress, cave-associated adaptations may buffer some of its downstream consequences, preserving selected physiological functions. Evidence is evaluated within the framework of the hallmarks of ageing, considering genomic instability, telomere dynamics, deregulated nutrient sensing, mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic inflammation, while identifying major knowledge gaps regarding epigenetic alterations, loss of proteostasis, macroautophagy, cellular senescence, stem-cell exhaustion, altered intercellular communication and dysbiosis. The available evidence supports A. mexicanus as a comparative model for investigating how chronic environmental and metabolic stress can be uncoupled from selected aspects of functional decline. Distinguishing delayed ageing from enhanced tolerance or compensation in response to accumulated damage will be essential to establish the extent and mechanisms of ageing resilience in this species.

articles.titulo: Molecular MRI Reveals Macrophage-Enriched Peritumoral Immune Remodeling After Incomplete Ablation in Liver Cancer.
articles.autores: He Y, Xu H, M M Rogasch J, Berndt N, Guo J, Schellenberger E, Häckel A, Heidemann L, Hesse F, Liu Y, Ramtke J, Beindorff N, Hofheinz F, Kader A, Mülleder M, Textoris-Taube K, Hamm B, Müller DN, Schmidt R, Hauptmann R, Traub H, Schannor M, Savic LJ
articles.resumo_original: Incomplete image-guided ablation can promote local tumor progression by reshaping the residual tumor microenvironment toward immunosuppression, yet noninvasive biomarkers of this process remain limited. Here, a translational multiparametric PET/MRI strategy was developed to monitor macrophage-associated microenvironmental remodeling after incomplete microwave ablation (iMWA) in orthotopic VX2 liver tumors. Twenty-four tumor-bearing rabbits were assigned to untreated control, early post-iMWA (short-term), or late post-iMWA (long-term) groups and underwent clinical 3 T PET/MRI, including diffusion-weighted imaging, dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI, [1 8F]FDG PET, and T2-weighted MRI before and after administration of Eu-VSOP. Eu-VSOP-enhanced MRI revealed a hypointense peritumoral rim after iMWA, with the largest rim-to-liver signal decrease and rim thickness observed in the long-term group. Prussian blue staining and LA-ICP-ToF-MS demonstrated preferential iron and europium enrichment in macrophage-rich, CD206-associated peritumoral regions. Histology and proteomics further demonstrated increased CD206 and MMP-9 expression, extracellular matrix remodeling, immunosuppressive myeloid-associated changes, and metabolic reprogramming in viable residual tumors, accompanied by altered [1 8F]FDG uptake. Together, these findings indicate that incomplete ablation induces a temporally evolving, macrophage-rich immunosuppressive peritumoral niche and support the potential of Eu-VSOP-enhanced multiparametric PET/MRI for noninvasive monitoring of post-ablation microenvironmental remodeling.

articles.titulo: Genome-wide identification and integrative analysis of the cytochrome P450 superfamily in pea (Pisum sativum L.) reveals candidate genes associated with Aphanomyces root rot response.
articles.autores: Tahir MS, Dhaubhadel S
articles.resumo_original: Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases (P450) constitute one of the largest and most functionally diverse enzyme superfamilies in plants, underpinning the biosynthesis of a plethora of primary and specialized metabolites involved in growth and development as well as stress response. Here, we present the first integrated genome-wide analysis of the pea P450 superfamily (CYPome), combining phylogenetic, structural, evolutionary, transcriptional, and genetic approaches to identify defense-associated candidates. We identified 210 P450 genes encoding 241 proteins in pea genome, classified into 45 CYP families across 10 clans. Comparative analyses revealed both highly conserved legume P450 lineages and a substantial fraction of pea-specific expansions, reflecting dynamic CYPome evolution. Gene structure and motif analyses confirmed conservation of core catalytic features, alongside family-specific variation consistent with functional diversification. A conserved core of many PsP450 genes induced across multiple pea cultivars at a wide range of time points post Aphanomyces euteiches infection together with their expression in root tissue was discovered. Integration of aphanomyces root rot resistance-associated quantitative trait loci further refined candidate prioritization, identifying PsP450s that co-localized with resistance loci, exhibited strong co-expression with PsIFS genes, and were rapidly induced upon infection. Collectively, this integrative analysis defines the pea CYPome and identifies a focused set of high-confidence P450 candidates likely involved in defense-associated metabolic reprogramming during A. euteiches infection. These findings provide a foundational resource for functional genomics and offer promising targets for improving disease resistance in pea and related legume crops.

articles.titulo: Innate immune memory in mucosa: where is it encoded?
articles.autores: Noye EC, Belz GT
articles.resumo_original: Trained immunity describes the capacity of innate immune cells to develop memory-like responses following a prior challenge. Early studies focused on myeloid cells and bone marrow progenitors. Extension of this concept to mucosal tissues, however, presents a more complex picture. These barrier sites harbor diverse, long-lived immune populations that interact with structural cells and neuronal circuits to actively shape immune responses. Emerging evidence suggests that memory-like programs extend beyond immune cells to include epithelial, stromal, and neuronal compartments. We propose that trained immunity in mucosal surfaces is distributed across the tissue ecosystem, encompassing progenitors, tissue-resident populations, and the tissue niche. This expanded framework redefines innate immune memory and has important implications for infections and chronic inflammatory diseases.

articles.titulo: Triggers of Gout Flares from Local to Systemic Perspectives.
articles.autores: Straton AR, Crisan TO, Joosten LAB
articles.resumo_original: Gout is the most common type of inflammatory arthritis, caused by MSU crystal deposition in the joint, resulting from chronic hyperuricemia. Typically, the first clinical presentation is a gout flare characterized by severe pain, redness, joint swelling, and limited mobility. Despite continuous exposure to increased serum urate concentration followed by MSU crystal formation, flares are unpredictable and intermittent when poorly managed. Acute gout flares follow a two-step model: firstly, MSU crystals build up and, secondly, an endogenous or exogenous triggering event is needed. Once both triggers are given, resident macrophages initiate an acute inflammatory response. However, these additional factors are still under debate and increased serum urate concentrations alone are insufficient to ignite gout flares. In this review, we aim to sharpen our understanding of the unique characteristics responsible for transitioning from an asymptomatic state to acute joint inflammation observed in gout patients. We focus on integrating joint mechanisms during a gout flare, such as NLRP3 inflammasome activation, macrophage heterogeneity changes, and local physicochemical conditions with systemic influences from immunometabolism and genetic variation to explain the interindividual variability in flare susceptibility.

articles.titulo: The metabolic reprogramming of T cells controls airway remodeling in severe asthma.
articles.revista: The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology
articles.autores: Steele H, Kato E, Dell G, Fink M, Ghastine A, Willicut A, Cheroutre H, Kronenberg M, Herro R
articles.resumo_original:
Mixed granulocytic asthma (MGA) is a severe Th2-low endotype, characterized by high Th17/neutrophilic burden and exacerbated airway remodeling. Both features confer resistance to inhaled corticosteroids and typical asthma treatments.
We aimed to address gaps in knowledge, including how Th17 cells induce pathological tissue remodeling and how Th17 differentiation occurs in response to allergens.
We generated a Th2-low murine model of asthma on the Il4rα-/- background that mimics the decrease in type 2 response seen in corticosteroid-resistant patients. We monitored major features of human disease including heightened airway reactivity to methacholine, Th17/neutrophilic inflammation, airway remodeling, and resistance to corticosteroid treatment. Comparative transfer of Th2 versus Th17 cells were analyzed. We further investigated how the mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) pathway modulates pathogenic Th17 cell reprogramming by in vitro T cell cultures and in vivo therapeutic blockades.
LIGHT (aka TNFSF14) and the OXPHOS pathway are enriched in human MGA and likewise upregulated in this mouse model. We show OXPHOS promotes the metabolic reprograming of Th17 cells, to sustain their survival despite steroid treatment and produce LIGHT that controls airway remodeling. Mechanistically, OXPHOS regulates RORγt expression and the subsequent transcriptional network to program differentiation of Th17 cells, whereas LIGHT drives airway remodeling by activating the MMP9-dependent TGFβ pathway. Additionally, OXPHOS+Th17 cells promote the expression of osteopontin necessary for fibroblast activation. LIGHT antagonistic blockade reduces airway remodeling, whereas OXPHOS inhibition kills Th17 cells and subsequent neutrophilia. Importantly, the dual blockade of LIGHT and OXPHOS reverses all features of MGA back to baseline and reciprocally increases the numbers of Treg cells.
The dual blockade of LIGHT and OXPHOS constitutes a promising target for clinical interventions in human MGA, possibly extending to other Th17-driven fibrotic diseases.

articles.titulo: Itaconate alleviates sepsis-induced acute lung injury by suppressing Peroxiredoxin 1 dimerization through covalent alkylates at Cys173.
articles.autores: Ma J, Chen Y, Zhang Y, Zhang Y, Zhang Z, Tu G, Liu Y, Shen Y, Deng Y, Wu J, Deng Z, Shen C, Zhan D, Li J, Li J
articles.resumo_original: Sepsis-associated acute lung injury (SALI) is characterized by overwhelming inflammation and oxidative stress, during which damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) exacerbate tissue injury. Peroxiredoxin 1 (PRDX1), a canonical intracellular antioxidant enzyme, paradoxically functions as a pro-inflammatory DAMP after extracellular release. This pathogenic transition depends on PRDX1 dimerization through intermolecular disulfide bonds. However, the endogenous metabolic mechanisms that restrain PRDX1 release remain unclear. Here, we identify the ACOD1-itaconate axis as a critical suppressor of PRDX1-mediated hyperinflammation in SALI. Clinical dataset analysis revealed that elevated PRDX1 expression strongly correlates with sepsis mortality. In a murine cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) model, Acod1 deficiency exacerbated SALI and amplified PRDX1 secretion, whereas therapeutic administration of 4-octyl itaconate (4-OI) robustly alleviated lung injury and the accompanying cytokine storm. Mechanistically, chemical proteomics and mutagenesis showed that itaconate directly targets PRDX1. Acting as an electrophile, itaconate covalently alkylates the highly conserved cysteine 173 residue of PRDX1 via Michael addition. This redox modification sterically blocks intermolecular disulfide bond formation, thereby preventing PRDX1 dimerization and subsequent secretion from primary macrophages. Consequently, the loss of extracellular PRDX1 dimers reduces Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) engagement and suppresses downstream MAPK and NF-κB signaling cascades. Strikingly, the PRDX1-C173S loss-of-function mutation abolished the inhibitory efficacy of 4-OI, confirming Cys173 as an indispensable pharmacological target. Together, our study bridges immunometabolism and redox biology by demonstrating that itaconate restrains systemic inflammation through covalent trapping of PRDX1 in a monomeric state, providing a targeted redox-based therapeutic strategy for acute inflammatory diseases.

articles.titulo: Jujuboside A ameliorates T2DM-associated MASH: Suppression of YY1/FAS axis-mediated hepatic de novo fatty acid biosynthesis.
articles.autores: Yang T, Chen L, Luo H, Wang L, Jiang X, Yang H, Chen L, Qian S, Wang T, Li B, Ji F, Yan X, Yin X, Lu Q
articles.resumo_original: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) represents a progressive subtype of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), and is predominantly driven by dysregulated hepatic fatty acid (FA) metabolism. Although Jujuboside A (Ju A), a major bioactive triterpene saponin isolated from Ziziphus jujuba Mill. (sour jujube), exhibits hepatoprotective properties, its precise regulatory mechanisms underlying T2DM-associated MASH remain poorly defined. This study investigated the dose-dependent protective effects and molecular mechanisms of Ju A using both in vivo and in vitro models. Combining targeted FA profiling and long-chain FAs (LCFAs)-specific metabolomics, alongside chromatin immunoprecipitation (Ch-IP), luciferase reporter assays, molecular docking with dynamics simulations, and Yin Yang 1 (YY1) gain-of-function and fatty acid synthase (FAS) inhibition (C75) studies, we characterized Ju A-mediated metabolic reprogramming and molecular targets involved. Ju A treatment markedly ameliorated MASH and hepatic lipid deposition in diabetic mice by restoring dysregulated hepatic FA homeostasis, particularly by blocking de novo lipogenesis (DNL)-derived LCFA accumulation. Mechanistically, Ju A exerted these effects by blocking the nuclear translocation of YY1. This inhibition diminished YY1 binding to the FAS promoter, subsequently downregulating FAS expression and inhibiting aberrant hepatic de novo FA biosynthesis. Collectively, these findings demonstrated that Ju A ameliorated T2DM-associated MASH by restoring hepatic FA homeostasis via inactivation of the YY1-FAS axis, highlighting its promising therapeutic potential against diabetic liver complications.

articles.titulo: Urinary oxidative DEHP metabolites and advanced cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome: Evidence from NHANES and mechanistic insights into MECPP-related macrophage inflammatory-glycolytic activation.
articles.autores: Liang L, Su S, Niu Q, Rao K, Zhang Y, Chen N, Wang L, Chen Y, Yao P
articles.resumo_original:
Phthalates are ubiquitous environmental contaminants, yet their relevance to advanced cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome remains unclear. We examined the associations between urinary phthalate metabolites and advanced CKM syndrome, and explored the potential mechanisms linking di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP)-related exposure to macrophage inflammatory-glycolytic activation.
We analyzed 4236 adults from seven cycles (2005-2018) of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). A total of ten urinary phthalate metabolites were quantified, and advanced CKM syndrome was defined as CKM stages 3-4 using an NHANES-adapted American Heart Association framework. Survey-weighted logistic regression, restricted cubic splines, and weighted quantile sum (WQS) regression were used to assess single-metabolite, dose-response, and mixture associations. Mono(2-ethyl-5-carboxypentyl) phthalate (MECPP) was further evaluated using network toxicology, molecular docking, Mendelian randomization, single-cell RNA sequencing, and macrophage reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR).
Among 4236 participants, 648 had advanced CKM syndrome. In fully adjusted models, oxidative DEHP metabolites were positively associated with advanced CKM syndrome. Compared with the lowest quartile, the highest quartile was associated with higher odds for mono(2-ethyl-5-oxohexyl) phthalate (MEOHP; odds ratio [OR], 1.64; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.12-2.42), mono(2-ethyl-5-hydroxyhexyl) phthalate (MEHHP; OR, 1.60; 95% CI, 1.05-2.42), and MECPP (OR, 1.84; 95% CI, 1.26-2.68), with significant trends. Restricted cubic spline analyses suggested non-linear associations. WQS regression indicated a positive mixture association, with MECPP receiving the highest weight. Network toxicology identified 33 overlapping genes enriched in pathways related to the renin-angiotensin system, insulin resistance, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor signaling, and diabetic cardiomyopathy. Among the candidate hub genes, tumor necrosis factor (TNF) and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARG) were further examined using molecular docking and Mendelian randomization. Single-cell analyses of public mouse heart and kidney datasets localized Tnf mainly to macrophages and Pparg to cardiac endothelial cells and renal monocytes. In RAW 264.7 macrophages, MECPP potentiated palmitic acid-induced expression of inflammatory and glycolysis-related genes.
Urinary oxidative DEHP metabolites, particularly MECPP, were positively associated with advanced CKM syndrome in US adults. These findings support MECPP as a potential biomarker of DEHP-related exposure and generate mechanistic hypotheses involving macrophage-centered inflammatory and glycolytic transcriptional activation. Prospective and experimental studies are warranted to clarify causality and to determine whether DEHP-related exposure contributes to the development and progression of CKM syndrome.
