articles.titulo: Temporal shifts in post-asthmatic immune responses define tumor outcomes via strain-specific monocyte reprogramming.
articles.autores: Wang X, Chen C, Wan Y, Dang B, Liu X, Gao Q, Zhang J, Cheng SC
articles.resumo_original: Epidemiological evidence linking asthma to lung cancer risk remains contradictory, presenting asthma as either a risk factor or a protective condition. We hypothesize that this heterogeneity stems from the temporal dynamics of inflammatory response and host genetic background. Using ovalbumin (OVA)-induced asthma models, we identify a temporal shift in immune effectors driving post-asthmatic tumorigenesis. During acute airway inflammation, eosinophil infiltration accelerates tumor growth across mouse strains. Following resolution, however, tumorigenic outcomes in recovery diverge along genetic lines. Prior asthma reshapes chromatin landscapes of bone marrow myeloid progenitors, establishing innate immune memory that differentially programs monocytes across strains. In C57BL/6 mice, trained monocytes adopt oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), acquiring a suppressive, tissue-remodeling phenotype that promotes tumor progression. Conversely, BALB/c-trained monocytes utilize glycolysis to maintain a pro-phagocytic state, enabling tumor clearance. These findings delineate a biphasic mechanism wherein temporal shifts in post-asthmatic immune responses define tumor outcomes via strain-specific monocyte metabolic reprogramming.

articles.titulo: FSTL1 and NLRP3 Inflammasome Activation in Lupus Nephritis: A Mesenchyme-to-Macrophage Hypothesis.
articles.autores: Li Y, Qiu H, Gao X, Li N
articles.resumo_original:
Lupus nephritis (LN) is a major cause of morbidity in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), and current therapies often fail to prevent end-stage renal disease. Follistatin-like protein 1 (FSTL1), a mesenchymal/stromal-derived glycoprotein, is implicated in renal inflammation.
To synthesize evidence for a proposed FSTL1-driven NLRP3 inflammasome axis in LN and to identify gaps relevant to biomarker development and targeted therapy.
We examine the hypothesis that stromal/tubular FSTL1 is internalized by macrophages and activates NLRP3 via dual signals: mitochondrial ATP production (activation) and transcriptional upregulation of Nlrp3/pro-caspase-1 (priming), with resulting IL-1β amplifying tubulointerstitial inflammation and fibrosis. We assess evidence that FSTL1 is elevated in SLE sera, whereas direct LN kidney evidence is limited to one Chinese-language immunohistochemical study and NLRP3 colocalization has not been demonstrated in biopsy-proven LN; CKD and UUO models suggest FSTL1 may be present in LN kidney but this remains untested. We also discuss post-translational modifications, extracellular vesicle shuttling, and immunometabolism as unexplored determinants of context-dependent FSTL1 behavior.
The proposed mesenchyme/stroma-to-macrophage axis may offer new opportunities for LN biomarkers and targeted therapy, but current evidence is largely indirect and should be interpreted as a mechanistic framework requiring rigorous translational validation.

articles.titulo: Mitochondria-protective polysaccharide augments burn wound repair through immunometabolic reprogramming.
articles.autores: Zhong G, Liang Q, Pu J, Zhai X, Hu Z, Wu H, Xu N, Hu C, Luo Y, Liu Y, Zhao J, Sun P, Wang Y, Chen F, Luo G, Yu Y, Zhong C
articles.resumo_original: Effective wound healing requires coordinated extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition, immune regulation, and metabolic adaptation-processes governed by fibroblast mitochondria. Conventional burn therapies fail to address the mitochondrial dysfunction that impedes tissue regeneration. Here, we show that colanic acid (CA), a microbial-derived exopolysaccharide, acts as a mitochondrial-protecting biomaterial that accelerates burn repair by restoring immuno-metabolic crosstalk. In a murine deep second-degree burn model, CA enhanced wound closure 3.1-fold over controls, reduced reactive oxidative species by 54%, and increased mature collagen deposition by 193%. Mechanistically, CA undergoes intracellular internalization with the assistance of the membrane receptor TLR4 and maintains mitochondrial integrity, evidenced by restored cristae ultrastructure, a 1.4-fold increase in oxidative phosphorylation flux, and a 1.5-fold elevation in ATP production-effects abolished upon silencing the mitochondrial regulator Thap11. Bulk RNA-seq indicated that CA reshaped the wound immune landscape by driving macrophage recruitment and M2 polarization via mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming. By synchronizing mitochondrial rescue with immune-guided ECM remodeling, CA outperformed hyaluronic acid dressings in wound closure and extracellular matrix remodeling.The preliminary translational proof-of-concept of CA was confirmed in a Bama minipig model of deep second-degree burn wound, where it enhanced re-epithelialization, angiogenesis, and tissue perfusion. Together, these findings suggest that CA is a multifunctional polysaccharide with mitochondrial protective effects capable of addressing the multifaceted pathology of burn wounds across species.

articles.titulo: Hepatocyte IRE1α-XBP1s axis prevents pro-metastatic niche formation through metabolic rewiring of inflammatory monocytes.
articles.autores: Zhang H, Liang P, Yang W, Chen X, Fu Y, Chen C, Yin Z, Li X, Pei X, Lei JH, Chu X, Zhao ZB, Hu H, Chen M, Pan H, Lian ZX, Ding X, Halberg N, Ramm GA, Hou J
articles.resumo_original: Inositol-requiring enzyme 1α (IRE1α) and the downstream spliced form of X-Box Binding Protein 1 (XBP1s) have been identified as tumor promotors. However, how IRE1α-XBP1s signaling affects tumor progression in a non-cell autonomous manner remains unclear. Here we show that the hepatocyte IRE1α-XBP1s axis unexpectedly inhibits liver metastasis by confining local metainflammation. Genetic ablation of IRE1α or XBP1 in mouse hepatocytes exacerbates liver metastasis due to the accumulation of inflammatory monocytes (IMs). Mechanistically, a non-canonical Forkhead box O1 (FoxO1)-glutamine synthetase (GS) pathway endows the IRE1α- or XBP1-null hepatocytes with the metabolic activity to secrete glutamine, which is necessary and sufficient for IM fitness. Reintroduction of hepatocyte XBP1s or blockade of glutamine metabolism effectively reduces IMs and mitigates disease progression. Importantly, clinical patient survival with liver metastases positively correlates with hepatocyte XBP1s expression. Our study defines a paradigm of hepatocyte-IM interaction that can be leveraged to treat liver metastasis.

articles.titulo: Lactylation of HSC70 Impairs Chaperone-Mediated Autophagy to Promote Pyrin Inflammasome-Dependent PANoptosis in Macrophages During Sepsis.
articles.autores: Chen Y, Zhang Y, Wang P, Ma J, Zhao X, Li Y, Deng Z, Meng X, Zhu J, Yao L, Li J
articles.resumo_original: Sepsis-related cytokine storm is associated with poor prognosis in septic patients. IFNγ/LPS can synergistically trigger a sepsis-associated proinflammatory cytokine storm and induce macrophage death in the form of PANoptosis. The ensuing release of proinflammatory cytokines further amplifies macrophage death, leading to subsequent multiple organ damage. Concurrently, the IFNγ/LPS induced inflammatory cascade also downregulates chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) activity, and this dysregulation further exacerbates the inflammatory response in macrophages and in vivo. Thus, a positive feedback loop between dysfunctional CMA and the inflammatory cascade is established. Enhancing CMA activation reduces macrophage death and organ damage, whereas inhibiting CMA exacerbates macrophage PANoptosis and organ injury. Mechanistically, impaired CMA leads to accumulation of the transcription factor CUX1, which subsequently upregulates Pyrin expression and promotes Pyrin-mediated PANoptosome assembly, thereby driving macrophage PANoptosis. In addition to the cytokine storm, the lacylation at lysine 561 (K561) of HSC70, a core component of the CMA machinery, is associated with reduced CMA activity. Blocking lactylation can similarly attenuate macrophage death and multiple organ injury in sepsis. Taken together, this "Kla-CMA-CUX1/Pyrin-PANoptosis" signaling axis, linking metabolic reprogramming to immune dysregulation in sepsis, suggests that targeting key nodes of this axis may represent a promising therapeutic strategy to reduce sepsis-associated mortality.

articles.titulo: Glioblastoma-associated microglia/macrophages (GAMs): Advances in knowledge and implications for glioblastoma (GBM) therapy.
articles.revista: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Reviews on cancer
articles.autores: Singh S, Mishra R
articles.resumo_original: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an exceptionally aggressive, therapy-resistant central nervous system malignancy. Within the tumour microenvironment, glioblastoma-associated microglia and macrophages (GAMs) constitute a highly heterogeneous population whose functional states profoundly influence disease progression, tissue architecture, immune evasion, and treatment response. In this review, we propose a conceptual framework in which distinct GAM phenotypes emerge from the integrated influence of vascular, tumoural, metabolic, biomechanical, neural, and immune inputs, together with glyco-immune interactions, extracellular vesicles, and epigenetic regulation. As GAMs process these cues, they actively remodel their surrounding ecosystem, sustaining a protumourigenic niche. We critically evaluate emerging therapeutic interventions-including those targeting GAM abundance, immunometabolism, mechanotransduction, and intercellular communication-as well as advanced platforms such as engineered myeloid systems, phytomedicines, targeted delivery vehicles, and gut-brain axis-based strategies. Furthermore, we address key translational bottlenecks, including extreme GAM plasticity, spatial heterogeneity, limitations of preclinical models, barriers to central nervous system delivery, and a lack of predictive biomarkers. We argue that the therapeutically relevant target is not the GAM population in isolation, but rather the diverse niche-GAM functional units and the cumulative signalling networks that sustain them. Ultimately, achieving durable clinical efficacy will require biomarker-guided, spatially informed combination regimens that selectively disrupt maladaptive myeloid states while preserving physiological microglial homeostasis.

articles.titulo: Biosafety level-3 cryo-electron tomography of active severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 virions.
articles.revista: Protein science : a publication of the Protein Society
articles.autores: Fukuhara H, Dokainish HM, Kita S, Tabata K, Takasu A, Huiskonen JT, Anraku Y, Nomai T, Someya T, Senda T, Stuart DI, Sasaki M, Orba Y, Suzuki Y, Sawa H, Maenaka K
articles.resumo_original: Understanding the structural properties of pathogenic viruses in their native, infectious state is critical for rational vaccine and drug development. However, conducting cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) under biosafety level 3 (BSL-3) containment presents significant challenges. Here, we established and validated a high-end cryo-EM workflow within a BSL-3 facility, comprehensively integrating facility design, containment measures, sample handling, cryo-transfer systems, and decontamination protocols. To demonstrate the utility and reproducibility of this workflow, we applied cryo-electron tomography to investigate severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 in its native, active state. Our observations confirm that unfixed viral particles display pleomorphic features comparable to those previously reported in fixed or inactivated preparations, validating that these structural characteristics represent native features rather than artifacts of chemical fixation. Furthermore, spatial redistribution of surface spikes was observed. The establishment of this robust BSL-3 cryo-EM workflow provides a practical blueprint for the structural characterization of emerging high-consequence pathogens, supporting pandemic preparedness, vaccine development, and antiviral discovery.

articles.titulo: Structure of the Chimalliviridae bacteriophage Goslar reveals host recognition and infection machinery.
articles.autores: Basu D, Gu Y, Li YX, Forman T, Ghassemian M, Min RK, Pogliano J, Corbett KD
articles.resumo_original: Large-genome bacteriophages (phages) of the Chimalliviridae family have a distinctive life cycle, building compartments inside infected bacterial cells that broadly protect their genomes from host defenses. Here, we use cryo-electron microscopy to determine a structure of the Escherichia coli-infecting Chimalliviridae phage Goslar. We combine manual modeling of 25 structural proteins with AlphaFold structure predictions of an additional three proteins to generate a composite model with 2888 protein chains from 28 different structural proteins, totaling more than 1.4 million amino acid residues. Our structure reveals the architecture of the Goslar capsid, portal, tail, and baseplate, highlighting structural similarities and differences with other tailed phages. Combining our structural data with quantitative mass spectrometry of Goslar virions, we identify several high-copy virion-associated proteins that likely play key roles when injected into host cells upon infection. We also identify a Chimalliviridae-specific family of proteins that form long, flexible filaments anchored at the phage baseplate and which incorporate carbohydrate-binding domains, suggesting a key role in host recognition.

articles.titulo: The structural basis of IL-36R proinflammatory signaling mediated by IL-36γ and IL-37.
articles.autores: Andries J, Toul M, Thierens L, Bekaert B, Felix J, Clancy DM, Savvides SN
articles.resumo_original: The interleukin-36 receptor (IL-36R) drives proinflammatory signaling and is therapeutically targeted by spesolimab in acute skin inflammation. Beyond its three canonical agonists (IL-36α, IL-36β, and IL-36γ), IL-36R was recently proposed to be activated by IL-37. Together with antagonism by IL-36R antagonist (IL-36RA) and IL-38, this creates a complex structure-function landscape that remains poorly understood. Here, we report the cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of human IL-36γ bound to IL-36R and the shared co-receptor IL-1R accessory protein (IL-1RAcP). IL-36γ engages IL-36R with low affinity, enabling high-affinity IL-1RAcP recruitment. IL-37 exhibits the opposite binding signature, binding IL-36R with high affinity but IL-1RAcP weakly. Functional comparison of IL-36R engagement by IL-36γ and IL-37 confirmed their common proinflammatory signature, with IL-36γ exhibiting markedly higher potency, consistent with its more stable signaling complex. Structural comparison of cytokine-bound versus antibody-antagonized IL-36R revealed that spesolimab acts as an allosteric antagonist. This study therefore provides a structural and mechanistic blueprint for IL-36R activation by distinct cytokines.

articles.titulo: Structural insights into West Nile virus programmed ribosomal frameshifting reveal coordinated regulation by RNA, ribosome, and nascent peptide.
articles.autores: Wu M, Zhou H, Jin Q, Wang Y, Yuan S
articles.resumo_original: Programmed -1 ribosomal frameshifting (-1 PRF) is essential for West Nile virus (WNV) gene expression and generates NS1', a protein implicated in viral replication and pathogenesis. However, the structural pathway by which translating ribosomes traverse the WNV frameshift signal remains poorly understood. Here, we combined cryo-electron microscopy, RNA structural modeling, molecular dynamics simulations, and functional analyses to investigate the mechanism of WNV -1 PRF. We resolved a pre-frameshift ribosomal complex together with four translocation intermediates, including a previously uncharacterized semi-rotated state in which the 40S subunit undergoes partial rotation while tRNAs remain in near-canonical A/A-P/P configurations. This intermediate is accompanied by remodeling of conserved peptidyl-transferase-center nucleotides, suggesting that active-site rearrangements can precede canonical tRNA movement during translocation. Structural modeling and simulations further suggest that the WNV frameshift-stimulatory RNA exists as a compact but conformationally heterogeneous ensemble capable of adopting multiple stable or metastable pseudoknot architectures. In addition, we identified direct interactions between the nascent viral peptide and the ribosomal exit tunnel, and disruption of the tunnel-occupying peptide reduced frameshifting efficiency. Together, our findings suggest that WNV frameshifting is governed not by a single stimulatory element but by the coordinated coupling of RNA dynamics, ribosome remodeling, and nascent-chain interactions.IMPORTANCEViruses often rely on a process called programmed ribosomal frameshifting to produce proteins important for infection. West Nile virus (WNV), a mosquito-borne pathogen that can cause severe neurological disease in humans, uses this strategy to generate NS1', a protein linked to viral replication and pathogenesis. However, how ribosomes are redirected into an alternative reading frame remains incompletely understood. Here, we provide structural insights into ribosome movement during translation of the WNV frameshift signal. Our findings also suggest that the viral RNA can adopt alternative conformations and that the emerging viral peptide may influence frameshifting efficiency. Together, these observations contribute to our understanding of how RNA structure, ribosomal dynamics, and nascent peptides may influence viral protein expression.

articles.titulo: On-virion structural dynamics reveal temperature- and receptor-coordinated activation of an alphacoronavirus spike.
articles.autores: Liang J, Peng C, Tan R, Song Y, Zhang Z, Yu J, Wang X, Li S
articles.resumo_original: Human alphacoronaviruses primarily infect the human upper respiratory tract, yet how temperature and receptor-binding coordinate viral spike (S) protein activation remains unclear. Using cryo-electron tomography and subtomogram averaging, we directly visualized the structural dynamics of S on human coronavirus 229E (HCoV-229E) virions under physiologically relevant temperatures and in the presence of the host receptor human aminopeptidase N (hAPN). We identified two prefusion S2 conformations, compact and loose, that interconvert reversibly by temperature, revealing intrinsic S2 "breathing" on virions. Receptor-binding domain (RBD)-up conformations are rare on apo virions but are promoted at 33°C and stabilized upon receptor binding. hAPN can bind bivalently to neighboring S, forming Gemini S-hAPN complexes. Receptor incubation further promotes conversion from prefusion to postfusion S, an effect enhanced at 33°C. Together, our results demonstrate an optimized temperature for the HCoV-229E viral fitness, and establish temperature and receptor binding as synergistic regulators of alphacoronavirus S activation. These findings provide a structural framework for understanding alphacoronavirus infectivity.

articles.titulo: Cryo-EM Analysis of Photosynthetic Complexes: From Purification to Data Collection.
articles.autores: Amelii A, Sanità G, Donadio F, Esposito E, Bassi R, Dall'Osto L, Capaldi S
articles.resumo_original: Oxygenic photosynthesis, the process that converts solar energy into chemical energy, begins with light capture by pigment-protein complexes in thylakoid membranes. Cryo-electron microscopy (Cryo-EM) can determine the structures of these complexes at near-atomic resolution, thereby unveiling the molecular basis of light harvesting, excitation energy transfer, and dissipation, and their regulation. Here, we present a workflow for studying plant photosynthetic complexes using Cryo-EM, from isolation and purification of pigment-protein complexes to sample preparation and data acquisition. Using plant Photosystem I as a case study, the protocol provides guidance on grid preparation, vitrification, and the collection of high-quality datasets. It further underscores how purification and sample-preparation strategies can be adapted to different plant sources and photosystem populations, while preserving the stability and integrity of these labile membrane assemblies. Coupled to Cryo-EM parameters tailored to the specific biophysical properties of distinct photosynthetic complexes, this workflow provides a robust and reproducible route from leaf tissue to near-atomic-resolution structures.

articles.titulo: A step toward molecular-scale views of human synapses: Cryo-ET of human induced neurons on EM grids.
articles.autores: Tao CL
articles.resumo_original: Stem cell-derived neurons offer an accessible model for studying human synaptic biology, but resolving their native ultrastructure remains challenging. In this issue of Structure, Houcek et al.1 present a workflow for culturing human induced neurons on cryo-EM grids over mouse glia, enabling the functional validation of synaptic transmission followed by plunge-freezing and cryo-ET imaging.

articles.titulo: Ribocentre-FoldBridge: a comprehensive database bridging RNA chemical probing data and 3D structures.
articles.autores: Sun H, Hu L, Peng X, Zhang W, Lin J, Huang J, Zhang C, Huang L, Miao Z
articles.resumo_original: RNA chemical probing generates nucleotide-resolved profiles in vitro and in cells, while X-ray crystallographic or cryo-electron microscopy models provide high-resolution structural models but remain comparatively low throughput. Aligning these experiments from different modalities may provide insights into RNA structure formation and molecular functions. Here, we present Ribocentre-FoldBridge (https://foldbridge.ribocentre.org/), an AI-assisted, curator-reviewed database linking curated chemical-probing profiles with experimentally determined 3D structures. This database catalogues 12 types of RNAs, linking 256 929 probing profiles across five experimental categories to 5321 structure-linked cases. It interactively visualizes the probing profiles that align with RNA secondary and tertiary structures at nucleotide resolution. We demonstrate probe-specific reactivity patterns across paired, unpaired, and solvent-accessible structural contexts. The database aims to provide a reproducible evidence layer for examining RNA structure-function relationships across heterogeneous experiments, and thus facilitate the development of new RNA structure or function prediction programs.

articles.titulo: Polyphosphate and Disordered Hfq Regions Drive DNA Compaction through Conformation-Dependent Interactions.
articles.autores: Navon Y, Levy Y
articles.resumo_original: The RNA-binding protein Hfq and inorganic polyphosphate (polyP) were previously suggested to promote DNA compaction of AT-rich regions by forming heterochromatin-like structures, yet the underlying molecular mechanism remains unclear. Here, we combine coarse-grained and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the interplay between Hfq, polyP, and DNA. Under physiological conditions, polyP electrostatically interacts with the distal faces of multiple Hfq hexamers, clustering them near DNA and leaving the proximal faces available to interact with the DNA minor groove via the disordered N-termini, thereby promoting compaction. While this mechanism shows limited dependence on DNA sequence, it is highly sensitive to environmental conditions. Under high-salt conditions, electrostatic interactions are screened, weakening polyP-Hfq association and limiting Hfq clustering, while stabilization of non-canonical DNA conformations exposes hydrophobic surfaces. These changes shift the mode of Hfq interaction with DNA toward its distal face and disordered C-termini, favoring hydrophobic interactions and reducing compaction. Together, our findings reveal a conformation-dependent switch in Hfq-DNA interaction modes governed by cellular conditions, providing a molecular framework for environment-responsive genome organization in bacteria.

articles.titulo: Membrane Scaffold Protein Engineering for Nanodisc Technology: Design Strategies, Scaffold Variants, and Rational Selection for Membrane Protein Studies.
articles.autores: Fapohunda O, Olatunde SK, Ogbonna CE, Olawade DB
articles.resumo_original: Membrane proteins account for about a third of the human proteome and half of all drug targets, yet their hydrophobic character makes them difficult to isolate and study. Nanodiscs, discoidal lipid bilayers girdled by two copies of an apolipoprotein A-I-derived membrane scaffold protein (MSP), provide a soluble, native-like environment that keeps them folded and active. The term now covers lipid nanoparticles stabilized by various amphipathic scaffolds; this review concerns the MSP-based family. It maps the design principles, variants, and applications that two decades of MSP engineering have produced, to help readers select a scaffold rationally. PubMed, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were searched for peer-reviewed literature on MSP design, nanodisc assembly, and membrane protein characterization, and the findings were organized thematically. Strategies fall into recurring categories: sequence truncation and extension to tune diameter, surface charge redesign to raise solubility, covalent circularization to improve homogeneity and thermal stability, and functionalization with tags, fluorophores, or reactive handles. Together, these give particles of roughly eight to seventeen nanometers with linear scaffolds, and about eight and a half to fifty nanometers when circularized. These variants have enabled higher-resolution cryo-electron microscopy, cleaner nuclear magnetic resonance spectra, and more reproducible screening against G protein-coupled receptors and ion channels. Constraints remain: modest expression yields, empirical lipid matching, and limited scalability. MSP engineering has matured nanodiscs into a programmable platform for structural biology, biophysics, and biotechnology, and computational design promises a further step change. Three tables consolidate variants, applications, and open challenges. This review is narrative rather than systematic, so its coverage is selective rather than exhaustive and reflects interpretive judgement about which studies best illustrate the field. No funding was received for this work.

articles.titulo: Mass Spectrometry-Based Footprinting Strategies for GPCR Structure Analysis.
articles.revista: Journal of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry
articles.autores: Jin YT, Roberts R, Smith CG, Sun J
articles.resumo_original: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are a major class of membrane proteins that mediate diverse signaling pathways and represent the largest family of drug targets. However, their conformational flexibility and structural sensitivity to membrane environments make it difficult to characterize using conventional structural methods such as X-ray crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy, and NMR. Mass spectrometry (MS)-based footprinting has been a powerful approach for probing GPCR structure and dynamics. Well-designed footprinting strategies report on solvent accessibility changes with distinct spatial and temporal resolutions. In this review, we discuss how temporal footprinting and native-like membrane mimetics such as liposomes, nanodiscs, picodiscs, and styrene maleic acid lipid particles (SMALPs) have expanded the ability to characterize GPCR dynamics under relevant physiological conditions. We also focus on four representative footprinting techniques, including fast photochemical oxidation of proteins (FPOP), synchrotron X-ray footprinting, carbene labeling, and hydrogen-deuterium exchange (HDX), and discuss the structural information on GPCRs that each method provides. We highlight the differences of each approach when analyzing GPCRs, including labeling chemistry, time scale, residue specificity, and structural resolution. We also summarize their applications in studying GPCR/ligand interaction and conformational transitions. Finally, we discuss current challenges and future opportunities for integrating footprinting techniques to achieve a more comprehensive understanding of the GPCR structure relevant to drug discovery.

articles.titulo: Mapping AMPA and NMDA receptors at mouse brain hippocampal synapses by cryo-ET.
articles.revista: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
articles.autores: Spangler CJ, Matsui A, Kim H, Shiltseva EV, Dhandapani G, Weingarten DJ, Arnold R, Sugiyama Y, Jackman S, Elferich J, Gouaux E
articles.resumo_original: AMPA and NMDA receptors are fundamental to synaptic transmission through the detection of released neurotransmitter. These ion channels open in response to glutamate binding, resulting in depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane and influx of calcium. Receptor localization plays a key role in synaptic strength, and changes in receptor number and location underpin synaptic plasticity, learning and memory. Here we apply receptor subunit-specific antibody fragments and multiplexed gold nanoparticle conjugates, together with cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), to elucidate the in-situ molecular organization of AMPA and NMDA receptors at hippocampal synapses in adult mouse brain tissue. AMPA receptors are predominantly found in densely packed liquid-like clusters, with interspersed NMDA receptors and adjacent NMDA receptor clusters. By direct localization of individual receptors, we provide molecular-resolution insight into the distribution of AMPA and NMDA receptors across the synapse, at peri and extrasynaptic sites, and within endocytosed vesicles. Visualization of multiple presynaptic vesicle fusion events suggests that receptors are near, but not always directly adjacent to, transmitter release sites. By mapping AMPA and NMDA receptors, and glutamate release sites, we provide receptor-resolution insight into the structure and function of brain hippocampal synapses.

articles.titulo: Brain-wide activity imaging with electron microscopy reveals a distributed brain network for processing threatening somatosensory stimuli.
articles.autores: Randel N, Wang C, Clayton MS, Wang K, Pang S, Xu CS, Champion AS, Hess HF, Cardona A, Keller PJ, Zlatic M
articles.resumo_original: To understand how brains work, neural activity must be overlayed onto synaptic-resolution circuit architecture. Recent advances in light-sheet microscopy (LSM) enable whole-brain, cellular-resolution imaging of activity of all cell bodies; however, most neurons from such datasets cannot be identified. In most organisms, neurons are identifiable based on their projections (and not based on cell body position), which, when densely labeled, cannot be resolved using LSM. Here, we present a novel methodology to overcome this by combining whole-brain activity imaging with subsequent volume electron microscopy imaging of the same brain to visualize neuronal projections and identify neurons with interesting activity. We used this approach to identify brain neurons that process input from multisensory (nociceptive and mechanosensory) Basin interneurons that trigger vigorous escape in Drosophila larvae in response to threatening somatosensory stimuli. After whole-brain imaging of neuronal activity during Basin activation, we imaged the same brain with an enhanced focused ion-beam electron microscope (eFIB-SEM). We registered the functional and anatomical volumes and reconstructed (in the eFIB-SEM volume) the projections of neurons that responded to Basin activation to determine their developmental lineage and identity. This revealed a distributed network for processing threatening somatosensory stimuli that trigger vigorous escape spanning 25 distinct lineages and many distinct brain areas. Our workflow provides a powerful framework for mapping neuronal activity onto structure across an entire brain, yielding novel insights into the distributed central processing of somatosensory stimuli.

articles.titulo: Stacking Up: The Expanding Catalog of Filament-Forming Enzymes.
articles.autores: Horton NC
articles.resumo_original: Enzyme filamentation has emerged as a widespread and functionally important mode of macromolecular organization. Once viewed as an unusual property of a few metabolic enzymes, reversible filament formation is now known for more than 50 enzymes across bacteria, archaea, plants, fungi, and animals. This review summarizes recent progress in the field, expanding substantially on our 2019 analysis and incorporating more than 300 new publications. We survey the known filament-forming enzymes, their catalytic activities, biological contexts, filament architectures, and available structural information from X-ray crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy, and in cellulo imaging approaches. Filamenting enzymes span five major enzyme classes and function in metabolism, stress responses, signaling, replication, and host defense. In many cases, polymerization occurs at critical metabolic branch points and appears to regulate enzyme activity, allostery, substrate channeling, localization, or sequestration. Distinct filament geometries, including linear stacks, solenoidal coils, tubes, and rings, are associated with specific functional outcomes and cellular roles. We also highlight emerging in cellulo structural studies of enzyme filaments, summarizing the insights they provide into filament organization and cellular assembly when available. Together, these findings highlight enzyme filamentation as a common mode of macromolecular organization with consequences for structure, assembly, and function in diverse biological contexts.

articles.titulo: Cryo-EM and NMR Reveal a Membrane-Gated Doc2B-Munc13-1 Complex and a Helical Doc2B-SNARE-Binding Interface.
articles.autores: Rastegar CT, Powell J, Wosztyl A, David G, Jaczynska K, Bai XC, Han Y, Chen Z, Rizo J
articles.resumo_original: Doc2s modulate neurotransmitter release through interactions with Munc13-1, SNAREs, lipids, and Ca2+, which involve the Doc2 C2 domains and Munc13-interacting domain (MID). However, it is unclear how these interactions are coupled, how Doc2s bind to Munc13-1, and how they bind to the SNAREs. Here we determined the cryo-electron microscopy structure of a Doc2B-Munc13-1 complex aided by an AI-designed Munc13-1 binder, revealing how Doc2B MID binds to a Munc13-1 hydrophobic pocket essential for opening syntaxin-1 and explaining why Doc2B inhibits SNARE assembly. NMR and fluorescence spectroscopy show that Doc2B MID binds lipids and that MID-lipid and MID-Munc13-1 interactions are mutually exclusive, suggesting that membrane binding helps release the inhibition of Munc13-1. NMR shows that Doc2B binds to the SNARE complex via two helices of C2B. Based on these results and liposome fusion assays, we propose a working model whereby: 1. Doc2B MID-Munc13-1 interactions facilitate synergistic binding of both proteins to the plasma membrane, with the MID inhibiting Munc13-1. 2. Membrane binding facilitates MID-lipid interactions that transiently relieve the inhibition of Munc13-1, allowing SNARE complex assembly. 3. Doc2B binding to the SNARE complex inhibits neurotransmitter release but generates a primed state that mediates neurotransmitter release by an as-yet-unknown mechanism.

articles.titulo: Axon Content of the Circumpapillary Nerve Fiber Layer in Experimental Glaucoma.
articles.autores: Kharal A, Sullivan M, Patel NB
articles.resumo_original:
To determine axonal content from optical coherence tomography (OCT)-derived circumpapillary retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) measures using histologically informed models in a non-human primate experimental glaucoma model.
Unilateral experimental glaucoma was induced in 22 animals (mean age, 6.1 ± 1.9 years; 10 females) who were monitored with OCT. At varying stages of neuropathy, animals were euthanized and perfusion fixed. For RNFL histology, circumpapillary tissue (∼0.75 × 0.75 mm) from six equally spaced regions was obtained and processed for serial block face scanning electron microscopy in five animals. A single high-resolution image of the block face was used to quantify axon size (cross-sectional area) and non-axonal tissue area within the RNFL. Using the 95% limits of the histological data as a starting point, models for estimating axon count from OCT RNFL area were optimized and compared to total retrobulbar optic nerve axon counts in 22 animals.
The mean circumpapillary RNFL thickness of control eyes was 112 ± 6 µm, and it was 70 ± 24 µm in eyes with experimental glaucoma. Axon size and non-axonal area varied across the circumpapillary regions (F5, 31 = 9.06 and F5, 36 = 3.94, respectively; both P < 0.01), but did not differ between the two eyes (F1, 22 = 0.59, P = 0.45 and F1, 15 = 2.10, P = 0.17). The optimized model for estimating axon content from the circumpapillary RNFL profile had good agreement with the retrobulbar axon count (mean difference = 25; 95% limits of agreement, -334,239 to 334,289).
The axon size distribution and non-axonal area in the circumpapillary RNFL are similar between healthy and stable glaucomatous eyes. Building on this, a location-specific model is proposed that estimates axon content from the circumpapillary RNFL profile after accounting for regional variability in axonal and non-axonal components.

articles.titulo: 3D Electron Diffraction Reveals Counterion Coordination in Co-Existing Polymorphs of Ag29 Nanocluster.
articles.autores: Nagar H, Gurung K, Kučeráková M, Som A, Palatinus L, Pradeep T
articles.resumo_original: We unravel the complete structural architecture of the polymorphic Na3[Ag29(BDT)12(TPP)4] nanocluster (NC) using three-dimensional electron diffraction (3D ED) of microscopic crystals. By drop-casting nanocluster solution directly onto microscopy grids, we achieve in situ crystallization of nanometer-sized polymorphs and independently resolve co-existing cubic and trigonal phases crystal-by-crystal from a single grid square. Using difference electrostatic potential (DESP) maps derived from empirical 3D ED data, we pinpoint the specific lattice locations of the elusive Na+ counterions and observe distinct coordination environments across the two polymorphs. In the densely packed, solvent-free cubic phase, Na+ binds exclusively to thermodynamically favored pockets formed by one core-anchored and two staple sulfur atoms. Conversely, within the open, solvated trigonal lattice, Na+ occupies both these core-anchored sites and alternative positions coordinated entirely by three sulfur atoms of an outer Ag3S3 staple motif. These findings establish 3D ED as a powerful tool for resolving nanoscale polymorphic mixtures and demonstrate how macroscopic crystal packing influences local ionic interactions, providing key structural insights for the design of cluster-based assemblies.

articles.titulo: RobPicker: a meta-learning framework for robust identification of macromolecules in cryo-electron tomograms.
articles.autores: Liang Y, Hosseini R, Rahmani H, Singh D, Zhang R, Zhang L, Guo H, Choe S, Lee J, Xu M, Segal E, Zou J, Williamson J, Villa E, Grotjahn DA, Xie P
articles.resumo_original: Accurate particle picking of macromolecules of diverse types, shapes and sizes in cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) is critical for understanding the molecular architecture of biological systems in their native state. Current deep learning methods have shown potential for identifying macromolecules in tomograms; however, they are vulnerable to annotation noise in the training data and to imbalanced distributions of macromolecule species. Here, to address these limitations, we developed RobPicker, a meta-learning framework that effectively mitigates these issues by automatically learning to correct label errors and by placing greater emphasis on smaller and rarer macromolecule species. In evaluations across diverse cryo-ET datasets with noisy labels and imbalanced species distributions, RobPicker substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in identifying small and rare macromolecules. The robustness and efficiency of RobPicker led to improved resolution in 3D density maps of protein structures, enabling high-resolution cellular structural biology analysis.

articles.titulo: An evaluation framework for sparse 4D (3D + time) imaging reconstruction via bootstrapped cross-validation.
articles.autores: Zhang Y, Yao Z, Hu Z, Ritschel T, Villanueva-Perez P
articles.resumo_original: Four-dimensional (4D; 3D + time) microscopic imaging has emerged as a powerful technique for investigating dynamic phenomena in complex systems, enabling direct visualisation of structural evolution in space and time. However, when pushing the limits of spatiotemporal resolution, most time-resolved imaging techniques yield inherently sparse 4D datasets. While deep learning-based reconstruction methods have shown promise in reconstructing 4D from sparse spatiotemporal measurements, a practical approach for evaluating their performance in the absence of a 4D reference has, to the best of our knowledge, been lacking. Here, we present a bootstrapped cross-validation framework that estimates reconstruction performance by quantifying correlations between reconstructions generated from independently sampled subsets of the acquired data, as inspired by the 3D validation strategy in cryo-electron microscopy, where reconstructions from split datasets are compared to assess resolutions. This enables both qualitative and quantitative assessment in the absence of ground truth. We investigate two representative scenarios with sparse and ultra-sparse X-ray datasets and validate this approach using 4D-ONIX, a 4D deep-learning reconstruction method, on simulated water droplet collision experiments. The proposed approach provides a reference-free framework for performance estimation and support for better-informed experimental strategies across a wide range of ultrafast imaging applications.

articles.titulo: Agentic cryo-EM structure determination with CryoPilot.
articles.revista: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
articles.autores: Punuru P, Klose T, Kihara D
articles.resumo_original: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) relies on mature computational tools, but experts must still inspect intermediate results, choose among alternative processing routes, and decide when earlier choices should be revised. Here we present CryoPilot, a system of two language-model agents that carries cryo-EM data from raw micrographs through three-dimensional reconstruction to validated atomic models. Rather than executing a predefined pipeline, its reconstruction agent evaluates intermediate images and quantitative diagnostics, selects and parameterizes CryoSPARC jobs, tests alternative strategies, compares their outcomes, and retains, revises, or reverts decisions accordingly. A persistent programming environment and session database preserve the complete processing history, making each decision traceable and allowing multi-day workflows to proceed with minimal human intervention. Its modeling agent determines map handedness, builds atomic models with CryoZeta, removes regions the density does not support, and optimizes each model by testing refinement steps against map fit, geometry, and DAQ, a measure of local model-map agreement. Across nine public EMPIAR datasets, eight reconstructions reached 2.61-3.51 Å resolution, and refined models from seven maps agreed with reference structures to within 0.4-4.9 Å Cα RMSD. For a challenging α-latrocrustotoxin dataset, a single change of particle-picking strategy that we suggested enabled CryoPilot to improve the reconstruction from 5.9 to 4.15 Å. CryoPilot establishes an adaptive and auditable framework for agent-driven cryo-EM structure determination.

articles.titulo: Structural basis for repeat-associated non-AUG translation initiation on C9orf72 mRNA.
articles.revista: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
articles.autores: Kaufhold R, Dong W, Purwar I, Saladin B, Wieland CM, Krans A, Laimon E, Malik I, Leskaj S, Havilio T, Sokabe M, Fraser CS, Todd PK, Querido JB
articles.resumo_original: A GGGGCC (G 4 C 2 ) hexanucleotide repeat expansion in the first intron of C9orf72 is the most common monogenic cause of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD). This element serves as a template for repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation, which generates neurotoxic dipeptide repeat (DPR) proteins that aggregate in patient brains and contribute to neurodegeneration in model systems. To understand the mechanisms underlying RAN translation initiation, we used cryo-electron microscopy to determine the structure of an in vitro assembled human late-stage C9orf72 translation initiation complex at 3.2 Å resolution and a near-native complex purified from human cell lysate at 3.5 Å resolution. RAN translation on C9orf72 mRNA initiates predominantly at a near-cognate CUG codon that is located 24 nucleotides upstream of the G 4 C 2 repeat and is flanked by a strong endogenous Kozak sequence. The structures further reveal a direct interaction between the G 4 C 2 repeat and 18S ribosomal RNA expansion segment 9 (ES9S) on the 40S small ribosomal subunit through a kissing-loop interaction. Preventing this RNA-RNA interaction using complementary antisense oligonucleotides significantly reduces RAN translation in vitro and in patient-derived iNeurons, indicating that this structural interaction is functionally important. These findings provide mechanistic insights into RAN translation initiation and highlight a novel potential therapeutic approach to mitigate toxic DPR production in C9orf72-associated neurodegenerative disease.

articles.titulo: Distinct modes of N-terminal remodeling through a conserved inhibitor pocket in connexin-46/50.
articles.revista: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
articles.autores: Jarodsky JM, Myers JB, Reichow SL
articles.resumo_original: Selective pharmacological control of gap junction communication remains challenging because existing small-molecule connexin inhibitors act across multiple isoforms. The structural basis of this broad activity remains incompletely understood. Here, we used single-particle cryo-electron microscopy to examine native connexin-46/50 gap junction channels treated with two commonly used and chemically distinct inhibitors, 2-aminoethoxydiphenyl borate (2-APB) and carbenoxolone (CBX). Both treatments perturb the hydrophobic N-terminal (NT)-docking groove, but produce distinct conformational ensembles. 2-APB yields ordered destabilized-open and gated NT states resembling conformations observed during physiological pH- and Ca 2+ -dependent gating, with ligand- and lipid-associated densities accompanying the gated state. In contrast, CBX-compatible density occupies the same groove and is associated with loss of an ordered NT conformation, consistent with steric competition and altered physicochemical complementarity at the NT-docking site. Comparison with inhibitor-treated connexin-32 and connexin-36 structures identifies this region as a structurally conserved, pharmacologically sensitive pocket. These findings reveal how chemically diverse inhibitors perturb a conserved element of the native gating machinery while producing divergent NT-gating ensembles, providing a structural rationale for broad cross-isoform activity and identifying sequence-variable pocket margins that may support more selective modulation.

articles.titulo: Engineering conditional peptide self-assembly using AlphaFold.
articles.autores: Futty H, Chinelli S, Sonani RR, Plivelic TS, Seddon A, Egelman EH, Thomson AR, Adams DJ
articles.resumo_original: Programming self-assembly from peptide sequence remains difficult because existing design rules are only weakly predictive of emergent supramolecular behavior. Here, we show that AlphaFold Multimer can be used to engineer conditional peptide self-assembly by simultaneously selecting for co-assembly and against assembly of the individual components. Using model confidence metrics as proxies for assembly propensity, we designed peptide pairs that largely remain unstructured in isolation but form defined tape-like nanostructures upon mixing. Experimental measurements including circular dichroism, small-angle X-ray scattering, and cryo-electron microscopy validate the predicted behavior across multiple systems. These results establish artificial intelligence-guided design as a practical route to programmable supramolecular peptide materials.

articles.titulo: Immunogenicity and structure of a stabilized HIV-1 clade C Env from a pediatric elite neutralizer in complex with an autologous bnAb.
articles.autores: Singh S, Kumar S, Chatterjee A, Malhotra L, Pervez M, Rahman A, Andrabi I, Mondal B, Katpara S, Sharma S, Bhakhri H, Gaur A, Bansal T, Iyer V, Hussain AW, Ahmed S, Kumar R, Ethayathulla AS, Lodha R, Dutta S, Luthra K
articles.resumo_original:
The envelope (Env) glycoproteins derived from circulating viruses in elite-neutralizers (ENs), who naturally develop potent broadly neutralizing antibody (bnAb) responses, serve as a potential template for HIV-1 vaccine design. Here, we investigated the immunogenicity and structure of a clade C HIV-1 Env trimer (330) derived from the pediatric elite-neutralizer AIIMS_330.
The 330 Env was engineered as SOSIP.664, NFL.664, and multivalent ferritin-nanoparticle (NP) immunogens. Biophysical and antigenic properties were assessed using HIV-1 trimer-specific bnAbs and non-neutralizing antibodies. Immunogenicity was evaluated in rabbits immunized with Addavax-formulated SOSIP.664, NFL.664, or ferritin NP immunogens (n = 4), with an adjuvant only placebo group (n = 2). Structural characterization was performed by cryo-electron-microscopy (cryo-EM) using the autologous Env 330 SOSIP.664 trimer in complex with the bnAb 44m.
The 330 Env trimers exhibited native-like antigenic properties, high thermostability, strong binding to trimer-specific bnAbs, and limited reactivity with non-neutralizing antibodies. Immunization of rabbits elicited strong autologous neutralizing antibody responses together with modest heterologous Tier-1 neutralization. Autologous neutralizing responses were significantly higher for ferritin-NP (P = 0.019) and SOSIP.664 (P = 0.048) than for NFL.664, with no significant difference between ferritin-NP and SOSIP.664 (P = 0.681). A 5.1 Å cryo-EM reconstruction of the autologous Env 330 SOSIP.664-44m complex revealed native-like presentation of the N332-V3 supersite. The structural analysis further suggested the interacting Env contacts E293, R327, K337, and K446, along with glycans N332, N326, N442, and N448 with the bnAb-44m. We identified R327 of the conserved GDIR-motif and the N332 glycan, within the V3-loop, as neutralizing determinants on the 330 Env, with a fold reduction of 116, on testing the mutant 330 viruses with autologous bnAb 44m.
Pediatric elite-neutralizer AIIMS_330 derived Env trimers represent structurally and antigenically well-characterized clade C immunogens with ability to elicit strong autologous neutralizing antibodies, with modest heterologous Tier-1 neutralization. Together, these findings advance our understanding of clade C Env antigenic variability. Further, the structural and immunological insights support the potential utility of AIIMS_330 derived Env as an antigenic probe and may inform future rational design of Clade C HIV-1 vaccines and structure-guided strategies for eliciting neutralizing antibodies.

articles.titulo: Revisit of the admitted control RND efflux pumps' inhibitor PAβN: use limitations, and structural revelation in complex with MexB.
articles.autores: Wehbi H, Olivier E, Cece Q, Mégret M, Sébastien M, Aissaoui N, Llanes C, Phan G, Broutin I
articles.resumo_original:
To bypass the health problem of antibiotic resistance in Gram-negative bacteria, a tempting approach is to use efflux pump inhibitors (EPI) to block the transporters before they expel antibiotics from the cell. One well-known EPI is the phenylalanine-arginine beta-naphthylamide (PAβN). Although it is described as toxic and therefore unsuitable for clinical use, it is highly effective and is commonly used as EPI reference compound in drug development. Nevertheless, the lack of toxicity on several cellular strains in our hands required us to revisit this known RND inhibitor, to redefine its limits.
The rational design of new EPIs requires the integration of complementary information on their microbiological activity, toxicity toward eukaryotic cells, and description of molecular interaction with their target at atomic resolution. These parameters should also be considered in comparison with those of an established reference compound such as PAβN. Accordingly, the effect of PAβN on Pseudomonas aeruginosa was evaluated by determining the minimum inhibitory concentrations of three β-lactam antibiotics in the presence or absence of PAβN and by defining concentrations that do not perturb the bacterial envelope. Its toxicity was assessed using four human cell lines and multiple cellular endpoints. Finally, the interaction of PAβN with the RND transporter MexB was characterized by cryo-electron microscopy and crystallography.
Microbiological analyses defined concentration ranges in which PAβN can be used to investigate efflux inhibition without causing detectable perturbation of the bacterial envelope. Across the four human cell models, PAβN displayed limited cytotoxicity, whereas β-naphthylamine was markedly more toxic. This points to the β-naphthylamide moiety as a potential contributor to PAβN toxicity, possibly resulting from metabolic proteolysis processing. Structural analyses revealed PAβN bound to MexB in the Tight conformation in both cryo-EM and crystal structures, but at distinct positions within the binding cavity. Comparison with the previously reported structure of PAβN bound to the artificially symmetric trimer of AcrB provides new insights into PAβN recognition and handling by RND pumps. Together, these microbiological, toxicological, and structural data refine the use of PAβN as a reference EPI and provide new perspectives on substrate transport by RND efflux pumps.

articles.titulo: Chronic fructose intake disrupts extracellular ATP-pyrophosphate homeostasis and increases susceptibility to aortic calcification.
articles.autores: Flores-Roco A, Villa-Bellosta R
articles.resumo_original:
Excessive fructose consumption has become increasingly prevalent in modern diets and is strongly associated with metabolic disorders and elevated cardiovascular risk. Vascular calcification, a major contributor to arterial stiffness, is regulated by the balance between pro-calcifying factors and endogenous calcification inhibitors such as extracellular inorganic pyrophosphate. However, the effects of chronic fructose intake on pyrophosphate homeostasis, as well as their contribution to vascular calcification, remain incompletely understood.
Male Sprague-Dawley rats were exposed to a 10% fructose-enriched drinking solution for three months. Metabolic, biochemical, and vascular parameters were assessed, including plasma glucose, insulin, inflammatory cytokines, uric acid, mineral metabolism markers, ATP and pyrophosphate levels, hepatic mitochondrial function, and aortic calcification. Extracellular pyrophosphate metabolism in the aortic wall was evaluated, and the effects of genetic or pharmacological dual inhibition of TNAP and eNTPD1 on vascular calcification were examined ex vivo.
Fructose-fed rats developed hyperglycemia, hyperinsulinemia, elevated inflammatory cytokines, and increased uric acid levels despite unchanged body weight. They also exhibited increased plasma calcium and reduced 25-OH vitamin D levels without changes in phosphate or magnesium concentrations. Plasma ATP and pyrophosphate levels were significantly reduced, indicating impaired systemic anti-calcifying capacity. High fructose intake induced marked hepatic mitochondrial dysfunction, characterized by reduced ATP synthesis, increased H₂O₂ production, decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, impaired respiratory chain activity, and reduced oxygen consumption. In the aorta, fructose feeding increased calcification, decreased extracellular pyrophosphate synthesis, and enhanced pyrophosphate degradation. Dual inhibition of TNAP and eNTPD1 significantly reduced aortic calcification ex vivo, supporting the role of pyrophosphate-regulating enzymes in fructose-induced vascular mineralization.
These findings show that chronic fructose intake disrupts both systemic and local pyrophosphate homeostasis promoting a pro-calcifying environment. Targeting pyrophosphate-regulating pathways may represent a therapeutic strategy to prevent fructose-associated aortic calcification.

articles.titulo: Key factors for growth and phosphate uptake by Acinetobacter tjernbergiae.
articles.autores: Brück J, Täuber S, Ackermann L, Schittkowski H, Neubauer P, Junne S
articles.resumo_original: Phosphorus-containing fertilisers are essential for global food production but depend on finite phosphate rock reserves. Recovery of phosphorus from waste streams, such as those in wastewater treatment plants, will be required to follow future regulations. Certain Acinetobacter spp. can accumulate 24-30% (w w-1) of phosphate intracellularly, making them promising candidates for microbial phosphorus recovery. However, previous studies have reported insufficient biomass formation to enable rapid phosphate uptake. Therefore, this work investigated key factors of biomass generation and phosphate uptake of Acinetobacter tjernbergiae in an empirical study. Increasing iron concentration by 1 mg L-1 enhanced growth six-fold in shake flask cultivations. A maximum biomass concentration of 12 ± 0.7 g L-1 was achievable during 14 h of bioreactor cultivation. The maximum volumetric phosphate uptake rate (rS,P) reached 280.2 ± 40.8 mg (L h)-1, the highest value reported so far for Acinetobacter spp., while specific rates of up to 41.0 ± 1.1 mg (g h)-1 were achieved. It was further shown that A. tjernbergiae exhibits both polyphosphate accumulation and the overplus phenomenon. Moreover, phosphate uptake was strongly correlated with carbon uptake, while carbon absence resulted in phosphate release.

articles.titulo: Role of phoU in P. aeruginosa virulence and the emergence of compensatory mutations in the ΔphoU mutant.
articles.autores: Machado GT, Picinin NG, Ferraz D, de Almeida LG, Thomaz L, Wolf SG, Elbaum M, Spira B
articles.resumo_original: Bacteria respond to phosphate (Pi) availability by modulating the PHO regulon, which encodes proteins for Pi scavenging. The phoU gene is part of the pst operon, a high-affinity phosphate transport system that also represses PHO regulon expression under Pi excess. In the absence of phoU, Pi transport continues but repression fails, resulting in constitutive PHO gene transcription. In Pseudomonas aeruginosa and other Proteobacteria, phoU knockouts display pleiotropic effects, including stress and antibiotic sensitivity and polyphosphate (polyP) accumulation. Here, using cryo-STEM imaging and EDX analysis, we show that the ΔphoU mutant of P. aeruginosa accumulates large polyP granules containing over seven-fold more phosphorus than the wild type. Moreover, ΔphoU was markedly less virulent in vivo in the Galleria mellonella model. We further isolated two suppressor classes from ΔphoU: low-constitutive alkaline phosphatase (LCAP) and not-constitutive alkaline phosphatase (NCAP). LCAP mutants remain PHO-constitutive, less virulent than wild type, and accumulate polyP similarly to ΔphoU. In contrast, NCAP mutants are not PHO-constitutive, do not accumulate polyP, and retain wild-type virulence. We also tested swarming motility, pyocyanin, and pyoverdine production. Significant differences were limited to swarming, where ΔphoU was substantially less motile than the wild type, with LCAP showing partial recovery and NCAP full restoration.

articles.titulo: A Glial Interplay Regulates Junctional Architecture at the Blood-Brain Barrier of Drosophila.
articles.autores: Contreras EG, Naffin E, Collins-Ramírez M, Surina NV, Rothermel M, Salazar-Tirado J, Schirmeier S, Klämbt C
articles.resumo_original: Neurons require a tightly controlled ion and metabolite homeostasis, which is maintained by an effective blood-brain barrier (BBB). Since the integrity of the BBB is essential for brain function, its maintenance during development represents a significant challenge. The Drosophila BBB is formed by two glial layers. Subperineurial glia (SPG) establish pleated septate junctions (pSJs) to generate the primary diffusion barrier. Abutting the SPG lies the mitotically active perineurial glia (PG). Only a small number of PG cells are specified during embryogenesis. The FGF8-like signal Pyramus presented by the SPG subsequently triggers proliferation of the PG, which ultimately covers the entire nervous system. To investigate the role of PG in the development and physiology of the BBB, we genetically ablated them. In these animals, glucose influx into SPG is unchanged following acute glucose perfusion. However, adult PG-ablated flies show increased sensitivity to glucose-only diet, indicating that while baseline carbohydrate transport can be maintained in the absence of most PG, the system fails under metabolic stress. SPG morphology and pSJ organization are largely preserved during larval stages upon PG ablation. In contrast, in PG-ablated pupae, moody expression is impaired in SPG and pSJs progressively split, producing ectopic junctional strands. Together, these results reveal the necessity of PG for the maturation and function of SPG, as well as the mutual interdependence between the two BBB glial layers.

articles.titulo: The Fat-Body Secreted Neuropeptide CCHa2 Signals Insulin-Producing Cells in the Brain to Promote Sleep.
articles.autores: Biglari S, Gong S, Wang MC, Payne CA, Kauffman MR, DiAngelo JR, Keene A
articles.resumo_original: Sleep is a fundamental behavior regulated by diverse environmental and physiological cues. While the central mechanisms underlying sleep regulation have been investigated in detail, far less is known about how nutrient signals from the periphery are communicated to the brain to modulate sleep. Here, we perform a targeted RNAi screen of genes enriched in the fat body and regulated by feeding state to identify genes that function in the fat body to regulate sleep in Drosophila. This analysis found that fat body-specific knockdown of CCHa2 significantly reduced sleep duration and sleep depth in fed flies, phenocopying sleep in starved flies. CCHa2-deficient flies exhibited reduced glycogen stores and diminished feeding drive. Analysis of single-cell transcriptomic atlases confirms that the CCHa2 receptor (CCHa2-R) is selectively expressed in insulin-producing cells (IPCs) of the fly brain. We find that knockdown of CCHa2-R in IPCs recapitulates the sleep loss phenotype of CCHa2 mutants, supporting a role in adipose-brain signaling. Further screening of genes identified in single cell atlases as being enriched in IPCs led to the identification of numerous genes that function in IPCs to regulate sleep, including modulators of wnt and insulin signaling. Together, these findings identify a fat body-IPC axis that is a critical modulator of sleep duration and intensity.

articles.titulo: Current advances in chemical ecology-based management tactics for the spotted lanternfly, Lycorma delicatula (Hemiptera: Fulgoridae).
articles.autores: Ruether BF, Tholl D, Leskey TC
articles.resumo_original: The spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula [White]), an invasive fulgorid planthopper of significant economic concern, relies on a complex suite of chemical signals to navigate host selection, aggregation, and reproductive success in its US invaded range. While initial research focused primarily on volatile attraction, recent advances have broadened to include a multitrophic understanding of the insect's chemical ecology. This review synthesizes the rapidly expanding body of literature on L. delicatula chemical ecology, with a focus on findings published since 2023, to delineate the mechanisms governing host selection, conspecific recruitment, and complex tritrophic interactions. Current management relies heavily on broad-spectrum insecticides, but studies are constantly attempting to shift the field toward more selective strategies as understanding grows regarding L. delicatula sensory biology, conspecific signaling, and host-mediated interactions. We propose that the next phase of management should move beyond viewing chemical ecology as a supplement to insecticides and instead treat semiochemical-based tactics as the foundation for integrated pest management (IPM). Specifically, we suggest the development of multimodal devices that combine host and conspecific volatiles with vibrational and visual cues tailored to specific life stages and seasonal behaviors. Future efforts should prioritize translating these ecological findings into spatially precise management tools, such as push-pull systems and attract-and-kill stations, while leveraging new genomic resources to improve semiochemical lure selectivity and efficacy. Ultimately, integrating chemical ecology into management programs should improve early detection and provide sustainable population suppression while minimizing non-target impacts.

articles.titulo: Ecological and social cues orchestrate concerted courtship in Drosophila.
articles.autores: Brand P, Keller K, Coleman RT, Eghbali NB, Zylka S, Prieto-Godino LL, Ruta V
articles.resumo_original: Mating decisions are often attributed to the sensory signalling between prospective sexual partners. Yet these interactions are also shaped by the broader environmental context in which they unfold, to appropriately align sexual arousal with reproductive opportunities1-6. Here we show that in Drosophila erecta mating is strictly contingent on the ecological and social environment generated as flies densely aggregate in groups on a food patch. We find that food volatiles directly promote male sexual arousal, triggering individuals to sample and pursue potential mates, giving rise to dynamic interactions across the group. The ensuing visual motion transforms each male's visual field, which in turn further amplifies his arousal, generating a multisensory feedback loop that coordinately promotes courtship across individuals. D. erecta's strict dependence on environmental cues appears latent in related species, such as Drosophila melanogaster, where food odour can promote arousal7 but is dispensable for vigorous courtship. Comparative circuit analyses show that species-specific thresholds for sexual arousal reflect variation in how olfactory input modulates conserved nodes controlling courtship drive, rendering food volatiles a strict sensory gate only in D. erecta. Together, our findings highlight how environmental cues not directly tied to sexual signalling can profoundly influence reproductive behaviour and reorganize the social landscape to ensure mating occurs in contexts where reproductive opportunities are abundant.

articles.titulo: Light pollution causes death, sleep loss, and cognitive impairments through systemic reactive oxygen species accumulation in bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) gynes.
articles.autores: Shi M, Guo Y, Wang Y, Wang S, Li J, Li Z
articles.resumo_original: Light pollution affects about one quarter of the Earth's land surface and is rapidly growing in both extent and intensity with accelerated global urbanization. Artificial light at night (ALAN) constitutes the major source of light pollution and poses significant challenges to the health of many organisms, including pollinators. However, whether and how ALAN exposure affects bumblebees' physiology remain unexplored. Our study aims to preliminarily investigate the effects of ALAN exposure on bumblebees and hypothesizes that it may cause physiological damage to gynes. As we expected, ALAN exposure causes precocious death in gynes. Extended light exposure leads to sleep loss and dysfunctional cognitive performance in gynes. In addition, light pollution also disrupts the nutritional homeostasis in gynes. Transcriptomic analysis revealed altered expression of genes associated with sleep, cognition, and nutrient metabolism, suggesting that ALAN exposure may disrupt gut-brain communication in gynes. Furthermore, systemic accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) is detected in ALAN-exposed gynes due to down-regulation of genes in the glutathione metabolic pathway. Importantly, both oral supplementation with antioxidants and dark recovery effectively suppress excessive ROS production and reverse the detrimental effects after ALAN exposure to gynes. Our study provides evidence of the detrimental effects of light pollution on gynes for the first time and reveals the pivotal role of oxidative stress in mediating light-induced sleep loss, cognitive impairment, and nutrient homeostasis disruption of bumblebees. This further implicates light pollution as a potential contributor to bumblebees' decline.

articles.titulo: Class-wide sequence, structural, and docking-profile diversity of insect odorant receptors and structural specialization of Orco.
articles.autores: Zhang T, Yang X, Fu Y, Xue W, Zhang Y, Duan S, Yin Y, Guo Y, Gao C, Liu Y, Li G, Xu C, Lu H
articles.resumo_original: Insect olfaction is facilitated by a heterotetrameric odorant receptor-odorant receptor co-receptor (OR-Orco) complex. However, extensive sequence divergence and lineage-specific expansion have complicated large-scale comparisons of OR repertoires across insects. Here, we integrated sequence similarity, structural similarity, and molecular docking to analyze ORs from 115 insect species. OR repertoire size was associated with adult diet, larval diet, and habitat, but not with circadian rhythm. We developed a 'trunk-branch' network framework to classify ORs according to sequence and structural similarity and used large-scale molecular docking to derive comparative docking profiles. Despite marked differences in sequence- and structural-community composition, almost all sampled orders contained ORs assigned to all six docking-profile communities. Holometabolous insects showed higher OR sequence-community diversity than non-holometabolous insects, and docking-profile composition differed between extant lineages whose order-level origins predate or postdate the end-Permian mass extinction. Most notably, we identified a highly conserved extracellular β-sheet in Orco that restricts ligand access to the binding pocket and may contribute to its reduced capacity to bind natural odorants. The emergence of Orco represents a key evolutionary transition from homomeric receptors to heteromeric OR-Orco complexes, and our results suggest that this transition may have been accompanied by pronounced specialization of the extracellular domain and binding pocket. Together, these analyses provide a class-wide framework for comparing insect OR diversity and generate testable hypotheses for future experimental and evolutionary studies.

articles.titulo: Motor Neurons in the Prothoracic Ganglion of the Praying Mantis, Tenodera sinensis.
articles.autores: Takaki K, Ikemoto H, Yamawaki Y
articles.resumo_original: To understand the neural mechanisms underlying a behavior, it is important to identify the motor neurons innervating the muscles involved in the target behavior. In this study, we comprehensively stained potential motor neurons in the prothoracic ganglion of the praying mantis (Tenodera sinensis Saussure) by dye filling from each lateral nerve. We registered potential motor neurons into the standard atlas of the prothoracic ganglion and classified them into 13 clusters on the basis of the position of primary neurites relative to neuropils. Cell bodies of most motor neurons clustered in the anterior region of the hemiganglion ipsilateral to the filled nerve. Two clusters were located in the posteroventral region and the dorsocentral region. The latter cluster is likely to be a group of dorsal unpaired median neurons. Other neurons showed morphological features specific to common inhibitor neurons and sensory neurons. Most sensory afferents terminated in the anterior, ventralmost, and lateral ventral association center. These results provide fundamental knowledge that is helpful for understanding the neural mechanisms underlying the motor control of foreleg movements in the mantis.

articles.titulo: Somatotopic Organization of Sensory Inputs From Taste Appendages in the Subesophageal Zone and Brain of the Honey Bee Apis mellifera.
articles.autores: Pitzalis M, Larcher V, Sanchez MGB, Giurfa M, Carcaud J, Sandoz JC
articles.resumo_original: The study of gustatory pathways from the periphery to the brain offers valuable insights into the neural mechanisms underlying taste processing and foraging choices, particularly in ecologically and economically relevant species such as the honey bee, Apis mellifera. While the neural substrates of other sensory modalities in bees, notably olfaction and vision, have been thoroughly characterized, the organization principles of gustatory pathways in the primary gustatory center (the subesophageal zone, SEZ) and brain of this species remain largely unexplored. Using anterograde mass staining with dextran-coupled fluorescent tracers applied into the main gustatory appendages (antennae, mouthparts, and foreleg tarsi), we identified the projection areas of their sensory afferents within the SEZ. Our results show that sensory circuits are confined to specific, distinct regions of the SEZ, suggesting the presence of somatotopic "maps" corresponding to the different appendages. Overlaps between projections, reflecting potential information exchange between appendicular domains in the SEZ, were most evident among inputs originating from similar appendages (e.g., between mouthparts-proboscis and mandibles) and were limited between domains of different appendages (e.g., antennae and mouthparts). We also confirm the subesophageal-calycal tract (SCT) as the main output of the SEZ. Combined retrograde staining of the SCT and anterograde staining of taste appendages revealed that SCT dendrites overlap specifically with sensory input from the maxillae in the SEZ. The functional significance of these findings is discussed in the context of gustatory information processing during bee feeding behavior, and the results are considered within a comparative framework across insect taxa.

articles.titulo: Spontaneous neural activity in the developing ant olfactory system.
articles.revista: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
articles.autores: Frank DD, Kronauer DJC
articles.resumo_original: Spontaneous neural activity is a pillar of mammalian neurodevelopment. In mammals, developing olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) show spontaneous activity patterns that depend on the olfactory receptor (OR) they express. This activity is necessary for proper sorting of OSN axons into olfactory bulb glomeruli. This contrasts with the simpler olfactory system of the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, where antennal lobe glomeruli form without functional ORs. Compared to Drosophila, ants have a vastly expanded olfactory system and, unlike Drosophila, require functional ORs for proper development. This raises the possibility that ants, like mammals, rely on spontaneous neural activity. To test whether developing ant OSNs are spontaneously active, we performed live calcium imaging in translucent pupae of the clonal raider ant Ooceraea biroi, using a transgenic line expressing the genetically encoded calcium indicator GCaMP6s in OSNs. Developing O. biroi OSNs exhibit spontaneous calcium transients from the earliest stages of glomerulus formation, and features of this activity change over the course of metamorphosis. During early stages, activity is faster, varies widely between cells, and is uncorrelated across the OSN population. By mid-metamorphosis, activity has slowed, with longer calcium events and fewer peaks per cell. As pupae approach eclosion, a new mode appears, with rhythmic, sawtooth-shaped calcium events that synchronously engage OSNs in both antennae. This stage-dependent spontaneous activity suggests that the expanded ant olfactory system may use a developmental logic more akin to mammals than to Drosophila.

articles.titulo: Heavy-tailed connections support robust neural communication.
articles.revista: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
articles.autores: Betancourt JM, Varanasi V, Clark DA, Lynn CW
articles.resumo_original: In the synaptic wiring between neurons, some rare connections are orders of magnitude stronger than most. This heavy-tailed connectivity is ubiquitous across different species, brain regions, and cell types, suggesting that it serves a general purpose for neural function. Here, we show, both analytically and in simulations, that heavy-tailed connections reduce communication errors in the presence of synaptic noise. In minimal models of individual neurons, noisy connections induce errors at a rate that depends only on a simple network statistic, which we refer to as robustness. For a fixed number of incoming synapses, neurons with broader distributions of connection strength are more robust and, therefore, admit fewer errors. Across several connectomes, we find that real neurons are consistently more robust than comparable null networks. In the whole brain of the fruit fly Drosophila, robustness increases with distance from the sensory periphery, such that central neurons are more robust than those involved in sensory processing. Together, these results indicate that heavy-tailed connections may arise universally to fortify the brain against noise in communication.

articles.titulo: The Role of Drosophila Toll Receptors in the Central Nervous System.
articles.autores: Ma Z, Xu J, Yu XL, Wang X, Gu Q, Meng H
articles.resumo_original: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are evolutionarily conserved pattern recognition receptors that play pivotal roles in innate immunity by detecting pathogen-associated molecular patterns. While initially characterized for their function in dorsoventral patterning and antifungal defense in Drosophila, the Toll family is now understood to have undergone a functional expansion in the nervous system. This review synthesizes the current understanding of the nine Drosophila Toll receptors (Toll-1 to Toll-9) and their roles in the central nervous system (CNS). We discuss how these receptors, particularly through non-canonical signaling pathways, function as neurotrophin receptors and cell surface recognition molecules. They mediate a wide range of cellular processes, from axon guidance to synaptic partner matching and the regulation of neuronal survival versus apoptosis through the competitive recruitment of adaptor proteins such as dMyD88 and Sarm. We further explore the involvement of Toll signaling in adult brain structural plasticity, sleep homeostasis, and behavioral responses to environmental stressors such as ethanol. Importantly, this article addresses the context-dependent duality of Toll signaling in neuropathology, dysregulation, and aberrant activation, which are closely related to neurodegeneration, lifespan determination, and infection responses.
